it wins more individual probes and gives the best sufficiency per token. The
slice-level caveat is important. Compact STM alone is strongest on early
high-continuity slices (`skip=180` and `skip=360`), normal RAG is narrowly best
only on `skip=1260`, and STM+LTM wins or ties most of the later slices. The
current policy implication is not "always add more context"; it is to make
compact STM+LTM the next live chat-demo prompt-policy candidate, expose compact
STM as a lower-token mode, and keep expanded history behind an explicit manual
or learned gate.

To test the actual STM-graph-to-LTM mechanism rather than treating LTM as
summary retrieval, we added an opt-in consolidation audit
(`CORTEXT_STM_LTM_AUDIT=1`) and reran the `skip=1980` corpus slice through the
live Cortext path with STM graph formation, deep consolidation, relabeling,
pruning, LTM retrieval, and OpenAI `gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17` judging enabled.
The audit is per consolidation cue and records the STM graph state entering the
relabeler, current labels, refined labels, labels kept/added/removed, durable
`derived_from` and `has_label` edges, relation/fact products, and whether each
durable cue still maps back to source memories with content. The run processed
180 messages, produced 16 judged probes, and wrote:

* `build/stm_ltm_audit_skip1980_180_openai.json`
* `build/stm_ltm_audit_skip1980_180_openai.sqlite`

The mechanism did create source-grounded LTM graph structure. Across 10
consolidation cycles, **160** STM label edges entered the relabeler, **31**
current cue labels were presented, **17** refined durable labels were accepted,
**17** labels were added, **0** labels were kept, and **0** labels were removed.
The run created **99** `derived_from` links, **17** `has_label` links, touched
**6** fact assertions, and all **99 / 99** source memories behind the durable
cues still had hydratable content. This confirms that the current LTM path is
not merely pruning or summarizing: STM graph evidence is being converted into
durable cue-label-source graph structure.

The original "removed" counter in that judged run counted only durable
`has_label` edges physically deleted from an existing cue. We tightened the
audit afterward so provisional STM labels that enter `current_labels` and are
not returned by the relabeler are counted as pruned even when they were never
promoted to durable edges. A current 80-message smoke rerun of the same slice
(`build/stm_ltm_audit_current_smoke_prune.json`) produced **52** STM label
edges entering the relabeler, **8** current labels, **6** refined durable
labels, **6** added labels, and **8** provisional labels pruned-by-omission
across **5** consolidation cycles while preserving **59 / 59** hydratable
source memories. This makes the audit align with the intended mechanism:
consolidation may keep, add, or decline to promote STM labels, not only delete
already-durable edges.

The same audit also explains why the current Cortext LTM-only retrieval remains
weak. OpenAI judged compact Cortext LTM at **0.625** sufficiency and **1.5625**
relevance using **81.8** tokens, while compact STM-only scored **2.1875**,
STM+LTM scored **2.25**, and normal RAG scored **4.0** at **196.8** tokens.
Counter diagnostics showed **15 / 16** probes with zero Cortext-LTM query
overlap, **16 / 16** probes where many memories were ranked but only four were
injected, and **15 / 16** probes where label-graph boosts were present but did
not recover query-overlapping evidence. The failure taxonomy for this slice is
therefore: missed identity/topic evidence during ranking, generic or weak label
boosts, under-admission of ranked evidence into the prompt packet, and no
observed source-mapping loss. The next hardening target is retrieval/ranking and
admission over the durable STM-derived graph, not summary generation.

The benchmark now emits this taxonomy directly as privacy-safe aggregate JSON.
A current judged short rerun of the same corpus slice wrote
`build/stm_ltm_taxonomy_judged.json` with 80 processed messages, 7 judged
compact-policy probes, 5 consolidation cycles, **52** STM label edges entering
the relabeler, **6** refined durable labels, **8** provisional STM labels
pruned-by-omission, **59 / 59** hydratable source memories, and **0** lost
source mappings. One consolidation cycle pruned all current labels to zero and
one ended with no durable `has_label` edge, while no cycle lost its
`derived_from` source links. Its failure counters were: **6 / 7** probes with
zero Cortext-LTM query overlap, **5 / 7** probes where label-graph boost existed
but did not recover LTM query overlap, **7 / 7** probes with many ranked
memories but only the admission-cap subset injected, **7 / 7** judged probes
where Cortext LTM scored below normal RAG, **6 / 7** where it scored below
STM-only, and **0** LTM wins. This makes the failure claim reproducible from
the benchmark artifact rather than only from prose inspection.

Manual inspection of that failure mode found one production-path source-routing
gap: retrieved durable `LABEL` nodes could be ranked by the graph, but hydration
did not follow `has_label -> ASSOCIATION -> derived_from` to display the
original source memories. We added that expansion path and a regression test
(`Cortext expands durable label retrieval nodes through association sources`) so
a label hit now remains a routing node while the prompt receives source content.
The follow-up judged artifact,
`build/stm_ltm_label_expansion_judged.json`, reran the same 80-message
`skip=1980` slice with OpenAI `gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17`. The audit was
unchanged in structure: **52** STM label edges entered the relabeler, **8**
current labels were considered, **6** refined labels were accepted, **8**
provisional labels were pruned, **59** `derived_from` links were created, **6**
durable `has_label` edges remained, and **59 / 59** source memories were
hydratable.

The routing fix improved but did not solve LTM retrieval. Non-compact
Cortext-LTM-only relevance moved from **2.43** to **2.71** and sufficiency from
**1.14** to **1.57** on the seven judged probes. Compact Cortext LTM sufficiency
rose from **0.57** to **0.71**, and low-LTM-relevance failures dropped from
**7 / 7** to **6 / 7**. However, compact Cortext LTM still had **0** wins,
**6 / 7** zero query-overlap probes, and stayed well below lexical LTM
(**3.14** sufficiency) and normal RAG with history (**3.57** sufficiency). The
current conclusion is therefore sharper: source grounding and label-to-source
hydration are now present, but durable graph ranking/admission still fails to
select enough query-relevant source memories. The next hardening target is
ranking over STM-derived durable cues and their source sets, not additional
summary text.

We then tested the most direct version of that next target: an opt-in
durable-source-set score that lets a retrieved `ASSOCIATION` or `LABEL` candidate
receive ranking credit from the best matching source memory reachable through
`derived_from` (or `has_label -> ASSOCIATION -> derived_from`). A deterministic
unit test verifies that this path can assign a nonzero source-set boost to a
durable label. The judged chat-replay ablation
(`build/stm_ltm_source_set_rank_judged.json`) showed that the naive source-set
boost was not a production default in that initial form. It activated on broad durable cues, but
non-compact Cortext-LTM-only relevance fell from **2.71** to **2.00** and
sufficiency from **1.57** to **0.86**; compact Cortext LTM fell from **0.71** to
**0.57** sufficiency. The scorer was therefore first left disabled as a
diagnostic, then reintroduced only with a Focus/Sensitivity/Stability-derived
weight and floor. This negative result
narrows the ranking problem: Cortext needs selective source admission within a
durable cue, not a coarse boost for any cue whose source set contains a
semantically nearby item.

We also separated two hydration/admission concerns that had been entangled in
the chat prompt path. First, hydration now preserves the ranked retrieval order
emitted by the graph retriever instead of relying on the iteration order of the
retrieved-embedding map. Second, query-aware ordering of sources inside a
durable cue was first tested as an isolated source-ordering variant. On the same
`skip=1980` seven-probe slice, rank-preserving hydration with query-aware source ordering
(`build/stm_ltm_query_source_admission_judged.json`) raised compact Cortext LTM
sufficiency to **1.00**, but non-compact Cortext-LTM-only sufficiency was only
**1.00**. Rank preservation without query-aware source ordering
(`build/stm_ltm_rank_preserve_judged.json`) also produced compact Cortext LTM
sufficiency **1.00**, but non-compact Cortext-LTM-only sufficiency dropped to
**0.43**. Because both variants still had **6 / 7** zero-overlap probes and **0**
LTM wins, the result is treated as negative evidence for source ordering as a
standalone quality fix, not as evidence against query similarity inside
production hydration. Production now preserves retrieval rank and uses
query-aware linked-source ordering by default, with
`CORTEXT_DISABLE_QUERY_AWARE_LINKED_SOURCE_HYDRATION=1` retained only as an
ablation/regression switch. The
best short-slice LTM-only result remains the label-to-source hydration run
(`build/stm_ltm_label_expansion_judged.json`), not either source-admission
variant.

Finally, we hardened and reran the relation side of the same STM-graph-to-LTM
path. The earlier audit showed **0** relation edges despite relation extraction
being enabled, so the persistence path was instrumented with relation-count,
missing-endpoint, and unsupported-predicate counters. Two implementation gaps
were then fixed in the production consolidation path: relation endpoints emitted
by the relabeler can now materialize as durable, evidence-gated `LABEL` nodes
even when the endpoint was omitted from the replacement label array, and
non-empty relation predicates outside Cortext's current edge ontology are
conservatively persisted as `co_occurs` rather than dropped. For multimodal
blob-backed relabeling, endpoint admission is allowed from the blob extraction
result rather than requiring exact appearance in the text-only evidence string.
Focused tests cover endpoint materialization, audit skip counters, and
blob-backed endpoint admission.

The judged replay artifact
`build/stm_ltm_relation_blob_endpoint.json` reran the same 80-message
`skip=1980` slice through Cortext only, with STM graph creation, deep
consolidation, relabel/prune, LTM retrieval, and OpenAI
`gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17` judging enabled. The audit now shows **64** STM label
edges entering the relabeler, **12** current labels, **11** refined durable
labels, **12** pruned labels, **59** `derived_from` edges, **11** durable
`has_label` edges, **3 / 3** extracted relations persisted as relation edges,
and **59 / 59** source memories hydratable. This closes the specific
under-linking defect in LTM construction on this slice: the relabeler/pruner is
now creating durable label, source, fact, and relation structure rather than
only deleting noisy labels. It does **not** close the retrieval-quality gap.
Compact Cortext LTM scored **0.857** mean sufficiency with **0** wins, while
normal RAG scored **4.000** and full history scored **4.857** in the compact
policy judge. Non-compact Cortext-LTM-only scored **0.714** sufficiency with
**0** wins. The failure has therefore moved downstream: durable graph
construction is source-grounded and connected, but ranking/admission still does
not reliably select the right original experiences for the prompt.

We then made the durable relation graph active during retrieval by allowing a
candidate's durable labels to contribute through one-hop label-to-label
relations with a Focus/Sensitivity/Stability-derived relation weight. The follow-up judged artifact
`build/stm_ltm_relation_label_propagation.json` kept the same construction
audit (**59 / 59** sources hydratable, **11** durable labels, and **3 / 3**
relations created) but raised compact Cortext LTM from **0.857** to **1.143**
mean sufficiency and from **1.857** to **2.143** mean relevance. The compact
STM+LTM union also improved to **2.286** sufficiency. This shows that the
relation graph is now participating in ranking, not merely being persisted.
However, normal RAG still scored **3.857** sufficiency and **2** wins, while
Cortext LTM had **0** wins and **6 / 7** zero-overlap probes. A query-aware
linked-source ordering repeat
(`build/stm_ltm_relation_label_propagation_query_sources.json`) did not improve
compact LTM as a standalone change, so the later production default treats it as
bounded source ordering rather than a retrieval-quality claim. The next
bottleneck is therefore not lost source grounding or missing relation persistence,
but overly broad or
weak label admission/ranking: relation propagation helps, yet it can still boost
generic labels that do not select the right underlying experiences. A direct
aggregate SQLite audit of the same artifact supports this diagnosis: the durable
graph contained **10** `LABEL` nodes, **9** single-token labels, **6.4** mean
label characters, and **23.1** mean label-relation degree. All labels had at
least one source `has_label` edge, so the problem is not unattached labels; it is
that many attached labels are too short and high-degree to be discriminative
retrieval anchors.

We tested a narrow degree-damping guard for this diagnosis without changing
consolidation: `1 / (1 + damping * degree)` is applied to label-graph retrieval
boosts, where degree counts durable `has_label` and label-relation edges. The
damping coefficient is now derived from Focus/Sensitivity/Stability. A focused
unit test verifies that equally similar high-degree labels receive lower
retrieval boost than low-degree labels. The original fixed-value replay did not
show that damping alone was sufficient. With damping **0.05**
(`build/stm_ltm_label_degree_damped.json`), compact Cortext LTM sufficiency was
**0.857** with **0** wins; with damping **0.01**
(`build/stm_ltm_label_degree_damped_001.json`), compact Cortext LTM again scored
**0.857** with **0** wins and retained **6 / 7** zero-overlap probes. The
non-compact LTM-only arm improved in the **0.01** run (**1.429** sufficiency),
but the compact chat-demo policy did not. Degree damping is therefore useful
generic-hub suppression, not the whole answer. The remaining fix likely has to
happen before or during label admission: the relabeler must produce more
discriminative durable labels, not merely downweight generic ones after they
already dominate the graph.

We then moved the hardening point upstream into the relabel/prune admission
path. The durable-label guard now rejects obvious function labels, chat roles,
pronouns, helper verbs, and transcript filler before they can become `LABEL`
nodes, while the Gemma relabel prompts now ask for durable anchors: named people,
places, organizations, pets, specific objects, and short event phrases. A
relation-predicate fallback was also added for blank predicates with valid
endpoints, mapping them to `co_occurs`; malformed non-alphanumeric predicates
are still rejected. Focused tests cover both the expanded filler rejection and
the blank-predicate fallback.

The live replay artifact
`build/stm_ltm_generic_label_guard_relation_fallback.json` shows this is a
partial construction hardening, not a retrieval-quality fix. The same
`skip=1980` Cortext-only replay still preserved **59 / 59** source memories, but
the final durable label surface tightened from **11** `has_label` edges to
**9**, with **13** labels pruned and **9** refined labels admitted. Compact
Cortext LTM noise dropped to **0.286**, and compact LTM relevance rose to
**2.429**, but compact LTM sufficiency remained **1.143** with **0** wins and
**6 / 7** zero-overlap probes; normal RAG still scored **4.286** sufficiency.
The stricter admission also exposed relation fragility: **4** relations were
emitted, but **0** relation edges were created because **2** lacked admissible
endpoints and **2** had unsupported malformed predicates. Thus, generic-label
filtering reduces some durable noise, but it does not solve the main problem.
The relabeler still needs to emit more discriminative endpoint labels and valid
relations, and retrieval still needs stronger query-specific admission before
compact Cortext LTM can replace normal RAG.

A second-pass stoplist tightened this further by rejecting modal/status labels
and generic abstract labels observed in the prior replay. The artifact
`build/stm_ltm_generic_label_guard_v2.json` improved the specific generic-label
failure counter (**3** label-boost-without-overlap probes, down from **5**) and
raised compact Cortext LTM sufficiency to **1.286** with lower noise
(**0.143**). However, it over-pruned: only **2** durable `has_label` edges
remained, **3 / 5** consolidation cycles ended with no durable labels, and
relation creation stayed at **0** because endpoints were still missing or
malformed. This marks the boundary of the stoplist approach. Rejecting obvious
non-memory words is useful, but a larger negative list is not the right
production mechanism. The next viable hardening target is a positive
discriminative-label contract for the relabeler: admit labels that carry enough
entity/object/event specificity and source support, and ask the model to repair
or expand weak endpoint labels before relation persistence.

The next production-path hardening added a small source-supported durable-label
floor during replacement-mode relabel/prune. If the relabeler returns too few
durable labels for an associative cue, Cortext now keeps up to the
Focus/Sensitivity/Stability-derived durable-label floor admissible current STM
graph labels before deleting stale `has_label` edges. This is not a retrieval-side heuristic: it is
part of the consolidation handoff and only admits labels that pass the same
durability and evidence checks as relabeler outputs. A focused regression test
simulates an under-admitting relabeler that returns one valid label while the STM
graph carries three source-supported durable labels plus generic noise; the new
path keeps the three durable labels and still drops the generic labels.

The corresponding live replay artifact
`build/stm_ltm_current_label_floor.json` shows that this fixes the construction
collapse but not the compact-LTM quality gap. On the same 80-message corpus slice,
cycles with current labels pruned to zero fell from **2** to **0** and durable
`has_label` edges rose from **2** to **5**. Source grounding remained intact
(**59 / 59** hydratable source memories and **59** `derived_from` links), and
cycles without durable labels fell from **3** to **1**. However, compact Cortext
LTM still scored only **1.000** sufficiency with **0** wins, while compact normal
RAG scored **3.857** sufficiency with **3** wins. A historical relaxed STM-label
admission diagnostic produced the same construction counters in
`build/stm_ltm_current_label_floor_more_stm.json`; the current production path
derives the similarity floor and label caps from Focus/Sensitivity/Stability, so
the immediate failure is not a standalone similarity threshold.

Finally, re-enabling the label bank exposed a separate realtime constraint. The
seeded-label path loaded roughly **6.5k** label memories, which is the intended
surface for STM graph label proposals, but the current STM label selector
recomputes k-means-like clustering over that label set per signal. In a bounded
smoke with reduced cluster settings, the run had processed only **6** signals
after roughly **2** minutes, so it was stopped before judging. This means the
label-bank path is architecturally important for avoiding circular label
starvation, but it needs precomputed or cached label clusters before it can be
used as the realtime production STM graph proposal surface.

We then moved that clustering work out of the per-signal STM graph update. The
processor now keeps a cached label-cluster assignment keyed by requested cluster
count, embedding dimension, and summary-cache size; label cache updates
invalidate it. `UpdateShortTermMemoryShadow` still ranks the nearest clusters
for each signal and selects Top-K labels inside each selected cluster, but it no
longer recomputes the full label k-means loop on every update. A focused test
checks both cache reuse and invalidation. Profiling the still-slow seeded-label
smoke then found the remaining hot path in `GraphRetrieve.seed_sql`: SQLite
vector KNN was treating label-bank `LABEL` rows as ordinary memory seeds. We
therefore excluded `LABEL` rows from the base KNN seed query and kept labels as
graph/ranking substrate rather than standalone retrieved memories.

With those changes, the same bounded label-bank smoke completed instead of
stalling. `build/stm_ltm_label_bank_cached_probe2.json` processed **12**
messages in **14.965 s** with the label bank enabled. It produced **28** STM
label edges, sent **11** current labels into relabel/prune, retained **4**
durable `has_label` edges, preserved **8 / 8** source memories, and still
created **0 / 1** relation edges because one endpoint was missing. The judged
bounded artifact
`build/stm_ltm_label_bank_cached_grounded_judged.json` processed **30** messages
in **39.517 s** with four consolidation cycles. The consolidation handoff is now
substantially less starved: **108** STM label edges, **38** current labels,
**13** refined durable labels, **31** labels pruned, **13** final `has_label`
edges, **25** `derived_from` links, and **25 / 25** hydratable source memories.
However, the retrieval verdict is still negative for LTM alone: compact Cortext
LTM scored **1.000** sufficiency and **2.000** relevance with **0** wins, while
compact normal RAG scored **4.000** sufficiency with **1** win on the two judged
probes. The STM+LTM union was much stronger (**3.000** sufficiency), which
suggests that source continuity remains available in working/short-term memory,
but the durable LTM graph is still under-linked. The next hardening target is no
longer label proposal starvation; it is relation/endpoint repair and mapping
durable labels back to source memories strongly enough for LTM-only retrieval.

A final bounded rerun on the same `skip=1980` slice, after endpoint repair and
non-durable-endpoint classification, supersedes the earlier "missing endpoint"
diagnosis. The artifact
`build/stm_ltm_drop_non_durable_relation_judged.json` processed **30** messages
with normal Cortext working memory, STM graph creation, deep consolidation,
relabel/prune, LTM retrieval, OpenAI `gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17` judging, and the
label-bank-backed STM graph path enabled. Four consolidation cycles sent **27**
STM items and **108** STM label edges into the relabeler. The relabel/prune pass
considered **30** current labels, accepted **17** refined durable labels, kept
**7**, added **10**, and pruned **23** by omission. It created **25**
`derived_from` links, **17** durable `has_label` links, and preserved **25 / 25**
source memories with hydratable content.

The relation audit improved in the specific way the prior run required:
`relation_edges_created=1`, `relation_edges_skipped_missing_endpoint=0`,
`relation_edges_skipped_non_durable_endpoint=1`, and
`relation_endpoint_rejected_ungrounded=0`. Thus the remaining skipped relation
was not caused by lost evidence or endpoint lookup failure; the endpoint was
available to the relabeler but failed the durable-label admission contract. This
is the right failure mode for a human-like LTM builder: unsupported or
non-durable endpoints should not become durable graph anchors merely because a
relation string mentions them.

The quality verdict remains negative for LTM-only retrieval. On the two judged
compact-policy probes, compact Cortext LTM averaged **1.000** sufficiency and
**2.000** relevance with **0** wins. Compact STM+LTM union averaged **3.000**
sufficiency and **4.000** relevance, matching lexical LTM but still losing to
compact normal RAG at **4.500** sufficiency, **5.000** relevance, and **2 / 2**
wins. The corrected claim is therefore narrow but important: Cortext now creates
source-grounded durable LTM by consolidating STM graph structure through
relabeling and pruning, not by summary text alone; however, the current durable
graph still underperforms RAG because retrieval/admission does not yet select the
right original experiences from that graph often enough.

An 80-message repeat of the same slice
(`build/stm_ltm_drop_non_durable_relation_80_judged.json`) strengthens the
negative side of that verdict. It processed **80** messages, ran **9**
consolidation cycles, and judged four compact-policy probes. Source grounding
remained intact: **63** STM items and **252** STM label edges entered
consolidation; **60** current labels were considered; **32** refined durable
labels were accepted; **44** labels were pruned; **70** `derived_from` links and
**32** durable `has_label` links were created; and **70 / 70** source memories
remained hydratable. But relation creation did not generalize from the shorter
run: the relabeler emitted **5** relations, **0** relation edges were created,
**3** relations were skipped for non-durable endpoints, **2** for unsupported
predicates, and **0** for missing endpoints. All five endpoint rejections were
non-durable, with **0** ungrounded endpoint rejections. Compact Cortext LTM again
averaged **1.000** sufficiency with **0** wins, while compact normal RAG averaged
**3.500** and compact full history averaged **4.000**. The durable graph builder
is therefore source-preserving and selective, but not yet sufficiently
relational or discriminative for LTM-only retrieval to behave like a human
long-term memory.

To make the raw-STM comparison explicit, we added a benchmark-only
`--stm-graph-bakeoff` arm. This does not change production retrieval. It reads
the STM/LTM audit table produced by normal Cortext consolidation, builds one
packet from source memories selected by provisional STM `current_labels`, builds
a second packet from the same source-backed cues selected by refined durable
labels after relabel/prune, and judges both against normal RAG and full history.
The artifact `build/stm_ltm_graph_bakeoff_80_judged.json` reran the same
80-message slice with this arm enabled. The construction counters matched the
prior repeat: **252** STM label edges entered consolidation, **32** refined
durable labels survived, **70 / 70** sources were hydratable, and **0 / 5**
relations became durable edges.

The graph-only retrieval result was more negative than the compact Cortext LTM
result. Across seven graph-bakeoff probes, both raw and relabeled graph packets
had **0 / 7** query-overlap hits and **0** positive label-query cycles. On the
four judged graph probes, raw STM graph and relabel/prune LTM both averaged
**0.000** sufficiency and **0.500** relevance with **0** wins, while normal RAG
averaged **2.250** sufficiency and full history averaged **3.000**. This isolates
the failure: the source memories are present, but neither the provisional STM
label surface nor the refined durable label surface carries enough
query-discriminative language to route back to the relevant experiences. The
next hardening target is therefore the label/relation contract and retrieval
selector, not additional source preservation.

A focused grounding fix then tightened the admission contract used by the
replacement-mode relabel/prune pass. Text blobs are now treated as ordinary text
evidence, not as multimodal grounding for the current-label floor; only audio
and image blobs can satisfy the blob-evidence path. The privacy-safe judged
artifact `build/stm_ltm_text_blob_grounding_fix_judged.json` reran the same
`skip=1980`, 30-message slice with compact-policy and graph-bakeoff arms
enabled. The relabeler still received **27** STM items and **108** STM label
edges across four consolidation cycles, and source preservation remained intact:
**25 / 25** source memories were hydratable with **25** `derived_from` links.
But the stricter grounding rule reduced the durable label surface from the
earlier **17** refined labels to **10**, retained **0** current labels through
the floor, and pruned **30** current labels. The generic-label-collapse
diagnostic improved in the intended direction:
`label_boost_without_ltm_query_overlap=0`, compared with **2** on the earlier
smoke slice. A regression test now covers this case directly by verifying that a
text blob plus textual evidence admits only labels supported by the text, not an
unmentioned current label.

The quality result did not improve. On two judged graph-bakeoff probes, both
raw STM graph and relabel/pruned LTM again had **0 / 2** query-overlap hits,
**0** positive label-query cycles, **0.000** sufficiency, and **0.500**
relevance. Compact Cortext LTM averaged **1.000** sufficiency and **2.000**
relevance with **0** wins, while compact normal RAG averaged **4.000**
sufficiency and **5.000** relevance. The fix therefore removed a false-positive
label-retention path, but exposed the opposite failure more clearly:
over-pruning and under-admission now leave the durable graph too sparse or too
unqueryable to recover the right source experiences.

To separate evidence-window loss from label-surface mismatch, we added
privacy-safe audit counters for how many current, removed, and refined labels
appear in the selected relabeler evidence versus the full source text behind the
same `derived_from` links. The diagnostic run
`build/stm_ltm_evidence_window_probe.json` used the same 30-message slice and
normal Cortext consolidation path. It preserved **25 / 25** source memories and
again produced **10** refined durable labels and **1** relation edge. The new
counters showed that **0 / 30** provisional current labels appeared in either
the selected relabeler evidence or the full source text, while **8 / 10**
refined durable labels appeared in both. Thus, on this slice, the problem is not
primarily that the selected relabeler window truncates away otherwise valid STM
labels. The provisional STM label surface itself is poorly grounded in the
source language that consolidation sees, and relabel/prune is correctly deleting
those labels rather than using them as durable memory anchors.

We then hardened the handoff rather than the STM label-clustering mechanism
itself. Clustered STM label edges are still kept in the short-term graph for
fast approximate attention, but the number of ungrounded STM labels allowed into
the relabeler is now bounded by Focus/Sensitivity/Stability instead of a
standalone runtime setting. The OpenAI-judged artifact
`build/stm_ltm_grounded_current_labels_openai.json` reran the same 30-message
slice. The noisy provisional label surface was eliminated: **0** current labels
were sent to relabel/prune, **0** labels were pruned by omission, and source
grounding stayed intact at **25 / 25** hydratable source memories. The relabeler
still created durable labels directly from evidence, but only **3** refined
labels and **3** `has_label` edges survived, with **0** relation edges. The
graph-only quality remained poor under `gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17`: raw STM graph
and relabel/prune LTM both scored **0.000** sufficiency and **1.000** relevance
on two probes, while normal RAG scored **3.000** sufficiency and **4.500**
relevance. This confirms that noisy current labels were a real defect in the
consolidation handoff, but removing them exposes the remaining bottleneck:
under-admission and weak relation formation leave the durable LTM graph too thin
to route back to the original experiences.

To classify that under-admission, we added aggregate extractor/post-processing
counters to the audit table. The OpenAI-judged artifact
`build/stm_ltm_under_admission_openai.json` showed that the relabeler proposed
**9** label candidates and **2** relation candidates across the four cycles, but
only **3** labels were admitted from the extractor. Post-processing rejected
**1** label as non-durable and **5** labels as ungrounded; there were **0**
duplicate rejects, **0** legacy-gate rejects, **0** current-floor insertions,
and **0** relation-endpoint label insertions. The two relation candidates still
created **0** relation edges: one was skipped for an unsupported predicate and
one for non-durable endpoints. Thus the bottleneck is no longer hidden inside a
single "few labels survived" counter: on this slice, the extractor proposes a
small candidate set and most rejected candidates are not supported by the source
text under the evidence contract.

We also tested whether the grounding rule was merely too literal for event
phrases. The label admission check now accepts multi-token labels when all
canonical label tokens appear somewhere in the evidence, even if the exact
phrase is not contiguous; a regression test covers the `car crash` / `car ...
crash` case. The follow-up artifact
`build/stm_ltm_token_grounding_openai.json` did not change the live personal-chat
counters: **9** label candidates, **5** ungrounded rejects, **3** admitted
labels, **2** relation candidates, and **0** relation edges. This rules out
simple phrase-contiguity as the cause of under-admission on this slice. The next
hardening target is the relabeler contract itself: it needs to propose more
source-token-supported durable anchors and supported predicates, not looser
post-hoc admission of labels that the evidence does not contain.

We tightened that relabeler prompt contract next. The Gemma text, audio, and
image relabel prompts now ask for **4--8** exact source spans when the evidence
contains enough anchors, require every important label word to appear verbatim
in the evidence, disallow paraphrased or inferred labels, and allow relations
only when both endpoints exactly match final labels and the predicate is in the
supported set. The comparable OpenAI-judged artifact
`build/stm_ltm_prompt_contract_openai.json` showed no construction improvement:
the relabeler again produced **9** label candidates, **3** admitted labels,
**5** ungrounded rejects, **2** relation candidates, and **0** relation edges.
Graph-only retrieval remained well below normal RAG despite a small score
fluctuation on this two-probe slice: raw STM graph and relabel/prune LTM both
averaged **0.500** sufficiency and **1.500** relevance, while normal RAG
averaged **4.000** sufficiency and **5.000** relevance. The prompt-only change
therefore did not solve under-admission. The current evidence points to a
stronger extractor/relabeler capability gap or a need for a deterministic
source-span candidate generator before the LLM relabel/prune pass.

We then added that deterministic source-span floor to the replacement-mode
relabel/prune path. For each consolidation request, the processor now extracts a
small bounded set of durable candidate labels directly from capitalized or
multi-token source spans in the same evidence sent to the relabeler. These
source-span candidates are included as relabeler hints and, if the extractor
under-admits, can fill the durable label floor only when they are still grounded
in the source text. A regression test covers the intended failure mode: when the
extractor returns no labels for `"Maria met Bailey at River Park."`, the
replacement path admits `Maria`, `Bailey`, and `River Park` as source-grounded
durable labels and records them separately from ordinary current-label carryover.
The audit migration was also hardened so older audit tables can accept the newer
per-cycle counters.

The comparable OpenAI-judged artifact
`build/stm_ltm_source_span_floor_openai.json` shows that this fixed the
emptiness problem but not retrieval quality. On the same `skip=1980`,
30-message Cortext-only replay, four consolidation cycles sent **27** STM items
and **108** STM label edges through relabel/prune, preserved **25 / 25**
hydratable source memories, generated **31** source-span candidates, inserted
**6** durable labels from the source-span floor, inserted **9** labels from the
extractor, and ended with **15** refined durable labels after pruning **21**.
Thus the relabel/prune stage is no longer merely deleting noisy STM labels; it
is creating grounded durable label structure from the source window when the LLM
under-admits.

The remaining failure is relation formation and query routing. The relabeler
emitted **7** relation candidates, but **0** relation edges were created because
all seven were skipped as unsupported predicates. Graph-only quality was
unchanged: raw STM graph and relabel/pruned LTM both averaged **0.000**
sufficiency and **1.000** relevance on two judged probes, while normal RAG
averaged **2.000** sufficiency and **4.000** relevance. Compact Cortext LTM
improved over graph-only but still trailed lexical memory: compact Cortext LTM
averaged **1.000** sufficiency and **2.000** relevance, compact STM+LTM union
averaged **3.000** sufficiency and **4.000** relevance, and compact normal RAG
averaged **4.000** sufficiency and **5.000** relevance. The verdict is
therefore sharper: source-grounded durable labels are now being created, but
human-like LTM retrieval still requires either supported relation extraction or
a retrieval selector that can use the durable labels to recover the original
experiences instead of behaving like a sparse label list.

We next separated two relation failures. First, malformed relation predicates
from the relabeler are no longer treated as fatal when the endpoints are
otherwise durable and grounded; they fall back to the weakest supported
`co_occurs` relation. On the same replay this moved the relation-failure counter
from unsupported predicates to non-durable endpoints, proving that the remaining
LLM relation objects still did not name acceptable durable anchors. Second, we
added a bounded deterministic co-occurrence fallback among the final admitted
labels for each replacement-mode cue. This is not a new summary heuristic: it
connects the labels that survived relabel/prune on the same source-backed STM
association, with a small weight and a cap of six labels per cue.

The artifact `build/stm_ltm_label_cooccurrence_openai.json` shows the result.
Construction improved in the intended graph-formation sense: the same four
cycles still preserved **25 / 25** source memories, admitted **15** durable
labels, and retained the **6** source-span-floor labels, but now created **24**
deterministic label co-occurrence edges. LLM relation candidates remained
unusable as direct edges: **7** relation candidates produced **0** direct
relation edges because **7** were skipped for non-durable endpoints. Retrieval
quality still did not improve in the graph-only arm. Raw STM graph and
relabel/pruned LTM both had **0 / 2** query-overlap hits and **0.000**
sufficiency; relabel/pruned LTM averaged **0.500** relevance versus normal RAG
at **4.000** relevance and **2.000** sufficiency. Full Cortext with working
memory plus LTM remained competitive on this tiny two-probe slice, but compact
LTM-only still trailed lexical memory. The current bottleneck is therefore no
longer absence of durable labels or absence of any label graph edges; it is that
the durable label graph is not query-discriminative enough for the current
selector to recover the correct original experiences without recent working
memory or lexical RAG.

We then corrected the graph-bakeoff packet itself so that the relabel/prune arm
uses the same source-backed durable LTM path that production retrieval exposes in
debug state, rather than ranking only by refined-label lexical overlap. The
artifact `build/stm_ltm_production_graph_packet_v11_openai.json` reran the same
30-message corpus slice with this production-shaped graph packet. The construction
audit remained stable: **27** STM items and **108** STM label edges entered four
relabel/prune cycles; **25 / 25** source memories were hydratable; **25**
`derived_from` links, **4** durable source-backed LTM nodes, **20** durable
label-source backing pairs, **4** `has_label` links, and **3** co-occurrence
edges were created; **0** durable relation edges were created. The corrected
packet did find the production durable candidates: across two judged probes it
hydrated **8** original source memories behind **2** source-backed durable LTM
candidates. However, quality still did not improve: raw STM graph and
relabel/pruned LTM both averaged **0.500** sufficiency and **1.000** relevance,
while normal RAG averaged **3.500** sufficiency and **4.500** relevance.

In the historical v12 OpenAI development artifact, we ran a retrieval-weight
sensitivity check,
`build/stm_ltm_durable_weight035_v12_openai.json`, with a historical fixed
durable-source weight of **0.35** instead of the earlier **0.12** default. This
moved a source-backed durable candidate to the top rank on one probe, showing
that source-backed durable LTM can affect production ranking. It still did not
make the relabeled/pruned LTM competitive: graph-only relabel/pruned LTM remained
at **0.500** sufficiency and **1.000** relevance, compact Cortext LTM fell to
**0.500** sufficiency and **1.000** relevance, and compact normal RAG remained at
**4.500** sufficiency and **5.000** relevance. The development claim should
therefore remain conservative: the failure is not just
a too-small durable-source boost. The durable nodes preserve sources, but the
relabel/prune output is too sparse and off-target for these probes: **24**
labels were pruned, only **4** refined durable labels survived, **28 / 33** label
candidates were rejected as non-durable, and **2 / 2** relation candidates were
skipped for non-durable endpoints. The development claim should remain
conservative:
Cortext has an STM-graph-to-LTM consolidation path that creates source-grounded
durable structure, but this path is not yet a RAG-quality human-like long-term
memory until the relabeler/pruner produces more query-discriminative labels and
relation endpoints.

We then hardened the relabel/prune admission path in two source-preserving ways.
First, relation endpoint repair now runs before non-durable endpoint rejection,
so a weak endpoint can still map onto an already admitted durable label instead
of being skipped solely because the endpoint string is generic. A regression test
covers the lowercase endpoint `dog` repairing to the admitted durable label
`Bailey dog` without creating a junk `dog` label. Second, source-span candidates
now complement the extractor up to the Focus/Sensitivity/Stability-derived
durable-label ceiling instead of only filling the minimum durable-label floor.
The source-span generator was also tightened so capitalized phrases do not cross
sentence boundaries or consume the cap with subspans inside an already admitted
proper phrase.

The OpenAI-judged artifact
`build/stm_ltm_source_span_complement_v14_openai.json` shows the effect on the
same 30-message corpus slice. The relabeler still processed **27** STM items and
**108** STM label edges across four cycles, with **25 / 25** source memories
hydratable. The durable LTM surface grew from **4** to **7** refined labels:
**4** came from the extractor and **3** from the source-span complement. Durable
source-backed LTM nodes rose from **4** to **7**, label-source backing pairs from
**20** to **35**, `has_label` links from **4** to **7**, and deterministic
co-occurrence edges from **3** to **15**. Over-pruning decreased from **24** to
**21** removed labels. Relation extraction did not improve on this slice:
**2 / 2** relation candidates were still skipped for non-durable endpoints, with
**0** direct relation edges.

Quality moved in the expected but still insufficient direction. LTM-only Cortext
improved to **3.500** relevance and **1.500** sufficiency, and full Cortext with
working memory plus LTM reached **4.500** relevance and **3.000** sufficiency.
However, the isolated graph packet remained poor: raw STM graph averaged
**0.500** relevance and **0.000** sufficiency, while relabel/pruned LTM also
averaged **0.500** relevance and **0.000** sufficiency; normal RAG remained ahead
at **3.500** relevance and **2.500** sufficiency. The current verdict is thus
more nuanced: bounded source-span complement makes the durable LTM graph less
sparse and improves production LTM retrieval, but the graph-only relabel/prune
arm still does not recover the right experiences without lexical/recent-context
support. The next hardening target is query-discriminative routing over the
source-backed durable labels, plus relation endpoints that name admitted labels.

We then tested that routing hypothesis directly in production retrieval. The
first change added a source-text route for durable labels: when a live text query
does not exactly name a durable label, retrieval can still score the original
source payloads behind source-backed label graph nodes and seed matching source
memories back into graph retrieval. A focused regression verifies this with a
durable label whose own text does not match the query but whose backing source
payload does. The second change preserves the best high-confidence durable-source
candidate near the front of the selected list so chat-demo injection caps do not
discard it after retrieval already found it. On the personal-chat replay
(`build/stm_ltm_durable_source_promote_v16_openai.json`), this worked
mechanically: a source-backed durable candidate with **8** backing sources and
durable-source boost **0.968** moved to the top retrieval-debug rank on the first
probe. The graph-isolation arm also improved over the v14 source-span run:
relabel/pruned LTM rose from **0.500 / 0.000** relevance/sufficiency to
**1.000 / 0.500**, while raw STM graph stayed at **0.500 / 0.000**. However,
standalone Cortext LTM still averaged only **2.000 / 0.500**, compact-policy
Cortext LTM averaged **1.000 / 0.500**, and compact normal RAG remained ahead at
**4.500 / 4.000**. This falsifies the simpler "we only failed to surface the
durable node" explanation. The remaining bottleneck is label quality and graph
connectivity: **7** durable source-backed label nodes and **35** source backing
pairs exist, but **2 / 2** relation candidates still fail endpoint durability and
the query overlap counters remain zero for isolated LTM. The next viable
algorithmic target is not another score boost; it is relabeler output that names
retrievable, query-discriminative anchors and relation endpoints that connect the
surviving labels.

The next run (`build/stm_ltm_relation_accounting_v17_openai.json`) tightened the
durable-label gate against leading numeric fragments and made deterministic
label co-occurrence explicit in the relation-edge audit. This prevents low-value
date/count fragments from becoming durable labels while still preserving proper
alphanumeric anchors, and it records source-grounded co-occurrence edges as
actual relation structure rather than only as a side counter. The replay again
preserved **25 / 25** source memories, **7** durable source-backed labels, and
**35** label-source backing pairs. It now reports **15** relation edges created,
all from deterministic co-occurrence among admitted labels; LLM relation
endpoints still failed durability (**2 / 2** skipped non-durable endpoints,
**4** endpoint rejects). The stricter gate reduced removed labels from **21** to
**20**, shifted one label from extractor output to source-span admission, and
kept the durable LTM surface at **7** labels. Quality did not improve:
graph-only relabel/pruned LTM averaged **0.500 / 0.000**
relevance/sufficiency, Cortext LTM-only averaged **2.500 / 1.000**, and compact
normal RAG remained stronger at **5.000 / 4.500**. This result is useful because
it closes another false explanation: the graph is not simply disconnected. The
connected durable graph still lacks the right human-facing anchors for the
queries, so future work should target label selection/reranking at consolidation
time rather than more retrieval boosts or edge-count fixes.

As a follow-on, we extended the compact-policy source-window sweep with new
held-out live Cortext runs. The first added `skip=1800` for
`source_stm_recent_k in {2,3,4}`; it initially suggested that widening the
recent working/short-term packet improved quality, with compact STM recent
increasing from **2.0625** at `k=2` to **2.3125** at `k=3` and **2.5000** at
`k=4`. We then added `k=4` runs at `skip=720` and `skip=1260` to test whether
that result transferred. It did not: `k=4` scored **2.4375** compact STM
sufficiency at `skip=720`, but dropped to **2.0625** at `skip=1260`, where
normal RAG remained slightly higher at **2.1250** despite using about **220**
tokens. All runs used the public Cortext processing and consolidation path, a
128-token active-history budget, deep consolidation every 20 messages, no label
bank, and 16 judged probes per slice. Aggregating all currently available k
sweep artifacts now gives the following non-uniform evidence:

| source STM k | judged probes | best compact packet | mean sufficiency | mean relevance | mean noise | mean tokens | wins |
|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 16 | STM+LTM union | 2.3750 | 2.6250 | 0.0000 | 78.3 | 0 |
| 2 | 48 | STM+LTM union | 2.3333 | 2.6667 | 0.0417 | 75.5 | 5 |
| 3 | 64 | STM recent | **2.7813** | **3.0156** | 0.0156 | **56.8** | 23 |
| 4 | 64 | STM recent | 2.5625 | 2.9688 | 0.0313 | 75.1 | **24** |

This reverses the provisional `k=4` interpretation. With equal judged support
for `k=3` and `k=4`, `k=3` is better on mean sufficiency, relevance, noise, and
tokens. `k=4` wins one more individual probe, but it costs roughly **+18.3**
tokens per probe and is less robust on the problem slice (`skip=1260`). The
practical update is to keep `k=3` as the current compact STM setting, keep
`k=1` as the extreme efficiency point (**2.1875** sufficiency at **21.4**
tokens in the single slice where it has been measured), and treat wider STM
windows as situational rather than default.

The remaining question was whether the `skip=1260` problem slice needed a wider
LTM sidecar rather than a wider STM window. We therefore reran `skip=1260` with
STM fixed at `k=3`, lexical LTM fixed at `k=5`, and varied the compact union
cap. The cap is important because the compact STM+LTM packet is capped by
`max_injected_memories`: with STM `k=3` and cap `4`, the union usually admits
only one LTM item. A fair cap-4 rerun matched the prior cap-4 result, then cap
6 and cap 8 were run through the same live Cortext bakeoff path:

| compact union cap | union items | STM sufficiency | STM+LTM sufficiency | normal RAG sufficiency | union tokens | normal RAG tokens |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 | 4.0 | 1.6250 | 1.7500 | 1.8125 | **98.2** | 220.1 |
| 6 | 5.2 | **2.5000** | **2.6875** | **2.4375** | 121.7 | 220.1 |
| 8 | 5.4 | 2.3750 | 2.5625 | 2.3125 | 136.1 | 220.1 |

This is the clearest targeted LTM-side improvement so far. On the hard slice,
allowing approximately two additional LTM sidecar memories made compact STM+LTM
beat both compact STM and normal RAG while still using about **45%** fewer tokens
than normal RAG. The effect is not monotonic: cap 8 costs more and performs
worse than cap 6. This argues for testing a conditional cap expansion when a
compact LTM sidecar has query overlap or when the fixed cap-4 union is weak, not
for increasing the global chat-demo memory cap unconditionally.

We then tested transfer by adding cap-6 runs at `skip=1080`, `skip=1440`,
`skip=900`, and `skip=1620`. Across the five-slice transfer set
(`skip=900`, `skip=1080`, `skip=1260`, `skip=1440`, `skip=1620`), cap 6
improved compact STM+LTM from **2.2125** to **2.3750** mean sufficiency and
stayed above normal RAG (**2.1250**) while using **104.2** tokens instead of
**196.9**. The cost is real: cap 6 spends **+24.4** tokens over cap 4, raises
noise from **0.0000** to **0.0625**, and is not uniformly better. It helps
`skip=1080` and `skip=1260`, ties `skip=1440`, and loses to cap 4 on `skip=900`
and `skip=1620`. The current policy candidate is therefore not "always cap 6";
it is a conditional LTM expansion: use compact STM `k=3` as the default, use
cap-4 STM+LTM as the compact LTM packet, and expand toward cap 6 only when
retrieval diagnostics indicate that the LTM sidecar is relevant or the compact
packet is likely undercovered.

We then scanned a posthoc cap-expansion gate over those same five cap4/cap6
pairs using only non-private per-probe counters: raw Cortext retrieval count,
compact-packet token counts, overlap rates, active-history size, and aggregate
retrieval-debug scores. The best posthoc rule selected cap 6 for **43 / 80**
probes and lifted mean sufficiency to **2.5250** at **91.4** tokens, compared
with fixed cap 4 at **2.2125** / **79.9** tokens and fixed cap 6 at **2.3750** /
**104.2** tokens. This looked like the desired conditional rescue behavior on
the training surface, but it did not transfer to held-out chronological slices.
On fresh `skip=180`, `skip=360`, and `skip=720` cap-6 live Cortext runs, compact
STM recent became the best held-out packet and fixed cap 4 remained the best
STM+LTM cap:

| held-out policy (`skip=180,360,720`) | cap6 choices | mean sufficiency | mean relevance | mean noise | mean tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| STM recent | -- | **2.9375** | **3.1875** | 0.0208 | **57.5** |
| fixed cap 4 | 0 / 48 | 2.8750 | 3.1250 | 0.0208 | 78.3 |
| fixed cap 6 | 48 / 48 | 2.6250 | 3.1250 | 0.0208 | 102.3 |
| posthoc top rule applied | 24 / 48 | 2.5417 | 2.9583 | 0.0208 | 86.0 |
| low-noise posthoc rule applied | 15 / 48 | 2.6458 | 2.9583 | 0.0208 | 85.2 |
| normal RAG | -- | 2.7917 | 3.0417 | 0.0208 | 195.6 |

The held-out set rejects the current cap-6 gate as a production policy. It also
clarifies the useful result: cap 6 can rescue specific hard slices, but the
available diagnostics are not yet reliable enough to decide when to spend those
extra LTM tokens. On `skip=180`, cap 6 still trailed cap 4 (**2.8125** versus
**2.9375**) and STM recent (**3.0000**); on `skip=360`, it lowered the union
from **3.1875** to **2.9375**; and on `skip=720` it fell farther behind
(**2.1250** versus cap 4's **2.5000**). The default remains compact STM `k=3`
with a cap-4 compact STM+LTM packet available as an optional compact LTM view;
cap expansion should stay an experiment until it has a held-out-positive
admission signal.

Finally, we evaluated simple posthoc adaptive policies using only non-private
per-probe counters already emitted by the benchmark. The judge scores are used
only as outcomes. The strongest deployable rule in this set was compact-only:
choose STM+LTM when the lexical LTM sidecar adds query-overlap coverage,
otherwise keep STM recent. It is equivalent to `compact_overlap_best` in the
artifact below.

| policy | four-slice sufficiency | four-slice tokens | fair skip-540 sufficiency | fair skip-540 tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| always STM recent | 2.7500 | **58.0** | 2.5625 | **56.1** |
| always STM+LTM union | 2.7031 | 78.2 | 2.8125 | 76.8 |
| compact overlap best | **2.7813** | 68.3 | **2.8958** | 70.5 |
| normal RAG if compact overlap is zero | 2.7188 | 133.9 | 2.7292 | 143.2 |
| oracle best packet | 3.0469 | 82.4 | 3.1875 | 110.1 |

The overlap gate is not a large gain, but it is the first non-leaky adaptive
policy that improves the four-slice average while keeping the packet compact.
Rules that fall back to normal RAG can help individual slices, but they spend
roughly 2x the tokens of the compact overlap rule and did not improve the
overall four-slice mean. The oracle row shows there is still headroom if a
better confidence signal can identify when the compact packet is insufficient,
but it is not deployable because it uses judge outcomes.

A leave-one-slice-out rule-selection check reduces this claim. When the best
non-oracle rule is selected on three chronological slices and evaluated on the
held-out slice, the selected rules average **2.6563** sufficiency at **86.8**
tokens. Always-STM on the same held-out rows averages **2.7500** sufficiency at
**58.0** tokens, while fixed compact-overlap averages **2.7813**. The rule
choice changes across folds, and one fold selects a normal-RAG fallback that
loses badly on the held-out `skip=360` slice. Therefore compact-overlap should
be treated as a candidate heuristic for future implementation tests, not yet a
validated adaptive policy.

We repeated this selector audit after extending the cap-4 compact-policy surface
to ten chronological slices (`skip=180,360,540,720,900,1080,1260,1440,1620,1800`;
160 judged probes). The fixed packets remain simple: compact STM `k=3` averages
**2.3563** sufficiency at **56.2** tokens, cap-4 STM+LTM averages **2.4063** at
**77.9** tokens, and compact normal RAG averages **2.2563** at **194.3** tokens.
An oracle over the three packets reaches **2.7125** sufficiency at **86.0**
tokens, so there is still meaningful headroom if a confidence signal can choose
the right packet. However, leave-one-slice-out rule selection over the same
non-private counters averages only **2.3125** sufficiency at **97.7** tokens,
selecting STM on **46 / 160** probes, STM+LTM on **79 / 160**, and normal RAG on
**35 / 160**. The learned selector is worse than always using cap-4 STM+LTM and
less efficient than always using compact STM. This larger audit rejects the
current counter-only selector family for production promotion; the next useful
test should be a stronger verifier signal or a direct learned abstention model,
not another hand-written normal-RAG fallback.

We then tested that next step without changing production behavior. A
leave-one-slice-out ridge verifier used **81** pre-judge features per probe:
compact packet token counts, overlap counters, active-history counters, and
aggregate retrieval-debug scores. Each fold trained only on the other nine
chronological slices. A direct "choose the maximum predicted packet" policy
improved over the failed hand-written selector but spent too many tokens:
**2.4500** sufficiency at **107.7** tokens. The best held-out policy was an
STM-default efficiency gate: keep compact STM unless the learned margin
justifies switching to STM+LTM or rare normal RAG. It selected STM on **69 /
160** probes, STM+LTM on **62 / 160**, and normal RAG on **29 / 160**, reaching
**2.4813** sufficiency at **90.5** tokens with zero mean noise. Paired bootstrap
deltas were positive against fixed STM (**+0.1250**, 95% CI **[+0.0563,
+0.1938]**) and fixed cap-4 STM+LTM (**+0.0750**, 95% CI **[+0.0063,
+0.1500]**), while still using **103.7** fewer tokens than normal RAG on
average. This is the first selector in the private-conversation bakeoff that
clears held-out transfer, but it remains benchmark-only: it uses a trained
surface over one corpus, and the normal-RAG branch fires often enough that the
next production test should be an explicit learned abstention/verifier module
rather than another static prompt policy.

We stress-tested that conclusion with constrained variants. Compact-only
verifiers could choose only between STM recent and cap-4 STM+LTM. The best
compact STM-default gate selected STM on **87 / 160** probes and STM+LTM on
**73 / 160**, reaching **2.4188** sufficiency at **67.0** tokens. This is a
modest held-out gain over fixed STM (**+0.0625**, 95% CI **[+0.0063, +0.1188]**)
and saves **10.9** tokens versus fixed cap-4 STM+LTM, but the quality delta
versus fixed cap 4 is only **+0.0125** with a CI crossing zero. Rare-RAG caps
did not recover the unconstrained gain: a 5 percent training-time RAG cap chose
normal RAG on **13 / 160** held-out probes and reached **2.4250** sufficiency at
**74.5** tokens, while a 10 percent cap reached **2.4125** at **76.4** tokens.
Both are positive versus fixed STM but inconclusive versus fixed cap 4. The
practical split is therefore clear: a compact-only learned gate is production
shaped as a cheaper cap-4 substitute, whereas the larger quality gain requires
a true learned verifier with an explicit expanded-history/RAG admission policy.

Finally, we ran a stricter forward-chaining check: train on earlier
chronological slices and evaluate only on future slices. The first four slices
(`skip=180,360,540,720`) served as warmup/training; reported aggregates cover
`skip=900,1080,1260,1440,1620,1800` (**96** probes). On these future slices,
fixed STM averages **2.0938** sufficiency at **55.7** tokens, fixed cap-4
STM+LTM averages **2.1979** at **77.9** tokens, and normal RAG averages
**2.0000** at **194.9** tokens. The compact STM-default gate reaches
**2.1563** at **65.6** tokens with no RAG choices. Its paired gain over STM is
**+0.0625**, but the CI crosses zero (**[-0.0104, +0.1354]**), and it trails
fixed cap 4 by **-0.0417** while saving **12.4** tokens. Rare-RAG and
unconstrained forward gates also fail to beat cap 4. This forward-transfer
audit downgrades the learned selector from "ready to promote" to "candidate
for explicit online verifier testing": LOO shows learnable signal, but purely
chronological deployment needs either more training history or a richer
confidence model before it should control expanded context in the chat demo.

To add new data rather than only reanalyze the same ten slices, we then ran
three later live Cortext bakeoff slices with the same public benchmark path and
settings (`skip=1980,2160,2340`; 180 processed messages, compact STM `k=3`,
cap-4 STM+LTM, 16 judged probes per slice). These are farther forward in the
private conversation timeline than the selector-training surface. The later
slice aggregate strengthens the compact-memory result: STM recent averages
**2.6458** sufficiency at **57.4** tokens, cap-4 STM+LTM averages **2.7083** at
**79.3** tokens, and normal RAG averages only **2.2917** at **194.6** tokens.
Full history is weak on these slices (**1.6875** sufficiency at **1080.0**
tokens), and lexical LTM alone reaches **2.1458** at **101.8** tokens. Paired
bootstrap deltas favor both compact packets over normal RAG: STM recent is
**+0.3542** sufficiency with **137.2** fewer tokens, and STM+LTM is **+0.4167**
with **115.4** fewer tokens. STM+LTM also beats lexical LTM alone by **+0.5625**
while using **22.5** fewer tokens. The STM+LTM-minus-STM quality delta is small
(**+0.0625**) with a wide CI, so these later slices do not decide the gate; they
do reinforce the main human-memory claim that bounded working/short-term
continuity plus a compact LTM sidecar can beat a conventional RAG packet at a
fraction of the prompt cost.

We extended that live Cortext check with three still-later slices
(`skip=2520,2700,2880`) using the same benchmark path and settings. Under the
local Gemma 4 judge used for the previous live runs, the 48 new probes had STM
recent at **2.5000** sufficiency and **55.3** tokens, cap-4 STM+LTM at
**2.6875** and **78.5** tokens, and normal RAG at **2.4792** and **199.5**
tokens. The paired STM+LTM-minus-normal-RAG delta was **+0.2083** sufficiency
with **121.0** fewer tokens, but the approximate 95% interval crossed zero
(**[-0.0832, +0.4999]**). STM+LTM was more clearly better than lexical LTM alone
(**+0.5000**, CI **[+0.3155, +0.6845]**) while using **26.5** fewer tokens, and
better than compact full history (**+0.7292**, CI **[+0.1951, +1.2632]**) while
saving **1018.6** tokens. On the local judge, the additional farther-forward
evidence preserved the deployment-shaped conclusion that compact STM+LTM is a
strong default packet, while standalone Cortext LTM remains too weak to carry
recall by itself.

Because judge choice can bias these close comparisons, we then rebuilt the same
six later-future slices (`skip=1980..2880`) with the benchmark judge routed
through OpenAI `gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17`. This reversed the strongest quality
claim. Across 96 OpenAI-judged probes, full rolling history averaged **4.6042**
sufficiency at **1088.6** tokens, normal RAG averaged **3.7188** at **197.1**
tokens, STM+LTM averaged **2.7604** at **78.9** tokens, STM recent averaged
**1.6354** at **56.4** tokens, lexical LTM averaged **2.1771** at **103.4**
tokens, and Cortext LTM alone averaged **0.4375** at **70.3** tokens. The paired
STM+LTM-minus-normal-RAG delta was **-0.9583** sufficiency with **118.2** fewer
tokens, and the interval was entirely below zero (**[-1.1613, -0.7553]**).
OpenAI therefore does not support a quality-superiority claim for compact
STM+LTM over normal RAG. It does support a narrower and more deployable claim:
STM+LTM is the best compact non-RAG packet, clearly beats STM recent
(**+1.1250**, CI **[+0.9213, +1.3287]**) and lexical LTM (**+0.5833**, CI
**[+0.4200, +0.7467]**), and provides much better sufficiency per prompt token
than normal RAG or full history. At the time, this made the hosted-judge result
the stricter adjudication than the earlier local Gemma 4 development signal.

After the private-evaluation lock-down, hosted OpenAI judging is no longer an
allowed path for personal-chat data. This comparison remains useful as historical
evidence that judge choice can change quality conclusions, but current
reproduction and release-gating runs must use the loopback-only Ollama Gemma 4
12B judge (`gemma4:12b-it-qat`). The older local Nemotron path is retained only
as a historical development result or optional local disagreement check, not as
the primary release judge.

We then added a probe-level bootstrap over the same 64 chronological probes to
separate quality evidence from token-efficiency evidence. Compact STM `k=3`
remains a strong low-token baseline, averaging **2.7500** sufficiency at
**58.0** tokens versus normal RAG's **2.6875** sufficiency at **192.8** tokens,
but the paired STM-minus-normal-RAG sufficiency delta is only **+0.0625** with a
95% bootstrap interval of **[-0.1563, +0.2813]**. The quality-superiority claim
therefore does not clear the current evidence bar; the robust claim is that STM
matches normal RAG quality while using far fewer tokens. STM is clearly better
than the compact full-history packet in this harness (**+0.8750**, 95% CI
**[+0.3750, +1.3750]**), and compact-overlap remains only a small heuristic gain
over always-STM (**+0.0313**, 95% CI **[-0.0469, +0.1094]**). The same bootstrap
confirms that naive fact proposal should not be promoted: fact replacement and
fact union are worse than current Cortext for both `k=1` and `k=3`, with paired
deltas from **-0.8125** to **-1.3750** and intervals entirely below zero.

We then added one more chronological slice at `skip=720` using the same
benchmark shape, `build/chat_replay_goal_explore/modelroot_256`, compact STM `k=3`,
and lexical LTM top-5. This slice changes the story in a useful way: compact
full history is weak (**1.3125** sufficiency), while STM+LTM union is best on
the compact-policy surface (**2.5000**) and STM recent remains close
(**2.3125**) at lower token cost. Over the resulting five-slice, 80-probe
surface, compact STM remains the best fixed low-token packet: **2.8125**
sufficiency at **57.4** tokens. Normal RAG averages **2.7125** at **192.3**
tokens, and STM+LTM union averages **2.8000** at **77.8** tokens. The paired
STM-minus-normal-RAG delta is still small (**+0.1000**, 95% CI
**[-0.1625, +0.3375]**), so the robust claim remains quality parity plus much
better token efficiency, not decisive quality superiority. The paired
STM+LTM-minus-STM delta is essentially neutral (**-0.0125**, 95% CI
**[-0.1875, +0.1875]**), but an oracle over STM, STM+LTM, and normal RAG reaches
**3.1750** sufficiency at **81.6** tokens. The practical interpretation is that
there is headroom for a packet verifier, but neither unconditional LTM nor
simple overlap/history-budget rules have found it yet.

To check whether the continuity window should simply keep growing, we then ran
the strongest chronological slice (`skip=360`) with compact STM `k=4`:

| skip-360 packet | STM k | mean sufficiency | mean tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| compact STM recent | 3 | **3.5000** | 59.6 |
| compact STM+LTM union | 3 | 3.1875 | 77.6 |
| compact STM recent | 4 | 3.2500 | 77.3 |
| compact STM+LTM union | 4 | 3.2500 | 77.3 |
| compact normal RAG | -- | 3.3125 | 196.5 |

The fourth turn did not help. It added prompt cost and lowered sufficiency
relative to `k=3`, suggesting a practical continuity-depth knee around three
prior turns on this slice. This still needs broader chronological validation,
but it argues against unbounded "more STM is always better" prompt policy.
