ordering policy. Using the exported item-level STM rows, we compared target
rank under raw score, recency, trace score, boundary-gated score, and a simple
recency-then-raw policy. This is a shadow-only analysis over item ordering; it
does not change retrieval. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_order_policy_audit/stm_order_policy_results.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_order_policy_audit/stm_order_policy_summary.csv`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_order_policy_audit/stm_order_policy_combined.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_order_policy_audit/stm_order_policy_cases.csv`.

Target rank by ordering policy:

| policy | class | mean rank | top-1 | top-3 | top-5 | top-8 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| raw score | ordinary | 5.93 | 0.183 | 0.442 | 0.533 | 0.742 |
| raw score | delayed | 9.46 | 0.067 | 0.108 | 0.258 | 0.417 |
| recency | ordinary | 1.00 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| recency | delayed | 8.50 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.125 | 0.500 |
| trace score | ordinary | 2.96 | 0.475 | 0.742 | 0.875 | 0.942 |
| trace score | delayed | 8.71 | 0.000 | 0.108 | 0.225 | 0.517 |
| recency then raw top-4 | ordinary | 2.29 | 0.333 | 0.808 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| recency then raw top-4 | delayed | 10.98 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.075 | 0.317 |

This explains why STM looks valuable as a substrate but unsafe as a direct
surface. Ordinary continuations can be recovered by recency-like policies, but
delayed targets are buried by every simple ordering. Raw score keeps 95% of
delayed targets somewhere in the top-16, yet only 10.8% are top-3. Recency
makes ordinary continuations trivial and delayed continuations invisible.
Therefore, a useful STM design should preserve ordered item sets and vector
features for downstream attention or sequence models. It should not expose only
a top-k list chosen by recency, raw score, or trace score.

### STM Attention-Window Audit

The order-policy audit implies that the downstream consumer needs a bounded
window of ordered STM items rather than just the best few items. We therefore
measured the attention window size required to include target items under each
simple ordering policy. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_attention_window_audit/stm_attention_window_results.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_attention_window_audit/stm_attention_window_summary.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_attention_window_audit/stm_attention_window_best_delayed.csv`.

Window size needed for target inclusion:

| policy | class | coverage at 3 | coverage at 8 | coverage at 12 | coverage at 16 | window for 80% | window for 95% |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| raw score | ordinary | 0.442 | 0.742 | 0.867 | 0.983 | 10 | 16 |
| raw score | delayed | 0.108 | 0.417 | 0.700 | 0.950 | 16 | 16 |
| recency | ordinary | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1 | 1 |
| recency | delayed | 0.000 | 0.500 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 12 | 12 |
| trace score | ordinary | 0.742 | 0.942 | 0.958 | 0.983 | 4 | 10 |
| trace score | delayed | 0.108 | 0.517 | 0.817 | 0.983 | 12 | 16 |

The design implication is concrete. If STM is only used for ordinary
continuations, a tiny recency/trace window is enough. If STM is meant to help
delayed continuity, a downstream model must see roughly 12-16 ordered STM
items. Smaller top-3 or top-5 views discard most of the delayed signal before
the consumer has a chance to reason over it. This supports a shadow-DOM style
STM interface: bounded, ordered, and vector-rich, with the consumer responsible
for attention over the window.

### Projection Attention Window Sweep

We then tested whether the inclusion-window result translates into actual
consumer behavior. Using the compact projection vectors, we trained the same
source-held-out projection-attention consumer while limiting the visible STM
window to top-4, top-8, top-12, or top-16 items. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_projection_window_sweep/stm_projection_window_sweep_results.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_projection_window_sweep/stm_projection_window_sweep_summary.csv`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_projection_window_sweep/stm_projection_window_sweep_frontier.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_projection_window_sweep/stm_projection_window_sweep_scores.csv`.

Best delayed-recovery row by false-positive budget:

| FP budget | window | attention | AUC | recovery | delayed | FP mix |
|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 0% | 16 | recent | 0.7805 | 36 / 240 | 8 / 120 | 0 stale, 0 topic |
| 2% | 12 | recent | 0.7640 | 52 / 240 | 20 / 120 | 2 stale, 2 topic |
| 5% | 4 | raw score | 0.7351 | 69 / 240 | 34 / 120 | 6 stale, 6 topic |
| 10% | 16 | uniform | 0.8002 | 122 / 240 | 53 / 120 | 7 stale, 17 topic |

The window sweep shows why STM should expose an ordered window rather than a
single fixed top-k policy. Larger windows help at strict false-positive budgets:
the zero-FP and 2% delayed frontiers use windows 16 and 12. At 5% FPR, a small
top-4 raw-score window is more aggressive and recovers 34 / 120 delayed cases,
but with weaker AUC and balanced stale/topic false positives. This is not a
promotion result; it is a consumer-design constraint. The right window size
depends on the risk budget, so the substrate should retain enough ordered items
for downstream policy to choose conservatively.

### Projection Window Threshold Transfer

We then repeated the window sweep with threshold transfer. Thresholds were
trained on one dataset or chronological prefix and applied to held-out splits,
then we selected the largest train-side FP budget whose maximum held-out FP rate
stayed below the target. This asks whether the apparent top-4 5% result survives
portable calibration. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_projection_window_transfer/stm_projection_window_transfer_results.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_projection_window_transfer/stm_projection_window_transfer_summary.csv`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_projection_window_transfer/stm_projection_window_transfer_guardband.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_projection_window_transfer/stm_projection_window_transfer_frontier.csv`.

Transfer-stable window frontier:

| target transfer FP | window | attention | train FP budget | max held-out FP | aggregate recovery | aggregate delayed | FP mix |
|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 2% | 12 | recent | 0% | 0.012 | 43 | 14 | 0 stale, 2 topic |
| 5% | 12 | recent | 2% | 0.024 | 70 | 27 | 3 stale, 3 topic |
| 10% | 12 | recent | 5% | 0.094 | 103 | 46 | 10 stale, 12 topic |

The transfer audit changes the interpretation of the within-surface sweep. The
top-4 raw-score row looked attractive at 5% FPR within the same surface, but
after transfer guardbanding it recovers only 15 delayed cases at the 5% target.
Window-12 with recent attention is the stable choice across all transfer
targets, recovering 27 delayed cases at the 5% target with max held-out FP
0.024. The STM substrate should therefore retain at least a 12-item ordered
window for delayed continuity. Smaller windows are too brittle once thresholds
must transfer.

### Window-12 Recent Failure Analysis

We then inspected the transfer-stable `window=12`, recent-attention policy at
the 5% transfer target. This uses the 2% train-side guardband thresholds from
the previous experiment and reports which classes survive or fail under those
transferred thresholds. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_window12_recent_failure_analysis/stm_window12_recent_failure_results.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_window12_recent_failure_analysis/stm_window12_recent_failure_summary.csv`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_window12_recent_failure_analysis/stm_window12_recent_failure_cases.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_window12_recent_failure_analysis/stm_window12_recent_failure_examples.csv`.

Class selection under transferred thresholds:

| split | ordinary selected | delayed selected | stale FP | topic FP |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Taskmaster -> TopicalChat | 7 / 36 | 5 / 36 | 1 / 36 | 0 / 36 |
| TopicalChat -> Taskmaster | 25 / 84 | 15 / 84 | 1 / 84 | 3 / 84 |
| chronological 60/40 | 11 / 48 | 7 / 48 | 1 / 48 | 0 / 48 |

Aggregated across these transfer evaluations, the policy recovers 70 positives
but misses 125 ordinary and 141 delayed positives, while allowing only 6 false
positives (3 stale, 3 topic). The stable policy is therefore safe because it is
conservative, not because it understands delayed continuity. The false positives
are rare high-scoring stale/topic outliers; the much larger failure is missed
positives sitting just below the transferred thresholds. This confirms that the
substrate is retaining useful information, but the current projection consumer
does not extract enough of it under portable thresholds.

### Dual-Window Consumer Probe

Because the window-12 recent policy was safe but conservative, we tested a
dual-window shadow consumer that combines the stable window-12 recent score
with the more aggressive window-4 raw score. This remains a diagnostic over
already-computed STM scores and does not change production retrieval. The
artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dual_window_probe/stm_dual_window_probe_results.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dual_window_probe/stm_dual_window_probe_summary.csv`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dual_window_probe/stm_dual_window_probe_guardband.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dual_window_probe/stm_dual_window_probe_frontier.csv`.

Best safe transfer points:

| target transfer FP | score family | train FP budget | max held-out FP | recovery | delayed | FP mix |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 2% | w12 recent | 0% | 0.0119 | 43 | 14 | 0 stale, 2 topic |
| 5% | avg(w12 recent, w4 raw) | 2% | 0.0312 | 60 | 32 | 4 stale, 3 topic |
| 10% | logistic(w12, w4) | 5% | 0.0714 | 108 | 57 | 8 stale, 12 topic |

The dual-window average improves delayed recovery at the 5% transfer point
(32 delayed positives versus 27 for w12 recent) while staying below the 5%
held-out false-positive target. It does not dominate the conservative
window-12 policy overall: total recovery drops from 70 to 60 and false
positives increase from 6 to 7 at the same 5% target. At the 10% target, the
logistic dual-window probe improves delayed recovery but carries a larger
topic/stale false-positive tail. The useful result is architectural rather
than promotional: STM should expose multiple ordered-window summaries or raw
ordered items to a future consumer, because short and long windows carry
different ordinary/delayed-risk tradeoffs.

We then split-audited the 5% transfer result. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dual_window_split_audit/stm_dual_window_split_audit.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dual_window_split_audit/stm_dual_window_split_audit.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dual_window_split_audit/stm_dual_window_split_deltas.csv`.
For avg(w12 recent, w4 raw) against w12 recent at the same 5% budget, the gain
is split-specific rather than universal:

| split | recovery delta | delayed delta | false-positive delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Taskmaster -> TopicalChat | -5 | 0 | -3 |
| TopicalChat -> Taskmaster | +10 | +8 | +3 |
| chronological 60/40 | -12 | -3 | -5 |

This narrows the interpretation. Dual-window scoring can recover delayed
Taskmaster positives that the conservative window-12 consumer misses, but it
also changes the calibration tradeoff by split. That makes it useful evidence
for a richer STM read surface, not a stable consumer policy.

Finally, we audited split-local Pareto choices across the dual-window score
families. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dual_window_pareto_audit/stm_dual_window_pareto_audit.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dual_window_pareto_audit/stm_dual_window_pareto_by_split.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dual_window_pareto_audit/stm_dual_window_global_guardband_top5.csv`.
At a 5% held-out false-positive target, each split selects a different best
readout:

| split | split-local best score | recovery | delayed | FP / FPR |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| chronological 60/40 | weighted 30% w12 / 70% w4 | 23 | 11 | 4 / 0.0417 |
| Taskmaster -> TopicalChat | weighted 30% w12 / 70% w4 | 17 | 9 | 3 / 0.0417 |
| TopicalChat -> Taskmaster | avg(w12, w16 uniform) | 65 | 28 | 6 / 0.0357 |

The global guardband still chooses w12 recent at the 5% target (70 aggregate
recovery, 27 delayed, 6 false positives, max held-out FPR 0.0238). At the 10%
target, the global best shifts to avg(w12, w16 uniform) (116 recovery, 49
delayed, 16 false positives, max FPR 0.0625), while logistic(w12, w4) recovers
more delayed positives (57) at the cost of more false positives (20). This
confirms that the STM substrate has multiple useful views, but split-local
optimization is not portable enough to become a runtime policy.

We also audited objective choice directly. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_objective_tradeoff_audit/stm_objective_tradeoff_audit.json`
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_objective_tradeoff_audit/stm_objective_tradeoff_audit.csv`.
Under the same transferred false-positive targets, maximizing total recovery
and maximizing delayed recovery choose different STM readouts:

| target FPR | objective | score family | recovery | delayed | FP | max FPR |
|---:|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2% | max total | avg(w12, w16 recent) | 47 | 12 | 1 | 0.0060 |
| 2% | max delayed | w12 recent | 43 | 14 | 2 | 0.0119 |
| 5% | max total | w12 recent | 70 | 27 | 6 | 0.0238 |
| 5% | max delayed | avg(w12, w4) | 60 | 32 | 7 | 0.0312 |
| 10% | max total | avg(w12, w16 uniform) | 116 | 49 | 16 | 0.0625 |
| 10% | max delayed | logistic(w12, w4) | 108 | 57 | 20 | 0.0714 |

This reinforces the design constraint: an STM substrate can support different
read objectives, but a future consumer must declare which objective it serves
and must pass transfer guardbands for that objective. Treating "more recovery"
as a single scalar hides the ordinary/delayed tradeoff.

The marginal cost of optimizing for delayed recovery is recorded in
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_delayed_objective_cost_audit/stm_delayed_objective_cost_audit.json`
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_delayed_objective_cost_audit/stm_delayed_objective_cost_audit.csv`.
Compared with the max-total-recovery readout at each transferred FPR target,
the delayed-optimized readout changes the aggregate outcomes as follows:

| target FPR | readout change | delayed gain | ordinary delta | FP delta | total delta |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2% | avg(w12, w16 recent) -> w12 recent | +2 | -6 | +1 | -4 |
| 5% | w12 recent -> avg(w12, w4) | +5 | -15 | +1 | -10 |
| 10% | avg(w12, w16 uniform) -> logistic(w12, w4) | +8 | -16 | +4 | -8 |

Delayed recovery is therefore not free. The current score families can trade
ordinary recovery and additional false positives for delayed positives, but
they do not provide a universally better readout. This supports keeping STM as
a richer substrate while requiring downstream consumers to choose and justify
their recovery objective.

We then made the robustness criterion stricter by selecting readouts that
maximize the worst split rather than aggregate totals. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_minimax_readout_audit/stm_minimax_readout_audit.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_minimax_readout_audit/stm_minimax_readout_audit.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_minimax_readout_audit/stm_minimax_readout_candidates.csv`.

Selected readouts:

| target FPR | objective | score family | aggregate recovery | delayed | min split recovery | min split delayed | max FPR |
|---:|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2% | max worst recovery | avg(w12, w16 recent) | 47 | 12 | 8 | 3 | 0.0060 |
| 2% | max worst delayed | w12 recent | 43 | 14 | 7 | 3 | 0.0119 |
| 5% | max worst recovery | weighted 70% w12 / 30% w4 | 63 | 29 | 13 | 7 | 0.0312 |
| 5% | max aggregate recovery | w12 recent | 70 | 27 | 12 | 5 | 0.0238 |
| 10% | max worst recovery | max(w12, w4) | 103 | 44 | 23 | 11 | 0.0729 |
| 10% | max aggregate recovery | avg(w12, w16 uniform) | 116 | 49 | 21 | 9 | 0.0625 |

Worst-split optimization changes the chosen STM view. At 5%, the robust
readout sacrifices aggregate recovery (63 versus 70) but improves the weakest
split (13 versus 12) and weakest delayed split (7 versus 5). At 10%, the
robust readout again gives up aggregate recovery (103 versus 116) for better
worst-split recovery and delayed recovery. This is a further non-promotion
result: if STM is exposed, the API should preserve enough ordered-window
information for downstream consumers, but the current scalar readouts are not
stable under aggregate, delayed, and minimax objectives at the same time.

We finally computed a multi-objective regret audit over the same feasible
readouts. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_multiobjective_regret_audit/stm_multiobjective_regret_audit.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_multiobjective_regret_audit/stm_multiobjective_regret_summary.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_multiobjective_regret_audit/stm_multiobjective_regret_candidates.csv`.
The objective set was aggregate recovery, aggregate delayed recovery, worst
split recovery, worst split delayed recovery, and false positives. The
least-max-regret choices were:

| target FPR | least-regret readout | recovery | delayed | FP | min split recovery | min split delayed | max regret |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2% | avg(w12, w16 recent) | 47 | 12 | 1 | 8 | 3 | 2 |
| 5% | w12 recent | 70 | 27 | 6 | 12 | 5 | 5 |
| 10% | avg(w12, w16 uniform) | 116 | 49 | 16 | 21 | 9 | 15 |

The 2% case is close to a stable scalar choice, missing only the best delayed
aggregate by 2. The 5% and 10% cases are not close: the least-regret readout
still misses 5 delayed positives at 5%, and at 10% it misses 8 delayed
positives plus 2 worst-split delayed positives while carrying 15 extra false
positives relative to the minimum-FP feasible option. This is the clearest
scalar-readout result: STM has usable signal, but a single promoted score
cannot satisfy the competing objectives without a trained or explicitly
objective-aware consumer.

As a synthesis, we audited which primitive STM views are required to reproduce
the objective winners above. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_read_surface_requirement_audit/stm_read_surface_requirement_audit.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_read_surface_requirement_audit/stm_read_surface_requirement_winners.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_read_surface_requirement_audit/stm_read_surface_requirement_families.csv`.
Across 21 winner selections from the objective-tradeoff, minimax,
multi-objective-regret, and global-guardband audits, the winning score families
use these primitive views:

| primitive STM view | why it is needed |
|---|---|
| window4 raw | delayed-optimized and worst-split aggressive readouts |
| window12 recent | conservative 5% aggregate and least-regret readout |
| window16 recent | 2% conservative aggregate / least-regret readout |
| window16 uniform | 10% aggregate and least-regret readout |

The winning derived score families include w12 recent, avg(w12, w16 recent),
avg(w12, w16 uniform), avg(w12, w4), logistic(w12, w4), max(w12, w4), and
weighted 70% w12 / 30% w4. Therefore the read surface implied by these
experiments is not "one STM score." It is a bounded ordered/windowed STM state
from which consumers can compute short, medium, and long-window views under
their own objective and guardband. This is the most concrete substrate
requirement from the STM experiment sequence so far.

We then ablated those primitive views from the winner set. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_view_ablation_audit/stm_view_ablation_audit.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_view_ablation_audit/stm_view_ablation_by_view.csv`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_view_ablation_audit/stm_view_ablation_removed_view.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_view_ablation_audit/stm_view_ablation_coverage_sets.csv`.
Removing each view makes the following objective winners unavailable:

| removed primitive view | unavailable winners | fraction |
|---|---:|---:|
| window12 recent | 21 / 21 | 1.000 |
| window4 raw | 6 / 21 | 0.286 |
| window16 recent | 5 / 21 | 0.238 |
| window16 uniform | 4 / 21 | 0.190 |

The ablation confirms that window12 recent is the central stable view, but the
other views are not decorative. Window4 raw is needed for delayed and
worst-split aggressive objectives, window16 recent for the 2% conservative
aggregate/least-regret objective, and window16 uniform for the 10%
aggregate/least-regret objective. That argues for a compact four-view read
surface, not a single score and not an unbounded memory dump.

We then checked whether the four-view surface breaks the STM complexity budget.
The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_four_view_budget_audit/stm_four_view_budget_audit.json`
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_four_view_budget_audit/stm_four_view_budget_audit.csv`.
Window-16 support requires a larger retained STM horizon than the previously
preferred TTL12/cap24 substrate. The measured substrate tradeoff is:

| substrate | supports window16 | p95 size | p95 update us | delta p95 update | source 5% recovery | prior cost-benefit dominated |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| TTL12 / cap24 | no | 13 | 9.750 | 0.000 | 63 | no |
| TTL16 / cap32 | yes | 17 | 11.583 | +1.833 | 57 | yes |
| TTL16 / cap64 | yes | 17 | 10.208 | +0.458 | 57 | yes |

The latency/size cost of a window-16-capable substrate is small in absolute
terms: TTL16/cap64 adds 4 p95 items and 0.458 us p95 STM update latency over
TTL12/cap24. However, the old simple consumer did not improve on that larger
substrate (57 source-held-out 5% recovery versus 63 for TTL12/cap24), so the
extra horizon is justified only if STM is exposed as a multi-view substrate for
downstream consumers. It should not be interpreted as evidence that larger TTL
alone improves retrieval.

We then summarized the complexity/coverage curve for primitive STM views. The
artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_view_subset_efficiency_audit/stm_view_subset_efficiency_audit.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_view_subset_efficiency_audit/stm_view_subset_efficiency_best.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_view_subset_efficiency_audit/stm_view_subset_efficiency_all.csv`.

Best objective-winner coverage by view count:

| primitive view count | best view set | covered winners |
|---:|---|---:|
| 1 | window12 recent | 6 / 21 |
| 2 | window12 recent, window4 raw | 12 / 21 |
| 3 | window12 recent, window16 recent, window4 raw | 17 / 21 |
| 4 | window12 recent, window16 recent, window16 uniform, window4 raw | 21 / 21 |

The best two-view surface covers the stable 5% and aggressive short-window
objectives but misses the 2% and 10% long-window aggregate/least-regret
objectives. The best three-view surface still misses the 10% window16 uniform
objective family. Full objective coverage requires all four primitive views.
This makes the complexity tradeoff explicit: a one- or two-view surface may be
reasonable for a minimal implementation, but it would knowingly discard parts
of the observed STM value.

We then converted the view-count curve into implementation tiers. The artifacts
are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_read_surface_tier_audit/stm_read_surface_tier_audit.json`
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_read_surface_tier_audit/stm_read_surface_tier_audit.csv`.

| tier | primitive views | substrate | covered winners | p95 size | p95 update us | old consumer source 5% |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| minimal stable | window12 recent | TTL12/cap24 | 6 / 21 | 13 | 9.750 | 63 |
| core short/medium | window12 recent, window4 raw | TTL12/cap24 | 12 / 21 | 13 | 9.750 | 63 |
| extended long-recent | + window16 recent | TTL16/cap64 | 17 / 21 | 17 | 10.208 | 57 |
| full four-view | + window16 uniform | TTL16/cap64 | 21 / 21 | 17 | 10.208 | 57 |

The two-view core surface doubles objective coverage over the one-view surface
without increasing the retained horizon. The full four-view surface covers all
recent objective winners and costs only +4 p95 items and +0.458 us p95 STM
update latency relative to TTL12/cap24, but it depends on a substrate that was
dominated for the old simple consumer. This gives a practical implementation
choice: use the two-view surface if minimizing complexity now, or the four-view
surface if the goal is to preserve the full observed STM signal for future
consumers. Neither choice changes production retrieval until a consumer passes
transfer guardbands.

The resulting STM decision gate is captured in
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_decision_gate_audit/stm_decision_gate_audit.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_decision_gate_audit/stm_decision_gate_criteria.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_decision_gate_audit/stm_decision_gate_tiers.csv`.

| component | status | action |
|---|---|---|
| STM substrate boundedness | pass | keep as bounded shadow substrate candidate |
| STM direct retrieval consumer | blocked | do not change production retrieval |
| single scalar STM score | blocked | do not expose one score as policy |
| two-view core read surface | candidate | use for minimal shadow interface if complexity must stay TTL12 |
| four-view full read surface | candidate | preferred research substrate if preserving observed signal matters |
| larger TTL as retrieval improvement | blocked | do not argue larger TTL alone improves retrieval |
| future STM consumer | required | train/evaluate shadow-only with declared objective and transfer guardbands |

This is the current experimental stopping point. STM is justified as a bounded
substrate/read surface, not as a production retrieval consumer. The next
implementation decision should be API shape: either the minimal two-view
TTL12/cap24 surface or the full four-view TTL16/cap64 surface. Retrieval
behavior should remain unchanged until a downstream consumer passes the same
transfer and control-tail gates.

We then audited those recommended policy/threshold points by dataset and
control class. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dataset_breakdown/stm_policy_dataset_breakdown.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dataset_breakdown/stm_policy_dataset_breakdown.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dataset_breakdown/stm_policy_dataset_cases.csv`.

Source-held-out dataset breakdown:

| config | policy | threshold | Taskmaster recovery / FP | TopicalChat recovery / FP |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| conservative zero-FP | TTL8 / cap16 | 0.8271 | 27 / 168, 0 FP | 7 / 72, 0 FP |
| balanced 2% FP | TTL12 / cap24 | 0.7535 | 43 / 168, 5 FP | 8 / 72, 0 FP |
| balanced 5% FP | TTL12 / cap24 | 0.7059 | 54 / 168, 11 FP | 9 / 72, 1 FP |
| high-recall 10% FP | TTL12 / cap24 | 0.6214 | 68 / 168, 22 FP | 12 / 72, 2 FP |

Control-class breakdown:

| config | ordinary recovery | delayed recovery | stale FP | topic-shift FP |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| conservative zero-FP | 30 / 120 | 4 / 120 | 0 / 120 | 0 / 120 |
| balanced 2% FP | 40 / 120 | 11 / 120 | 0 / 120 | 5 / 120 |
| balanced 5% FP | 45 / 120 | 18 / 120 | 2 / 120 | 10 / 120 |
| high-recall 10% FP | 51 / 120 | 29 / 120 | 7 / 120 | 17 / 120 |

This breakdown sharpens the interpretation. The current STM consumer is useful
but not uniformly useful: Taskmaster carries most of the recovery, while
TopicalChat remains low-recall. The false-positive burden is mostly topic
shift, not stale same-source carryover. A future shadow consumer therefore
needs topic-shift / discourse-boundary discrimination; stale decay alone is not
the missing piece.

We then tested whether TopicalChat's low recovery was caused by weak STM signal
or by a global threshold calibrated mostly on Taskmaster. This diagnostic uses
dataset-local thresholds only to inspect score calibration; it is not a
production strategy. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dataset_local_thresholds/stm_dataset_local_thresholds.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dataset_local_thresholds/stm_dataset_local_thresholds.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_dataset_local_thresholds/stm_dataset_local_best_by_budget.csv`.

Best dataset-local policies by false-positive budget:

| dataset | FP budget | policy | recovery | false positives | precision | ordinary | delayed | threshold |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Taskmaster | 0% | TTL16 / cap32 | 28 / 168 | 0 | 1.000 | 25 | 3 | 0.8919 |
| Taskmaster | 2% | TTL16 / cap32 | 39 / 168 | 4 | 0.907 | 31 | 8 | 0.7809 |
| Taskmaster | 5% | TTL8 / cap16 | 49 / 168 | 9 | 0.845 | 33 | 16 | 0.6922 |
| Taskmaster | 10% | TTL12 / cap24 | 58 / 168 | 17 | 0.773 | 37 | 21 | 0.6832 |
| TopicalChat | 0% | TTL12 / cap24 | 8 / 72 | 0 | 1.000 | 8 | 0 | 0.7233 |
| TopicalChat | 2% | TTL12 / cap24 | 12 / 72 | 2 | 0.857 | 11 | 1 | 0.6244 |
| TopicalChat | 5% | TTL12 / cap24 | 21 / 72 | 4 | 0.840 | 15 | 6 | 0.4891 |
| TopicalChat | 10% | TTL16 / cap32 | 31 / 72 | 8 | 0.795 | 22 | 9 | 0.4343 |

This changes the diagnosis. Under the global 5% threshold, TopicalChat
recovered only 9 / 72; with a dataset-local 5% threshold, it recovers 21 / 72
at similar precision (0.840). TopicalChat therefore contains usable STM signal,
but its score scale is lower. A future shadow consumer needs calibration
features that explain corpus/domain shift without using dataset identity
directly. Candidate features include score distribution statistics, boundary
pressure, discourse entropy, source duration, and recent topic-shift indicators.

To test a dataset-free calibration feature, we normalized the TTL12/cap24
source-held-out scores within each conversation/source group. This is still a
diagnostic: the benchmark groups are not a streaming production calibrator. The
goal was only to test whether local score statistics can reduce the Taskmaster /
TopicalChat scale mismatch. The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_score_normalization/stm_score_normalization_results.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_score_normalization/stm_score_normalization_frontier.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_score_normalization/stm_score_normalization_cases.csv`.

At the 5% false-positive budget:

| score | recovery | precision | Taskmaster recovery | TopicalChat recovery | stale FP | topic FP |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| raw calibrated score | 63 / 240 | 0.840 | 54 | 9 | 2 | 10 |
| source-centered | 60 / 240 | 0.833 | 42 | 18 | 4 | 8 |
| source z-score | 61 / 240 | 0.836 | 46 | 15 | 3 | 9 |
| source percentile | 62 / 240 | 0.838 | 48 | 14 | 3 | 9 |
| source robust z | 43 / 240 | 0.782 | 26 | 17 | 5 | 7 |

At zero false positives:

| score | recovery | Taskmaster recovery | TopicalChat recovery |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| raw calibrated score | 31 / 240 | 24 | 7 |
| source-centered | 24 / 240 | 13 | 11 |
| source z-score | 27 / 240 | 16 | 11 |
| source robust z | 13 / 240 | 5 | 8 |

The diagnostic does not beat the raw score on total recovery, but it improves
domain balance. At 5% FP, source-centering doubles TopicalChat recovery (9 to
18) while reducing Taskmaster recovery (54 to 42) and keeping precision similar.
This suggests the future consumer should include local score-distribution
features alongside the raw calibrated score, then let held-out calibration
decide when normalization is helpful.

We then tested fixed, training-free score combinations over the TTL12/cap24
scores to see whether local normalization can complement the raw calibrated
score. Features were standardized using control-score statistics only in this
diagnostic; no dataset identity or production retrieval path was used. The
artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_score_ensemble/stm_score_ensemble_results.json`
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_score_ensemble/stm_score_ensemble_frontier.csv`.

At the 5% false-positive budget:

| score | recovery | precision | Taskmaster recovery | TopicalChat recovery | delayed recovery | stale FP | topic FP |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| raw calibrated | 63 / 240 | 0.840 | 54 | 9 | 18 | 2 | 10 |
| source-centered | 60 / 240 | 0.833 | 42 | 18 | 15 | 4 | 8 |
| max(raw, centered) | 63 / 240 | 0.840 | 47 | 16 | 17 | 2 | 10 |
| avg(raw, centered) | 60 / 240 | 0.833 | 47 | 13 | 15 | 4 | 8 |
| avg(raw, source z) | 60 / 240 | 0.833 | 48 | 12 | 16 | 4 | 8 |
| avg(raw, source percentile) | 65 / 240 | 0.844 | 53 | 12 | 18 | 2 | 10 |

At the 2% false-positive budget:

| score | recovery | precision | Taskmaster recovery | TopicalChat recovery | delayed recovery | stale FP | topic FP |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| raw calibrated | 51 / 240 | 0.911 | 43 | 8 | 11 | 0 | 5 |
| source-centered | 46 / 240 | 0.902 | 31 | 15 | 10 | 1 | 4 |
| max(raw, centered) | 51 / 240 | 0.911 | 38 | 13 | 10 | 1 | 4 |
| avg(raw, centered) | 54 / 240 | 0.915 | 42 | 12 | 11 | 0 | 5 |
| avg(raw, source percentile) | 51 / 240 | 0.911 | 42 | 9 | 12 | 0 | 5 |

This is a modest but useful result. Fixed combinations do not eliminate the
domain shift, but they show local distribution features can complement the raw
score. At 5% FP, `avg(raw, source percentile)` improves total recovery from 63
to 65 without reducing precision. At 2% FP, `avg(raw, centered)` improves
recovery from 51 to 54 and slightly improves precision. The next real consumer
should therefore train or calibrate over raw score plus source-local
distribution features, rather than choosing one score family manually.

We then made the calibration test stricter. Instead of choosing thresholds on
the evaluation set, we trained / calibrated on one split and transferred the
thresholds to a held-out dataset or chronological holdout. This used no dataset
identity at runtime, but the diagnostic reports dataset-held-out failure modes.
The artifacts are
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_consumer_transfer/stm_consumer_transfer_results.json`
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_consumer_transfer/stm_consumer_transfer_results.csv`.

At the nominal 5% false-positive budget:

| transfer | score | recovery | false positives | precision | observed FPR |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| train TopicalChat -> test Taskmaster | raw | 105 / 168 | 65 / 168 | 0.618 | 0.387 |
| train TopicalChat -> test Taskmaster | avg(raw, percentile) | 60 / 168 | 15 / 168 | 0.800 | 0.089 |
| train TopicalChat -> test Taskmaster | logistic local features | 68 / 168 | 21 / 168 | 0.764 | 0.125 |
| train Taskmaster -> test TopicalChat | raw | 8 / 72 | 0 / 72 | 1.000 | 0.000 |
| train Taskmaster -> test TopicalChat | avg(raw, percentile) | 10 / 72 | 1 / 72 | 0.909 | 0.014 |
| train Taskmaster -> test TopicalChat | logistic local features | 13 / 72 | 2 / 72 | 0.867 | 0.028 |
| chronological 60/40 | raw | 26 / 96 | 3 / 96 | 0.897 | 0.031 |
| chronological 60/40 | avg(raw, percentile) | 28 / 96 | 7 / 96 | 0.800 | 0.073 |
| chronological 60/40 | logistic local features | 24 / 96 | 5 / 96 | 0.828 | 0.052 |

At nominal zero false positives:

| transfer | score | recovery | false positives | precision | observed FPR |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| train TopicalChat -> test Taskmaster | raw | 48 / 168 | 9 / 168 | 0.842 | 0.054 |
| train TopicalChat -> test Taskmaster | avg(raw, percentile) | 41 / 168 | 4 / 168 | 0.911 | 0.024 |
| train TopicalChat -> test Taskmaster | logistic local features | 28 / 168 | 2 / 168 | 0.933 | 0.012 |
| train Taskmaster -> test TopicalChat | raw | 7 / 72 | 0 / 72 | 1.000 | 0.000 |
| train Taskmaster -> test TopicalChat | avg(raw, percentile) | 8 / 72 | 0 / 72 | 1.000 | 0.000 |
| train Taskmaster -> test TopicalChat | logistic local features | 8 / 72 | 0 / 72 | 1.000 | 0.000 |
| chronological 60/40 | raw | 12 / 96 | 0 / 96 | 1.000 | 0.000 |
| chronological 60/40 | avg(raw, percentile) | 14 / 96 | 0 / 96 | 1.000 | 0.000 |
| chronological 60/40 | logistic local features | 12 / 96 | 0 / 96 | 1.000 | 0.000 |

This is the strongest caution so far. Local features improve some transfers,
but threshold calibration is not stable across datasets. Training on TopicalChat
and testing on Taskmaster badly violates the intended false-positive budget for
the raw score. The fixed ensemble and logistic local-feature consumer reduce
that damage, but they do not make the budget reliable. The next STM consumer
must therefore report threshold transfer, not just within-surface budget
frontiers, before it can be treated as a safe shadow candidate.

## STM-Conditioned Anchor Attention Rerun

We then reran the anchor-attention question using the proposed STM substrate
instead of a special anchor model. This is a benchmark-only diagnostic; it
does not change production retrieval. The command was:

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_anchor_replay_bench \
  --stm-attention-anchor-shadow-only \
  --models=models \
  --output-dir build/stm_attention_anchor_shadow_ttl16_cap64_full
```

This pass builds `STM_before_t` chronologically with the proposed TTL16/cap64
substrate, then evaluates attention readouts over `window4_raw`,
`window12_recent`, `window16_recent`, `window16_uniform`, the core two-view
surface, and the proposed four-view surface. The artifacts are
`build/stm_attention_anchor_shadow_ttl16_cap64_full/stm_attention_anchor_results.json`,
`build/stm_attention_anchor_shadow_ttl16_cap64_full/stm_attention_anchor_ablation.csv`,
`build/stm_attention_anchor_shadow_ttl16_cap64_full/stm_attention_anchor_scores.csv`,
and
`build/stm_attention_anchor_shadow_ttl16_cap64_full/stm_attention_anchor_failure_examples.csv`.

| STM attention view | target/control AUC | inverted AUC | target top-3 | zero-FPR recovery | 5% FPR recovery |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| window4 raw | 0.1185 | 0.8815 | 97 / 240 | 1 / 240 | 6 / 240 |
| window12 recent | 0.1371 | 0.8629 | 90 / 240 | 2 / 240 | 10 / 240 |
| window16 recent | 0.1372 | 0.8628 | 90 / 240 | 2 / 240 | 10 / 240 |
| window16 uniform | 0.1216 | 0.8784 | 83 / 240 | 2 / 240 | 6 / 240 |
| core two-view | 0.1342 | 0.8658 | 93 / 240 | 2 / 240 | 10 / 240 |
| proposed four-view | 0.1348 | 0.8652 | 89 / 240 | 2 / 240 | 10 / 240 |
| proposed four-view + entropy/margin gate | 0.1536 | 0.8464 | 89 / 240 | 2 / 240 | 10 / 240 |

The matching 120-case repaired anchor-attention baseline remained stronger:
direct hierarchical attention had delayed AUC 0.589 with 1 / 36 zero-FPR
recovery, and the attention readouts recovered 4-5 / 36 low-FPR cases. The
STM-conditioned attention run is therefore a negative result for replacing the
special anchor-model question with STM attention alone.

The failure mode is the same one seen in earlier STM consumer probes. STM
contains useful recent evidence, but topic-shift and stale controls can attract
strong attention mass. The proposed STM surface is still useful as a bounded
read substrate, but attention over STM by itself is not a safe commitment
mechanism.

## Current STM Experimental Decision

The latest STM decision gate is recorded in
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_decision_gate_audit/stm_decision_gate_audit.json`,
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_decision_gate_audit/stm_decision_gate_criteria.csv`,
and
`build/short_term_memory_processor_shadow_stm_decision_gate_audit/stm_decision_gate_tiers.csv`.

| component | status |
|---|---|
| bounded STM substrate | pass |
| direct retrieval consumer | blocked |
| single scalar STM score | blocked |
| two-view core read surface | candidate |
| four-view full read surface | candidate |
| larger TTL as retrieval improvement | blocked |
| future consumer | required, shadow-only |

STM is experimentally justified as a bounded internal substrate/read surface.
It is not justified as a production retrieval consumer. The practical API
choice is between a minimal two-view TTL12/cap24 surface (window12 recent and
window4 raw) and a full four-view TTL16/cap64 surface that also exposes
window16 recent and window16 uniform. Production retrieval should remain
unchanged until a downstream consumer declares its objective and passes
transfer guardbands.

## ESS-AIST Preview Runtime Smoke

We added benchmark-only support for the first preview checkpoint,
`augmem/ESS-AIST-81M-preview-GGUF`. This is not an anchor-head checkpoint from
Cortext's point of view: the GGUF exposes a triembed semantic output but no
AAIT `anchor_key`, `anchor_action_logits`, `anchor_confidence`, or
`salience_delta` tensors. The integration therefore treats it as an embedding
slice model, not as an ingress-anchor model, and production retrieval remains
unchanged.

The preview contract is a 1536-dimensional vector split into three normalized
512-dimensional views:

| view | dimensions | intended diagnostic use |
|---|---:|---|
| semantic | 0:512 | normal semantic retrieval |
| subject | 512:1024 | subject/person/place/object continuity |
| event | 1024:1536 | event/situation continuity |
| prefix 1024 | 0:1024 | semantic + subject |
| prefix 1536 | 0:1536 | semantic + subject + event |

The runtime smoke command was:

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_anchor_replay_bench \
  --ess-aist-runtime-smoke \
  --models=models \
  --output-dir build/ess_aist_runtime_smoke
```

Artifacts:

- `build/ess_aist_runtime_smoke/ess_aist_runtime_smoke.json`
- `build/ess_aist_runtime_smoke/ess_aist_runtime_latency.json`
- `build/ess_aist_runtime_smoke/ess_aist_model_metadata.json`
- `build/ess_aist_runtime_smoke/ess_aist_gguf_tensor_name_audit.json`

Result:

- native GGUF triembed execution succeeded;
- output dimension: `1536`;
- semantic, subject, and event slice dimensions: `512` each;
- all emitted view norms were finite and approximately `1.0`;
- q8_0 is now the preferred checkpoint for ESS-AIST preview smoke runs;
- single-sample native Eigen fallback inference latency in the current debug
  build was `446.66 ms` after model load;
- the optimized native path now uses the custom GGUF parser plus a full GGML
  text graph, bypassing the installed llama.cpp tensor-name loader failure for
  the preview checkpoint while keeping attention, layer norms, pooling,
  projection, and L2 normalization inside backend graph execution;
- the verified local kernel backend was `MTL0 (Apple M3 Max)`;
- single-sample latency with the incremental ggml/Metal dense-kernel path was
  `216.47 ms` after model load;
- full-graph parity against the old per-linear debug path passed on the same
  Jared reference sentence: cosine `1.000000`, L2 diff `0.000589`, max absolute
  diff `0.000056`, and both output norms `1.000000`. The old per-linear debug
  path took `145.25 ms`; the full graph first measured call took `10.62 ms`;
- a sequential fair cache-miss comparison against the regular LEAF-IR q8 path
  used `cortext_text_encoder_bench --vary-text` with the same Jared reference
  sentence, 10 warmup rows, and 100 measured rows. Regular LEAF-IR
  (`models/llama_cpp/mdbr-leaf-ir-q8_0.gguf`) produced 256d embeddings at
  `3.24 ms` mean latency (`309.02` embeddings/s). ESS-AIST q8 produced 1536d
  embeddings through the full GGML graph at `2.28 ms` mean latency (`438.60`
  embeddings/s);
- the runtime smoke now reports `kernel_ops_granularity = full_text_graph`,
  `slice_benchmark_ready = true`, and single-sample inference `7.07 ms`;
- the 25-case ESS-AIST slice shadow run completed without debug overrides in
  `10.66 s` with `1596` uncached semantic requests. This is sweep-ready from a
  runtime standpoint, but it remains benchmark-only;
- on that 25-case slice, target ordering improved but commitment did not:
  repaired-real hierarchical attention over the subject slice reached target
  AUC `0.9870`, top-1 `0.8824`, and top-3 `1.0000`, while no-anchor AUC stayed
  near chance (`0.4787`) and wrong-active rejection remained poor (`0.1144`);
- the GGUF tensor audit found `999` tensors and confirmed `architecture =
  triembed`;
- no anchor-head tensors were present, so this run is embedding-slice readiness
  only.

We also added `--ess-aist-anchor-slice-shadow-only`, which evaluates
`semantic_key`, `subject_key`, `event_key`, `full_key`, and the 512/1024/1536
prefixes on the repaired real replay plus hard-synthetic v3 surfaces. This mode
now requires the full-text GGML graph by default. The native Eigen fallback
remains available only for debug shape checks via
`CORTEXT_ESS_AIST_ALLOW_EIGEN_FALLBACK=1`; it is too slow and should not be used
for replay evidence. The incremental per-linear ggml kernel path is also
debug-only and must be explicitly forced with
`CORTEXT_AAIT_DISABLE_FULL_GGML_GRAPH=1` plus
`CORTEXT_ESS_AIST_ALLOW_INCREMENTAL_GGML_KERNELS=1`. A direct llama.cpp
kernel-backed probe on
`ESS-AIST-81M_q8_0.gguf` still fails before execution because the installed
loader rejects one of the preview tensor names (`64 >= 64`), so the next
engineering task is no longer basic text speed; it is larger slice sweeps and
consumer ablations over the semantic/subject/event views.

Interpretation: ESS-AIST is now a high-performance benchmark runtime, not a
shape-only preview. The previous 50x slowdown was an implementation artifact of
the per-linear debug graph path. The full graph makes ESS-AIST comparable to the
regular LEAF-IR q8 path while producing a 1536d semantic/subject/event vector.
The first slice run does **not** show anchor readiness: it improves target
reachability but leaves no-anchor and wrong-active commitment unresolved. Any
promotion decision must continue to use no-anchor and wrong-active rejection,
zero-FPR recovery, and low-FPR recovery as primary metrics, not target AUC
alone.

### ESS-AIST Ingress-Native Shadow Ledger

Because ESS-AIST is designed for ingress rather than retrieval-time reranking,
we then replaced the slice/rerank diagnostic with an ingress-native shadow
ledger:

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_anchor_replay_bench \
  --ess-aist-ingress-anchor-shadow-only \
  --models=models \
  --output-dir build/ess_aist_ingress_anchor_shadow_full
```

For each repaired case, the benchmark replays the source conversation
chronologically up to the held-out current ingress step. Each prior signal is
encoded once and used to update separate shadow ledgers over:

| learned slice | dimensions | ingress role |
|---|---:|---|
| semantic_key | 0:512 | ordinary semantic continuity / diagnostic |
| subject_key | 512:1024 | provisional subject/person/place/object tracks |
| event_key | 1024:1536 | provisional episode/context tracks |

The runtime ledger does **not** see retrieval candidates. It does not receive
candidate labels, target flags, track ids, gold actions, or candidate classes.
Those fields are used only after chronological replay to audit whether the
pre-current ledger had formed the right state.

The full repaired-surface run covered `270` reference cases and `151`
no-anchor controls. It used `5220` uncached ESS-AIST view-cache entries and
completed in `16.25 s` with `kernel_ops_granularity = full_text_graph`.

Ingress-native results were negative:

| policy | target subject existed before current | safe target selected | no-anchor abstain | wrong-active distinct before current | zero-FPR | 5% FPR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| subject_only_loose | 1.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0/270 | 0/270 |
| subject_only_strict | 1.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0/270 | 0/270 |
| event_only | 1.000 | 0.000 | 0.026 | 0.000 | 0/270 | 0/270 |
| subject_event_agreement | 1.000 | 0.000 | 0.020 | 0.000 | 0/270 | 0/270 |
| subject_event_high_split | 1.000 | 0.004 | 0.119 | 0.015 | 0/270 | 0/270 |
| subject_event_very_strict | 1.000 | 0.007 | 0.278 | 0.026 | 0/270 | 0/270 |

This is the right failure mode to see from an ingress test. The target subject
track almost always exists before the held-out current signal, which means the
ingress ledger is not losing reachability. The failure is that wrong-active
turns are usually attached to the same subject track as the target. Earlier
diagnostics could accidentally count such a merged track as a target hit; the
ingress benchmark now treats that as unsafe and requires the selected target
track to be distinct from the wrong-active track.

Interpretation: evaluating ESS-AIST at ingress was the right correction, but the
preview checkpoint still does not solve anchoring as a pure vector-similarity
ledger. The subject/event blocks preserve broad stream continuity, not
human-level subject identity under wrong-active competition. This does not
invalidate the ESS-AIT vector contract, but the next checkpoint needs explicit
training/evaluation for subject-track splitting, no-match abstention,
wrong-active separation, and stale event closure. Cortext should not promote the
preview slices as an anchor mechanism from target reachability alone.

branch or tag; the repository only advertised `main`. The current `main`

`ess_aist_full_v9_subjectfix_l4k/best_model.pt`, so we downloaded it into a

`models/ESS-AIST-81M-preview-GGUF-v9/ESS-AIST-81M_q8_0.gguf`. The q8 artifact

This covered `270` references and `151` no-anchor controls, used `5220`

| policy | safe target selected | no-anchor abstain | wrong-active distinct | selected wrong-active | zero-FPR | 5% FPR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| subject_only_loose | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 1.000 | 0/270 | 0/270 |
| subject_only_strict | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.989 | 0/270 | 0/270 |

Relative to the earlier preview checkpoint, v9 improves the strict split and

`0.289`, and no-anchor abstention rises from `0.278` to `0.437` under the
strictest policy. It still does not pass the anchor gate. Safe target selection
is only `0.026`, zero-FPR recovery remains `0`, and 5 percent FPR recovery is
only `2 / 270`.

The v9 slice/rerank diagnostic also shows reachability without commitment:

| score family | best repaired-real view | target AUC | top-1 | top-3 | no-anchor AUC | wrong-active rejection AUC | zero-FPR | 5% FPR |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline retrieval | subject key | 0.5943 | 0.1259 | 0.2778 | 0.5212 | 0.4047 | 0 | 0 |
| micro-anchor | subject key | 0.6928 | 0.1556 | 0.4074 | 0.5015 | 0.1981 | 0 | 2 |
| hierarchical attention | semantic key | 0.7394 | 0.2667 | 0.4593 | 0.5151 | 0.2097 | 0 | 0 |
| latent ranker only | subject key | 0.8231 | 0.3370 | 0.6222 | 0.5017 | 0.1491 | 0 | 0 |

Interpretation: v9 confirms that the model-side subject/event training improved
offline subject and event geometry, and it helps the ingress split/abstain curve
relative to the first preview. The repaired replay still fails safe commitment:
no-anchor and wrong-active remain near the historical failure surface, and
low-FPR recovery is effectively absent. ESS-AIST v9 therefore remains
benchmark-only.

### ESS-AIST v9 Ingress Subject/Event Attention

We next tested whether a transformer-like ingress attention consumer over the
frozen v9 subject and event slices could avoid a special anchor head. This is a
different experiment from retrieval-time attention. The benchmark replays each
conversation chronologically, forms causal prior-track tokens from ESS-AIST
subject/event slices, and lets the current ingress signal attend over those
prior subject/event states. It still does not use retrieval candidates, target
ids, candidate classes, track labels, or future labels at runtime.

The command was:

```bash
CORTEXT_AAIT_REQUIRE_FULL_GGML_GRAPH=1 ./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_anchor_replay_bench \
  --ess-aist-ingress-attention-shadow-only \
  --models=models \
  --teacher-model models/ESS-AIST-81M-preview-GGUF-v9/ESS-AIST-81M_q8_0.gguf \
  --output-dir build/ess_aist_v9_ingress_attention_shadow_full
```

The ablation included separate subject/event attention, cross-event agreement
penalties, entropy and margin split gates, and joint subject+event keys. The
full repaired-surface run covered `270` references and `151` no-anchor controls,
used `5220` ESS-AIST view-cache entries, completed in `21.86 s`, and used the
Metal full-text graph.

| policy | safe target selected | no-anchor abstain | wrong-active distinct | selected wrong-active | zero-FPR | 5% FPR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| attention_loose | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 1.000 | 0/270 | 0/270 |
| attention_cross_split | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 1.000 | 0/270 | 0/270 |
| attention_very_strict | 0.004 | 0.040 | 0.030 | 0.937 | 0/270 | 0/270 |
| joint_attention_cross_split | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.993 | 0/270 | 0/270 |
| joint_attention_very_strict | 0.004 | 0.060 | 0.044 | 0.911 | 0/270 | 0/270 |
| joint_attention_ultra_split | 0.000 | 0.993 | 1.000 | 0.004 | 0/270 | 0/270 |

The result is a clear negative. Loose attention preserves broad continuity but
selects wrong-active on nearly every reference. Ultra-strict joint subject/event
attention creates distinct tracks and abstains on almost all no-anchor controls,
but it also loses all safe target binding. In other words, attention over frozen
ESS-AIST subject/event slices moves along the same split-versus-bind tradeoff as
the cosine ledger; it does not create the missing human subject anchor by
itself. The next defensible path is either a learned ingress attention adapter
over frozen ESS-AIST slices or a future embedding checkpoint trained directly on
bind/no-bind, wrong-active, and no-anchor subject continuity cases.

### ES-AIST-81M Preview GGUF

We then tested `augmem/ES-AIST-81M-preview-GGUF`, whose model card reports a
different contract from ESS-AIST v9. ES-AIST should not be interpreted as a
three-way 512d semantic/subject/event embedding. Its release metrics use a 768d
semantic prefix and a 768d entity tail:

| view | dimensions | intended use |
|---|---:|---|
| semantic_768_key | 0:768 | semantic retrieval |
| entity_key | 768:1536 | entity/subject continuity |
| full_key | 0:1536 | full embedding |

The first smoke proved that the GGUF executed, but the old ESS 3 x 512 slice
contract was wrong for this model. The benchmark was therefore patched to expose
`semantic_768_key`, `entity_key`, and `prefix_768`; ingress tests now use the
entity key as the identity track. The third ingress view is the full 1536d key,
not an independently trained event block.

The downloaded q8 file is
`models/ES-AIST-81M-preview-GGUF/ES-AIST-81M_q8_0.gguf`, SHA-256
`3c77c5aa277c1041c325723d47221970686ec0194b0aa59f3617a7f1192a5699`. The source
checkpoint in the manifest is
`es_aist_full_v13_anchor_memory_eventboost_er125_bs4096_nw0_l4b/best_model.pt`.

The release metadata is strong:

| metric | value |
|---|---:|
| entity same/different AUC | 0.9953 |
| same-topic different-entity rejection AUC | 0.9953 |
| same-entity different-event rejection AUC | 0.8001 |
| stale same-source rejection AUC | 0.9241 |
| wrong-active rejection AUC | 0.8799 |
| weak-reference entity candidate R@1 | 1.0000 |
| anchor-memory entity candidate R@1 | 0.9647 |

Runtime smoke used the Metal full graph:

```bash
CORTEXT_AAIT_REQUIRE_FULL_GGML_GRAPH=1 ./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_anchor_replay_bench \
  --ess-aist-runtime-smoke \
  --models=models \
  --teacher-model models/ES-AIST-81M-preview-GGUF/ES-AIST-81M_q8_0.gguf \
  --output-dir build/es_aist_runtime_smoke_q8_contract
```

The smoke passed with 1536d output, finite normalized 768d semantic/entity
views, `kernel_ops_granularity = full_text_graph`, backend
`MTL0 (Apple M3 Max)`, and `7.08 ms` single-sample inference.

We then promoted the runtime from a text-only smoke path to the engine's native
trimodal signal encoder. ES-AIST q8 now executes text, image, and audio through
GGUF tensors and GGML backend kernels. Text uses the full LEAF-IR-style graph.
Image uses the native image encoder/projection graph after 384 x 384 RGB
ImageNet-style preprocessing. Audio uses the native audio encoder/projection
graph after converting public 16 kHz mono PCM ingress into the model's 32 kHz,
128 x 1000 log-mel input. No Python, safetensors helper, or Eigen fallback is
used for normal execution.

The engine preserves the existing compact retrieval/storage shape by taking a
normalized 256d retrieval view when the encoder emits a larger vector. It also
attaches the normalized full 1536d ES vector to the ingress signal for Soft
Anchor formation. GGML backend loading is process-wide and idempotent so ES-AIST
can coexist with AAIT, LFM, and EmbeddingGemma paths without repeated backend
registration. Internal consolidation signals no longer insert or evict
working-memory chat slots, which keeps consolidation from perturbing the
visible chat tail while still driving consolidation jobs.

Verification:

```bash
cmake --build build -j 8 --target cortext_tests
./build/tests/cortext_tests "ES-AIST GGUF executes native text image and audio kernels" -s
./build/tests/cortext_tests "AAIT encoder load executes native triembed inference" -s
./build/tests/cortext_tests "Integration: scripted chat preserves turn-shaped working memory" -s
./build/tests/cortext_tests "Integration: scripted chat consolidation preserves prompt shape and graph integrity" -s
ctest --test-dir build -R cortext_tests --output-on-failure
cmake --build build -j 8 --target cortext_chat
```

The ES-AIST test verifies `architecture=triembed`, output dimension `1536`,
native runtime availability, corrected `semantic_768_key` and `entity_key`
slices, and finite unit-norm embeddings for text, image, and audio. The verbose
run shows GGML/Metal kernels for text attention/projection, image
im2col/convolution/pooling/projection, and audio convolution/activation
/pooling/projection.

| policy | safe target selected | no-anchor abstain | wrong-active distinct | selected wrong-active | zero-FPR | 5% FPR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

Correct-contract slice/rerank diagnostic on repaired replay:

| score family | best view | target AUC | top-1 | top-3 | no-anchor AUC | wrong-active rejection AUC | zero-FPR | 5% FPR |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline retrieval | semantic 768 | 0.5528 | 0.1074 | 0.2667 | 0.5401 | 0.4278 | 0 | 0 |
| micro-anchor | semantic 768 | 0.6740 | 0.1963 | 0.4444 | 0.5096 | 0.2364 | 0 | 2 |
| hierarchical attention | semantic 768 | 0.7219 | 0.2000 | 0.4444 | 0.5187 | 0.2263 | 0 | 0 |

Interpretation: ES-AIST has substantially better entity/rejection metadata than
ESS-AIST v9 and improves strict ingress split behavior, but it still does not
solve safe anchoring on the repaired Cortext replay. The best plain ingress
policy selected the safe target in only `0.093` of references. The strictest
useful policy abstained on `0.517` of no-anchor controls and split wrong-active
in `0.581` of references, but safe target selection dropped to `0.048`.
Low-FPR recovery remained zero. Attention over the corrected entity/full views
did not escape the same split-versus-bind tradeoff. These direct anchor-policy
benchmarks remain diagnostic only: ES-AIST is useful as a trimodal signal
encoder, but it is not a standalone hard anchor resolver, and retrieval ranking
is not changed by the anchor experiments.

### ES-AIST as Signal + WM/STM/LTM Context

The previous ES-AIST runs still implicitly asked the embedding model to behave
like a standalone anchor-binding policy. That is the wrong contract. ES-AIST
does not know the stream state by itself; it emits semantic/entity signals. The
engine must combine those signals with working memory, short-term memory, long
term candidate memory, recency, active-state, thresholding, and abstention
logic.

We added a benchmark-only contextual policy surface:

```bash
CORTEXT_AAIT_REQUIRE_FULL_GGML_GRAPH=1 ./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_anchor_replay_bench \
  --es-aist-contextual-anchor-shadow-only \
  --models=models \
  --teacher-model models/ES-AIST-81M-preview-GGUF/ES-AIST-81M_q8_0.gguf \
  --output-dir build/es_aist_contextual_anchor_shadow_full_contract
```

This mode treats ES-AIST as a signal source only. For each current ingress
signal it builds features over:

- `semantic_key = z[0:768]`
- `entity_key = z[768:1536]`
- `full_key = z[0:1536]`
- working-memory prior turns
- STM prior turns
- LTM candidate memories
- recency/source/window metadata
- WM/STM/LTM attention support, entropy, and margins

The run covered `421` repaired replay cases with `7696` candidate feature rows.
It used the Metal full graph (`MTL0`, Apple M3 Max) and completed in `25.81 s`.
Production retrieval remained unchanged.

| policy | target AUC | top-1 | top-3 | no-anchor AUC | wrong-active rejection AUC | stale rejection AUC | zero-FPR | 5% FPR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| semantic signal only | 0.5528 | 0.1074 | 0.2667 | 0.5401 | 0.4278 | 0.4833 | 0 | 0 |
| entity signal only | 0.5463 | 0.1148 | 0.2630 | 0.5338 | 0.4301 | 0.4812 | 0 | 0 |
| full signal only | 0.5505 | 0.1074 | 0.2593 | 0.5375 | 0.4283 | 0.4819 | 0 | 0 |
| entity + STM context | 0.5762 | 0.1407 | 0.2926 | 0.5248 | 0.4034 | 0.4773 | 0 | 0 |
| WM/STM/LTM attention | 0.6185 | 0.1481 | 0.3519 | 0.5268 | 0.3574 | 0.4704 | 0 | 1 |
| learned context policy, all-fit | 0.8579 | 0.3630 | 0.6741 | 0.4895 | 0.0219 | 0.6443 | 3 | 10 |
| learned context policy, delayed prequential | 0.8581 | 0.3667 | 0.6481 | 0.5001 | 0.0216 | 0.7424 | 2 | 7 |
| learned context policy, source-held-out | 0.7837 | 0.2444 | 0.6519 | 0.4860 | 0.0149 | 0.5958 | 0 | 0 |

Interpretation: adding WM/STM/LTM attention improves reachability over raw ES
slices, and a lightweight learned context policy can recover much more target
signal. However, wrong-active rejection collapses under the learned policies,
especially source-held-out. The source-held-out learned policy produced target
AUC `0.7837` and top-3 `0.6519`, but wrong-active rejection AUC was only
`0.0149` and low-FPR recovery stayed at zero. This means ES-AIST is useful as a
candidate/entity signal, but the current engine policy is not sufficient for
safe human-subject anchoring.

The policy-vs-signal audit separates the failures. Under the source-held-out
context policy, `66` reference cases had a useful signal where the target was
top-3 and separated from stale/wrong-active, but the calibrated policy still
abstained. Another `204` reference cases remained signal-ambiguous or bad, most
often because a wrong-active candidate scored slightly above the target.
Seven controls remained high-scoring false-bind risks and likely need explicit
no-anchor/boundary calibration.

This result reframes the next step. ES-AIST should not be promoted as an anchor
policy. It is a signal model that can feed an engine-owned policy. The next
engine-side experiment should train a small policy over ES signal features plus
causal WM/STM/LTM state with a direct wrong-active/no-anchor objective, rather
than relying on direct thresholds or generic target ranking loss.

#### Two-stage attention retrieval + safety commit

We then split the contextual policy into the architecture we actually want:

1. **Attention retrieval:** use ES semantic/entity/full signals over WM, STM,
   and LTM candidates to propose top-k anchors.
2. **Safety commit:** evaluate only the proposed top-k candidates using margins,
   memory-tier agreement, recency, source continuity, active-track competition,
   and boundary/no-anchor pressure; then bind or abstain.

The same run writes:

- `es_aist_attention_retrieval_stage1.csv`
- `es_aist_safety_commit_stage2.csv`
- `es_aist_two_stage_attention_safety_examples.csv`

Stage 1 confirms that attention over memory state is useful for recall:

| stage-1 policy | top-1 | top-3 | top-5 | selected wrong-active | selected stale | selected remote |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| semantic key | 0.1074 | 0.2667 | 0.3741 | 0.3563 | 0.1401 | 0.1259 |
| entity key | 0.1148 | 0.2630 | 0.3704 | 0.3515 | 0.1283 | 0.1283 |
| full key | 0.1074 | 0.2593 | 0.3852 | 0.3682 | 0.1425 | 0.1354 |
| WM/STM/LTM attention | 0.1481 | 0.3519 | 0.5000 | 0.5416 | 0.1093 | 0.0214 |

The attention layer raises target recall, especially top-5, and suppresses
remote candidates. However, it over-selects wrong-active recent candidates. This
is an acceptable retrieval-layer behavior only if the next layer is a strong
safety gate.

Stage 2 shows the current safety head is not yet good enough:

| safety policy | safe target selected | no-anchor abstain | selected wrong-active | target AUC | top-3 | wrong-active rejection AUC | zero-FPR | 5% FPR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| all-fit top-5 safety | 0.0037 | 0.9536 | 0.0000 | 0.6187 | 0.2481 | 0.3883 | 0 | 3 |
| delayed-prequential top-5 safety | 0.0296 | 0.9536 | 0.0185 | 0.6437 | 0.4000 | 0.3362 | 2 | 8 |
| source-held-out top-5 safety | 0.0000 | 0.9536 | 0.0037 | 0.5833 | 0.1296 | 0.3817 | 0 | 0 |

This is the expected failure mode for an early safety layer: it blocks most
no-anchor and wrong-active commits, but it also blocks nearly all safe binds.
The examples show both sides: several wrong-active top-1 attention selections
are prevented by safety, while several target-in-top-5 cases are incorrectly
abstained. The architecture direction remains correct, but the safety head needs
better calibration/training. The next policy experiment should train a commit
head directly on top-k ES+WM/STM/LTM features with explicit objectives for:
safe target bind, no-anchor abstain, wrong-active split/reject, and stale
closure/reject. Target ranking should remain Stage 1's job.

We then ran that next commit-head ablation by replacing the single generic
safety head with four explicit heads over the same top-5 attention proposals:
bind target, no-anchor risk, wrong-active risk, and stale risk. The run remained
shadow-only, used the same q8 ES-AIST artifact, and wrote
`build/es_aist_contextual_anchor_shadow_set_aware_fast/`.

Source-held-out results:

| safety policy | safe target selected | no-anchor abstain | selected wrong-active | top-3 | wrong-active rejection AUC | zero-FPR | 5% FPR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| single safety head | 0.0000 | 0.9536 | 0.0037 | 0.1296 | 0.3817 | 0 | 0 |
| multi-head bind only | 0.0037 | 0.9536 | 0.0519 | 0.3593 | 0.3269 | 1 | 2 |
| set-aware multi-head bind only | 0.0148 | 0.9536 | 0.0296 | 0.3333 | 0.3328 | 1 | 4 |
| multi-head recall-biased | 0.0000 | 0.9536 | 0.0000 | 0.2741 | 0.3411 | 0 | 0 |
| multi-head balanced | 0.0000 | 0.9536 | 0.0000 | 0.2148 | 0.3560 | 0 | 0 |
| set-aware multi-head balanced | 0.0000 | 0.9536 | 0.0000 | 0.1926 | 0.3553 | 0 | 0 |
| multi-head guarded | 0.0000 | 0.9536 | 0.0000 | 0.1852 | 0.3657 | 0 | 0 |
| set-aware multi-head guarded | 0.0000 | 0.9536 | 0.0000 | 0.1593 | 0.3734 | 0 | 0 |

This clarifies the current bottleneck. The separated heads do contain more
target signal: bind-only source-held-out top-3 rises to `0.3593` and low-FPR
recovery becomes nonzero (`1` at zero FPR, `2` at 5% FPR). But that recovery
comes with a wrong-active commit rate of `0.0519`. We also added a set-aware
top-k feature surface in which each candidate row is augmented with top-k mean,
max, standard deviation, and candidate-minus-summary features. The bind-only
set-aware variant reduces wrong-active commits to `0.0296` and improves 5% FPR
recovery to `4`, but guarded variants still recover zero safe binds. The
optimized set-aware run used `240` safety features and completed in `70.69 s`.

ES-AIST plus WM/STM/LTM attention should therefore be treated as a proposal
layer. The remaining missing component is a compact sequence- or item-level
commit model over the top-k proposal set, not another scalar threshold over the
same scores.

We then tested that compact nonlinear consumer directly. The added consumer uses
four small deterministic MLP heads over the same top-5 proposal rows: bind,
no-anchor, wrong-active, and stale. It remains shadow-only and production
retrieval is unchanged. The run wrote
`build/es_aist_contextual_anchor_shadow_sequence_mlp/`, with `10` hidden units
and `60` training epochs per head.

Source-held-out results:

| policy | safe target selected | no-anchor abstain | selected wrong-active | top-3 | zero-FPR | 5% FPR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| set-aware logistic bind-only | 0.0148 | 0.9536 | 0.0296 | 0.3333 | 1 | 4 |
| MLP bind-only | 0.0000 | 0.9536 | 0.0333 | 0.2148 | 0 | 0 |
| set-aware MLP bind-only | 0.0074 | 0.9536 | 0.0593 | 0.4185 | 0 | 2 |
| set-aware MLP balanced | 0.0000 | 0.9536 | 0.0519 | 0.1741 | 0 | 0 |
| set-aware MLP guarded | 0.0000 | 0.9536 | 0.0481 | 0.1778 | 0 | 0 |

The nonlinear consumer increases target top-3 in one source-held-out variant,
but it does so by selecting more wrong-active candidates. It does not improve
zero-FPR recovery over the set-aware logistic result. Delayed-prequential looked
better--the set-aware MLP bind-only variant reached top-3 `0.4593`, zero-FPR
recovery `4`, and 5% FPR recovery `10`--but that does not transfer across
sources. The run took `204.22 s`, so this is also too expensive as an
unfocused sweep.

This is a useful negative. More nonlinear capacity over the current scalar
ES/WM/STM/LTM top-k feature surface does not solve safe commitment. The
remaining anchor work should change the input/supervision surface toward
item-level or entity-track evidence, rather than continuing to tune scalar
commit scores.

We closed this sequence with an offline entity-track oracle headroom audit over
the same repaired replay candidate pool. This audit is not a runtime policy and
does not use labels as runtime features; it only asks whether an upstream
entity/track signal would have enough candidate coverage.

The artifact is
`build/es_aist_contextual_anchor_shadow_sequence_mlp/entity_track_oracle_headroom.json`.

| metric | value |
|---|---:|
| cases | 421 |
| references | 270 |
| controls | 151 |
| references with target in candidate pool | 270 |
| references missing target candidate | 0 |
| controls with target label present | 0 |
| oracle safe target selected | 1.0000 |
| oracle no-anchor abstain | 1.0000 |
| oracle zero-FPR recovery | 270 / 270 |

This shows the repaired replay surface is not failing because LTM candidate
coverage is missing. A perfect entity/track signal could select the target in
every reference case and abstain on every control. Current ES/WM/STM/LTM
attention reaches only top-5 `0.5000` and over-selects wrong-active candidates,
so the missing component is observable entity continuity, not memory
availability. The next model/system direction should therefore provide
entity/object/voice/track observations to the engine, or train the embedding
model so its entity key can support that track state directly.

We then quantified how good that missing entity/track signal must be. The
offline sweep starts from the existing `WM/STM/LTM attention` score and injects
a synthetic track boost with controlled target-track recall, false track-match
rate, and signal strength:

```bash
python3 tools/entity_track_signal_headroom.py \
  --artifact-dir build/es_aist_contextual_anchor_shadow_sequence_mlp
```

The artifacts are:

- `entity_track_signal_quality_sweep.csv`
- `entity_track_signal_quality_sweep.json`

Baseline `WM/STM/LTM attention` has top-1 `0.1481`, top-3 `0.3519`, top-5
`0.5000`, zero-FPR recovery `0`, and 5% FPR recovery `1`.

With zero false track matches and target-track recall `1.0`, the signal-strength
breakpoints were:

| target recovery | zero-FPR strength | 5% FPR strength |
|---:|---:|---:|
| >= 25% | 0.30 | 0.20 |
| >= 50% | 0.30 | 0.30 |
| >= 80% | 0.45 | 0.45 |
| >= 95% | 0.60 | 0.45 |

The decisive result is the false-track sensitivity. At target recall `1.0` and
signal strength `0.60`, zero-FPR recovery fell from `270 / 270` to `25 / 270`
when the false track-match rate rose to only `0.005`; at `0.01`, it fell to
`10 / 270`.

| false track rate | zero-FPR recovery | 5% FPR recovery |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.000 | 270 | 270 |
| 0.005 | 25 | 90 |
| 0.010 | 10 | 38 |
| 0.020 | 10 | 27 |
| 0.050 | 7 | 22 |
| 0.100 | 0 | 10 |

This reframes the model requirement. The missing entity signal must be
precision-first. High target recall is not enough: even very rare false track
matches destroy the zero-FPR operating point. Any future modality-agnostic
anchor model should therefore optimize false-track rejection at least as
strongly as target reachability.

Finally, we tested the structure of the motivating multimodal anchor chain
directly. The repaired replay results above show that a precise track signal is
needed, but the user-facing behavior is not just person continuity: it includes
person references, media/object handoff, and mixed relation questions such as
"How long has he had it?" We added a deterministic synthetic headroom audit:

```bash
python3 tools/multimodal_anchor_chain_headroom.py \
  --episodes 200 \
  --output-dir build/multimodal_anchor_chain_headroom
```

The artifacts are:

- `multimodal_anchor_chain_cases.csv`
- `multimodal_anchor_chain_headroom.csv`
- `multimodal_anchor_chain_headroom.json`

The benchmark generates `1200` cases over person pronouns, media/object
references, owner-object relations, wrong-active person references,
cross-modal image handoff, and no-anchor topic shifts. Candidate units include
person tracks, media/object tracks, and relation candidates such as
`owner(Jared, dog)`.

| policy | safe target selected | selected wrong-active | relation top-1 | media top-1 | zero-FPR safe recovery |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| recency only | 0.2000 | 0.8000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 200 / 1000 |
| entity only | 0.4000 | 0.6000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 400 / 1000 |
| entity + object/media | 0.8000 | 0.2000 | 0.0000 | 1.0000 | 800 / 1000 |
| entity + object/media + relation | 1.0000 | 0.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1000 / 1000 |

This makes the architecture requirement sharper. Entity tracks alone are not
enough for the target product behavior. They handle "he" but not "it", media
continuity, or "he had it" style owner/object relations. Entity plus
object/media tracks solves the image handoff but still fails mixed relation
questions. A modality-agnostic anchor substrate therefore needs relation/event
edges--owner, sender, depicts, attached-to, and similar links--in addition to
entity and object tracks.

As a final audit for this experiment sequence, we mapped the objective to the
artifacts in `docs/anchor-experiment-audit.md`. The audit records which claims
are covered by evidence and which are not. The covered claims are:

- ES-AIST + WM/STM/LTM attention is useful as a proposal layer.
- Single scalar, multi-head, set-aware, and small MLP commit consumers do not
  solve source-held-out safe commitment.
- The repaired replay candidate pool is not the blocker: every reference case
  contains its target candidate.
- Entity-only anchoring is insufficient for the motivating chain; object/media
  tracks and relation/event edges are required.

The uncovered requirement is a real high-precision modality-agnostic
entity/object/relation signal. Without that input, more policy sweeps over the
same scalar ES/WM/STM/LTM surface are not a productive path. The next valid
experiment needs a new input surface: a model artifact trained to emit
precision-first entity/object/relation signals, upstream multimodal track
proposals, or real/high-fidelity entity-object-relation episode labels.

We captured that next input surface in `docs/anchor-signal-contract.md`. The
contract requires typed entity, object/media, event, and relation proposals;
strict false-proposal gates; repaired replay evaluation; multimodal chain
evaluation; and manual-gold validation. This makes the current stopping point
explicit: the next experiment should test a new signal artifact or upstream
proposal interface, not another policy sweep over the existing scalar feature
surface.

We then made that contract executable as a benchmark scaffold:

```bash
python3 tools/evaluate_anchor_signal_contract.py \
  --episodes 200 \
  --output-dir build/anchor_signal_contract_eval
```

The artifacts are:

- `anchor_signal_contract_eval_cases.jsonl`
- `anchor_signal_contract_results.json`
- `anchor_signal_contract_summary.csv`
- `anchor_signal_false_proposal_audit.csv`
- `anchor_signal_failure_examples.csv`

The built-in proposal modes are headroom scaffolds, not model evidence. The
tool exists so future signal artifacts can be evaluated with the same schema
and gates through `--cases-jsonl` and `--proposals-jsonl`.

| proposal mode | required gates | target gates | entity recall | object/media recall | relation recall | entity false / case | object false / case | relation false / case |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| empty | fail | fail | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |
| entity only | fail | fail | 1.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |
| entity + object/media | fail | fail | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |
| entity + object/media + relation | pass | pass | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |
| entity + object/media + relation, noisy 0.005 | pass | fail | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.0025 | 0.0033 | 0.0042 |
| entity + object/media + relation, noisy 0.01 | fail | fail | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.0083 | 0.0092 | 0.0092 |

This executable audit reinforces the same conclusion. Entity-only proposals are
not enough for the anchor product behavior; object/media and relation proposals
are required. A complete scaffold can pass the minimum gates, but the noisy
0.005 condition already fails the stricter target false-proposal gate. The next
artifact therefore has to be evaluated as a high-precision signal source, not
as a generic embedding or retrieval reranker.

As a final check on the current ES-AIST surface, we asked whether the existing
scalar candidate features could be thresholded into that signal contract:

```bash
python3 tools/es_aist_signal_contract_threshold_audit.py \
  --artifact-dir build/es_aist_contextual_anchor_shadow_sequence_mlp \
  --output-dir build/es_aist_signal_contract_threshold_audit
```

The artifacts are:

- `es_aist_signal_contract_threshold_results.json`
