The audit evaluates semantic, entity, full, margin, context-only, and
stage-1-attention views over the `421` repaired replay cases. It calibrates
thresholds by false candidate proposal rate and reports target recovery.

| gate | best view | false candidate rate | target recall | selected targets |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| required false gate `<0.005` | full margin | 0.00498 | 0.0296 | 8 / 270 |
| strict target false gate `<=0.001` | entity margin | 0.00094 | 0.0037 | 1 / 270 |

The stage-1 attention view selected only `1 / 270` targets at the required
false gate. At a much looser 5% false-candidate rate, it selected `27 / 270`,
which is still weak and outside the required precision regime. Therefore the
current ES-AIST + WM/STM/LTM scalar surface cannot be converted into the missing
anchor signal by thresholding. It remains a proposal/ranking input; it is not a
high-precision entity/object/relation proposal source.

To keep the next benchmark aligned with the desired architecture, we replaced
the synthetic chronological ingress benchmark with a storage-time ES-AIST
attention benchmark over real conversation streams. This benchmark is not a
retrieval reranker and does not consume retrieved candidates. Its runtime
process is:

1. load PersonaChat, TopicalChat, and Taskmaster conversation turns;
2. replay each conversation chronologically;
3. at turn `t`, encode only the current incoming signal with
   `ES-AIST-81M_q8_0.gguf`;
4. before writing the current memory, attend over already-stored prior memories:
   WM is age `<=4`, STM is age `5..32`, and LTM is age `>32`;
5. update the selected shadow anchor only if score and margin pass; otherwise
   create a new shadow anchor for the current memory;
6. apply labels only after the storage-time action to audit target reuse,
   no-anchor safety, wrong-active selection, and stale selection.

The audit output records `retrieved_candidate_count=0`,
`uses_retrieved_candidates=0`, and `runtime_policy_uses_labels=0` for every row.
The final run also verified zero duplicate current-ingress steps per policy.

```bash
cmake --build build -j 8 --target cortext_ingress_anchor_formation_bench

CORTEXT_AAIT_REQUIRE_FULL_GGML_GRAPH=1 \
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_ingress_anchor_formation_bench \
  --models models \
  --teacher-model models/ES-AIST-81M-preview-GGUF/ES-AIST-81M_q8_0.gguf \
  --max-conversations 96 \
  --max-turns 96 \
  --max-cases 421 \
  --output-dir build/ingress_storage_attention_es_aist
```

This is now the correct architectural test: ES-AIST is used as a storage-time
signal over real prior WM/STM/LTM memory state, before retrieval, with
production retrieval unchanged. The result is still negative for replacing a
dedicated anchor model with the current hand-built attention policy. Loose
attention recovers targets but false-binds no-anchor and wrong-active cases.
Strict/high-precision attention protects no-anchor controls but collapses target
reuse and still has zero zero-FPR recovery. The bottleneck is therefore not
benchmark location anymore; it is the missing commit/safety policy or a stronger
model-side entity/event/object signal.

Because a fixed trained commit model would not naturally adapt to a user's
evolving memory stream, we then added a model-free adaptive ledger in the same
benchmark. This variant still uses ES-AIST only as an ingress signal, but the
ledger state evolves online:

- every stored memory creates or updates a provisional/active anchor;
- anchors carry support count, confidence, stability, contradiction count, and
  status;
- update decisions are relative over active anchors, using attention entropy,
  score margin, confidence, support, recency tier, and entity-vs-event split
  pressure;
- unsafe or ambiguous evidence creates/splits a new anchor instead of consuming
  an existing one.

We then re-read the same real chat run as a soft-anchor benchmark. In this
view the engine may return tentative references instead of pretending that
every reference must be a durable hard bind. This matters because humans also
carry ambiguous references: returning two plausible memories can be useful, but
writing the wrong one as settled memory is not.

| adaptive policy | hard selected target | tentative target top-3 | useful uncertain references | hard wrong commits | no-anchor hard binds |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| evidence loose | 266 / 270 | 270 / 270 | 4 / 270 | 153 / 421 | 151 / 151 |
| evidence mid | 252 / 270 | 268 / 270 | 16 / 270 | 156 / 421 | 149 / 151 |
| hysteresis | 237 / 270 | 261 / 270 | 24 / 270 | 156 / 421 | 141 / 151 |
| split guard | 247 / 270 | 268 / 270 | 21 / 270 | 159 / 421 | 149 / 151 |
| high precision | 165 / 270 | 226 / 270 | 61 / 270 | 142 / 421 | 119 / 151 |
| ultra precision | 5 / 270 | 118 / 270 | 113 / 270 | 14 / 421 | 11 / 151 |

The model-free online ledger does produce the expected continuity behavior.
Loose adaptive evidence keeps the correct target anchor in `266 / 270`
references with only `2 / 270` wrong-active selections. But it does that by
becoming too sticky: no-anchor abstention collapses to `0 / 151`. Increasing
hysteresis, split pressure, and precision thresholds gradually restores
no-anchor safety, but the tradeoff returns; ultra precision abstains on
`140 / 151` controls while recovering only `5 / 270` targets. This tells us
natural online state evolution helps continuity but still does not expose a
reliable hard no-anchor/split signal from ES-AIST plus scalar WM/STM/LTM state
alone.

Manual review changed the criterion rather than the core mechanics. In the
high-precision policy, several benchmark no-anchor "false binds" were
acceptable tentative conversational links: for example, "that is terrible i am
sorry . why do they hate you ?" pointed to the earlier family-hate turn, and
"they will try to acquire it . lol" pointed to the prior bank/tin-market turn.
These are useful as uncertain context but should not be durable identity facts.
The manual sample contains `12` real chat rows: `2` acceptable hard binds, `3`
acceptable tentative-only references, `2` acceptable no-hard-bind cases, `2`
ambiguous-but-useful rows, and `3` bad or generic signals. The next engine
contract should therefore preserve uncertainty:

- keep top-k tentative anchors with scores and memory-tier evidence;
- allow ambiguous references to be returned as uncertain context;
- require repeated support before durable consolidation;
- treat generic matches such as "Ok" or "Bye" as tentative at most;
- evaluate useful uncertain references and wrong durable commits, not zero-FPR
  alone.

We then made that contract explicit in the benchmark artifacts. Each adaptive
candidate, case, link, and final anchor state now includes `anchor_strength`, a
continuous evidence value in `[0, 1]`, and `anchor_label`, a derived policy
label (`none`, `tentative`, `ambiguous`, `durable`, `decayed`, or `rejected`).
The labels are derived from score, attention, margin, entropy, support count,
contradiction count, confidence, and decay state. They are not runtime labels
or gold supervision.

The anchor-strength/label pass wrote:

- `build/ingress_storage_attention_es_aist_anchor_strength_label/ingress_adaptive_anchor_cases.csv`

- `build/ingress_storage_attention_es_aist_anchor_strength_label/ingress_adaptive_anchor_manual_review_sample.csv`

| adaptive policy | target top-3 | hard wrong commits | durable selections | ambiguous selections | tentative selections | no-anchor durable binds |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| evidence loose | 270 / 270 | 153 / 421 | 379 | 29 | 13 | 138 / 151 |
| high precision | 226 / 270 | 142 / 421 | 158 | 175 | 88 | 64 / 151 |
| ultra precision | 118 / 270 | 14 / 421 | 9 | 186 | 226 | 3 / 151 |

The terms are right, and the audit is now legible. The current label derivation
is still too willing to call sticky no-anchor matches durable under
loose/high-precision policies. Ultra precision shows the opposite corner: very
few durable false binds, many tentative/ambiguous links, and much lower hard
target recovery. This supports the engine design but not the current thresholds
as production policy. `anchor_strength` should be the stored continuous value;
`anchor_label` should be a derived/cached view that can be recalibrated without
rewriting evidence.

We then swept the derived-label and knob-shaped promotion rules without changing
the underlying storage-time ES-AIST signal or the production retrieval path.
This pass kept ES-AIST as a signal model only: the engine consumed
`semantic_key`, `entity_key`, and `full_key` together with already-stored
WM/STM/LTM state, online support, contradiction, entropy, margin, recency, and
source continuity. No retrieved candidates or labels were runtime inputs.

| adaptive policy | target top-3 | hard target commits | hard wrong commits | no-anchor hard binds | no-anchor durable binds | durable | ambiguous | tentative |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| evidence loose | 270 / 270 | 266 / 270 | 153 / 421 | 151 / 151 | 138 / 151 | 379 | 29 | 13 |
| high precision | 226 / 270 | 165 / 270 | 142 / 421 | 119 / 151 | 64 / 151 | 158 | 175 | 88 |
| high precision + generic guard | 226 / 270 | 165 / 270 | 142 / 421 | 119 / 151 | 57 / 151 | 144 | 175 | 102 |
| high precision + margin guard | 226 / 270 | 165 / 270 | 142 / 421 | 119 / 151 | 53 / 151 | 130 | 175 | 116 |
| high precision + conservative label | 226 / 270 | 165 / 270 | 142 / 421 | 119 / 151 | 45 / 151 | 114 | 175 | 132 |

| ultra precision | 118 / 270 | 5 / 270 | 14 / 421 | 11 / 151 | 3 / 151 | 9 | 186 | 226 |

This strengthens the contract boundary. Label-only guards improve durable
safety without changing candidate reachability: the conservative
high-precision label reduces no-anchor durable binds from `64 / 151` to
`45 / 151` while preserving target top-3 (`226 / 270`) and hard target commits
(`165 / 270`). That is useful but not sufficient. The knob-shaped high-focus
corner reduces no-anchor durable binds to `16 / 151` and hard wrong commits to
`87 / 421`, but target top-3 drops to `168 / 270`. Ultra precision is the safe
extreme (`3 / 151` no-anchor durable binds), but it recovers almost no hard
targets. Therefore ES-AIST should be treated as a proposal signal. The engine
should persist `anchor_strength` and top-k tentative evidence, derive
`anchor_label` from knobs, and promote to durable only after repeated support or
stronger typed evidence.

The follow-up research synthesis agrees with this interpretation. The next
engine candidate is **Soft Anchor v1**: an ingress-time evidence accumulator.
ES-AIST remains a signal model that emits semantic, entity, and full-signal
views. Cortext owns the soft-anchor policy: view blending,
source/recency/boundary pressure, support and contradiction counts, generic
suppression, entropy/margin labels, decay, and durable promotion are derived
from Focus, Sensitivity, and Stability.

The accepted soft-anchor contract is not a hard referent resolver. It stores a
ranked hypothesis set:

```text
SoftAnchorLink {
  memory_id
  anchor_id
  anchor_strength
  anchor_label
  evidence_kind
  memory_tier
  score
  margin
  entropy
  support_count
  contradiction_count
  created_step
  updated_step
}
```

The design corrections are important. First, formation belongs at ingress and
must not alter production retrieval ranking. Second, generic suppression must be
modality-general; text shortcuts for "ok", "yeah", "bye", and filler are
allowed as an optional source of evidence, not as the anchor mechanism. Third,
durable promotion should be rare and require repeated non-generic support or
exceptionally strong low-entropy evidence. This makes the next experiment target
concrete: test the soft-anchor policy pieces directly with ablations for generic
suppression, repeated-support promotion, boundary pressure, WM-only versus
WM+STM versus WM+STM+LTM, semantic-only versus entity-only versus combined ES
views, contradiction penalties, a null/no-anchor hypothesis, and entropy/margin
labeling.

We then ran that first Soft Anchor policy ablation. This pass changed
engine-side policy only; ES-AIST remained the same signal model and production
retrieval remained unchanged. The run wrote
`build/ingress_storage_attention_es_aist_soft_anchor_fst_sweep/ingress_storage_attention_results.json`
and
`build/ingress_storage_attention_es_aist_soft_anchor_fst_sweep/soft_anchor_ablation_summary.csv`.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| high precision baseline | 226 / 270 | 165 / 270 | 142 / 421 | 119 / 151 | 64 / 151 | 32 / 151 | 3 |
| generic action suppressor | 218 / 270 | 149 / 270 | 135 / 421 | 104 / 151 | 52 / 151 | 47 / 151 | 8 |
| no contradiction penalty | 226 / 270 | 163 / 270 | 130 / 421 | 106 / 151 | 42 / 151 | 45 / 151 | 4 |
| no entropy/margin gate | 239 / 270 | 189 / 270 | 151 / 421 | 129 / 151 | 77 / 151 | 22 / 151 | 4 |
| null hypothesis | 176 / 270 | 154 / 270 | 120 / 421 | 99 / 151 | 69 / 151 | 52 / 151 | 3 |
| null + generic suppressor | 170 / 270 | 145 / 270 | 113 / 421 | 91 / 151 | 66 / 151 | 60 / 151 | 9 |
| repeated-support update gate | 132 / 270 | 0 / 270 | 0 / 421 | 0 / 151 | 0 / 151 | 151 / 151 | 0 |
| semantic-only view | 247 / 270 | 214 / 270 | 154 / 421 | 134 / 151 | 88 / 151 | 17 / 151 | 7 |
| entity-only view | 215 / 270 | 139 / 270 | 141 / 421 | 108 / 151 | 43 / 151 | 43 / 151 | 6 |
| full-only view | 230 / 270 | 181 / 270 | 149 / 421 | 124 / 151 | 65 / 151 | 27 / 151 | 4 |
| semantic+entity view | 225 / 270 | 169 / 270 | 152 / 421 | 122 / 151 | 65 / 151 | 29 / 151 | 4 |
| WM only | 242 / 270 | 167 / 270 | 143 / 421 | 120 / 151 | 66 / 151 | 31 / 151 | 3 |
| STM+LTM, no WM | 21 / 270 | 1 / 270 | 39 / 421 | 36 / 151 | 3 / 151 | 115 / 151 | 0 |

The result sharpens the soft-anchor design. Semantic evidence is the recall view:
semantic-only keeps the target in top-3 for `247 / 270` and hard-binds
`214 / 270` references, but it also produces `88 / 151` no-anchor durable
binds. Entity evidence is the safer view: entity-only reduces no-anchor durable
binds to `43 / 151` and increases no-anchor abstention, but loses target
recall. The engine should therefore not collapse the ES views into one scalar;
semantic evidence should carry tentative reachability and entity evidence
should guard durable promotion. Generic action suppression helps (`8`
references recovered at 5% FPR versus `3` for high precision), but it is not
promotion-ready. The null/no-anchor cutoff and repeated-support update gate are
too crude: null lowers hard commits but hurts durable-label quality, while
support-before-update achieves safety by preventing all hard target commits.
Repeated support should gate durable promotion, not all tentative updates.
Finally, removing the current contradiction penalty improved durable safety,
so the existing contradiction formula is not yet reliable.

We then implemented the first full Soft Anchor v1 hypothesis pass in the
same benchmark. This pass adds explicit `H_none` and `H_new` hypotheses, writes
top-k `SoftAnchorLink` rows, distinguishes tentative `soft_update` from hard
`update_existing`, and keeps durable promotion conservative. The run wrote
`build/ingress_storage_attention_es_aist_soft_anchor_fst_sweep/ingress_storage_attention_results.json`,
`build/ingress_storage_attention_es_aist_soft_anchor_fst_sweep/soft_anchor_v1_update_sweep_summary.csv`,
and
`build/ingress_storage_attention_es_aist_soft_anchor_fst_sweep/ingress_adaptive_anchor_soft_links.csv`.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| high precision baseline | 226 / 270 | 165 / 270 | 142 / 421 | 119 / 151 | 64 / 151 | 32 / 151 | 0 | 75 / 270 |
| soft anchor v1 | 261 / 270 | 0 / 270 | 0 / 421 | 0 / 151 | 0 / 151 | 151 / 151 | 1408 | 0 / 270 |
| v1 high focus | 261 / 270 | 0 / 270 | 0 / 421 | 0 / 151 | 0 / 151 | 151 / 151 | 1408 | 0 / 270 |
| v1 high sensitivity | 261 / 270 | 0 / 270 | 0 / 421 | 0 / 151 | 0 / 151 | 151 / 151 | 1408 | 0 / 270 |
| v1 update strict | 261 / 270 | 0 / 270 | 0 / 421 | 0 / 151 | 0 / 151 | 151 / 151 | 1367 | 7 / 270 |
| v1 update very strict | 242 / 270 | 0 / 270 | 0 / 421 | 0 / 151 | 0 / 151 | 151 / 151 | 1135 | 51 / 270 |
| v1 no generic | 270 / 270 | 0 / 270 | 0 / 421 | 0 / 151 | 0 / 151 | 151 / 151 | 1459 | 0 / 270 |

This is the first pass that gives a useful soft anchor behavior: default v1
keeps the target in retained top-3 for `261 / 270` references while producing
zero hard and durable false binds on no-anchor controls. But the same result
also shows why this is not yet finished human subject anchoring. The default
soft-update threshold collapses most of a conversation into one continuity
anchor, so wrong-active distinct-anchor preservation is `0 / 270`. The
very-strict update variant restores some separation (`51 / 270`) while keeping
hard and durable false binds at zero, but target top-3 drops to `242 / 270`.

The conclusion is therefore narrower than "anchors are solved." ES-AIST plus
WM/STM/LTM can power a soft, uncertainty-preserving soft anchor. The current
engine policy is not yet a reliable subject/person/place splitter. Future
policy work should improve split/new-anchor pressure using boundary, source,
and entity-specific evidence, while preserving top-k soft links and
conservative durable promotion.

and
`build/ingress_storage_attention_es_aist_soft_anchor_fst_sweep/soft_anchor_fst_monotonicity.json`.
Across all 27 settings the durable safety gate held: hard wrong commits,
no-anchor hard binds, no-anchor durable binds, and durable retained soft links
were all zero.

| Sensitivity | 0.75 | 261.0 | 1415.7 | 64.3 | 1.3 | 75.0 | 1403.7 |
| Stability | 0.25 | 259.2 | 1413.9 | 115.4 | 7.1 | 104.1 | 1373.3 |
| Stability | 0.50 | 259.2 | 1413.9 | 115.4 | 7.1 | 104.1 | 1373.3 |
| Stability | 0.75 | 259.2 | 1413.9 | 115.4 | 7.1 | 104.1 | 1373.3 |

The monotonicity checks were mixed. Focus behaved as a precision/split knob:
target top-3 recall decreased or stayed flat in `18 / 18` adjacent checks, and
wrong-active separation improved in `18 / 18`. Sensitivity behaved as a recall
knob: target top-3 improved in `18 / 18`, and retained soft links increased in
`12 / 18`. We then repaired the Stability mapping by removing Stability from
soft-update acceptance thresholds and leaving it on TTL/support-window
parameters. Configured active TTL now increases in `18 / 18` checks, actual
soft updates are preserved or increased in `18 / 18`, and create count is
preserved or lowered in `18 / 18`. On this short replay, the behavioral
metrics are flat across Stability because no long decay gap is being stressed;
that is preferable to the earlier bug where high Stability became a stricter
commit filter.

The resulting policy interpretation is: Focus should control precision and
split pressure; Sensitivity should control tentative recall and soft context
volume; Stability should control decay, link half-life, support windows, and
pruning separately from soft-update acceptance thresholds. A longer
decay-heavy replay is still required before this mapping is promoted into the
engine algorithms.

We then added a separate Soft Anchor **consumption** pass to the same
chronological ingress benchmark. This is intentionally distinct from formation:
formation stores ranked soft links; consumption decides which links would be
surfaced as uncertain context to a human or LLM. The run wrote
`build/soft_anchor_consumption_full_ablation_v2/soft_anchor_consumption_results.json`,
`build/soft_anchor_consumption_full_ablation_v2/soft_anchor_consumption_ablation_summary.csv`,
`build/soft_anchor_consumption_full_ablation_v2/soft_anchor_consumption_knob_sweep_summary.csv`,
`build/soft_anchor_consumption_full_ablation_v2/soft_anchor_consumption_cases.csv`,
and
`build/soft_anchor_consumption_full_ablation_v2/soft_anchor_consumption_surfaces.csv`.

| consumer policy | useful target surfaced | no-anchor surfaced | wrong-only surfaced | harmful contexts | useful / harmful | mean links | p95 chars |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| no consumption | 0 / 270 | 0 / 151 | 0 | 0 | 0.00 | 0.000 | 0 |
| default | 15 / 270 | 8 / 151 | 0 | 8 | 1.88 | 0.055 | 69 |
| high recall top-k | 252 / 270 | 139 / 151 | 5 | 148 | 1.70 | 0.950 | 208 |
| low-F / mid-S | 29 / 270 | 16 / 151 | 0 | 16 | 1.81 | 0.107 | 101 |
| low-F / high-S | 155 / 270 | 77 / 151 | 1 | 78 | 1.99 | 0.553 | 176 |
| high-F / mid-S | 2 / 270 | 0 / 151 | 0 | 0 | 2.00 | 0.005 | 0 |
| durable only | 0 / 270 | 0 / 151 | 0 | 0 | 0.00 | 0.000 | 0 |

The consumption result answers a different question than the formation result.
Soft Anchor formation is useful because it preserves the target in retained
top-k links for most reference cases without making hard commits. Direct
consumption is not yet ready as a default surfaced context policy. The
high-recall consumer finds `252 / 270` targets, but it also surfaces context on
`139 / 151` no-anchor controls. The strict/default consumers avoid most harm,
but they surface only `15 / 270` useful targets. In between, the best simple
knob settings improve volume but do not reach a clean useful/harmful ratio.

The consumption knob sweep confirms that Focus and Sensitivity move the user
experience predictably: Focus increased safety and reduced surfaced volume in
all adjacent checks; Sensitivity increased target surfacing and surfaced volume
in all adjacent checks. Stability still shows little behavioral movement on this
short replay: only `1 / 18` adjacent target-surfacing checks and `2 / 18` mean
link-count checks changed at all, and no LTM surfaces were produced. This means
the replay is useful for Focus/Sensitivity consumption calibration, but not a
complete Stability validation. The next evidence requirement for consumption is
a manually reviewed chat slice where uncertain hints are rated as useful or
harmful, rather than treating every no-anchor surfaced hint as equally bad.

We then wrote the next Soft Anchor consumption experiment program in
`docs/soft-anchor-consumption-experiments.md`. The plan enumerates the plausible
ways formed anchors could be consumed: silent safety, possible-continuity hints,
anchor-neighborhood context, ambiguous top-k candidate sets, clarification,
structured LLM self-selection, UI-only human hints, retrieval annotation without
ranking changes, context packing, same-anchor neighborhood expansion,
current-turn anchor recall, durable-only fact consumption, decayed-link
reminders, group anchors, cross-modal evidence, correction-aware recovery, and
an ask-or-show hybrid. These are experiment variants, not product modes.

The next evidence sequence is: replay consumption contract, manual chat
usefulness audit, LLM answer-quality A/B, prompt-shape ablation, context-budget
sweep, neighborhood expansion, clarification strategy, F/S/T consumption
semantics with a long Stability stress, multimodal audit, correction/recovery,
human UI consumption, and agent/tool consumption. A consumption behavior can
move into the engine only if manual review shows a useful/harmful ratio of at
least `5`, no-anchor harmful hints below `2%`, wrong-only replay hints below
`1%`, bounded p95 context and latency, monotonic Focus/Sensitivity behavior,
validated long-horizon Stability behavior, uncertain phrasing that never becomes
fact language, and no durable fact formation from tentative or ambiguous links.

We then added the executable replay test for that plan:

```bash
python3 tools/soft_anchor_consumption_contract_test.py \
  --input-dir build/soft_anchor_consumption_full_ablation_v2 \
  --output-dir build/soft_anchor_consumption_contract_test_packet

python3 tools/soft_anchor_consumption_contract_test.py \
  --input-dir build/soft_anchor_consumption_full_ablation_v2 \
  --output-dir build/soft_anchor_consumption_contract_test_all_packet \
  --all-formation-policies
```

The test reads formed Soft Anchor candidate rows and evaluates consumption
policies without rerunning retrieval, using retrieved candidates, or using gold
labels at runtime. Labels are applied only after policy selection to score
whether a surfaced hint would have helped or harmed the replay case. It writes
`soft_anchor_consumption_contract_results.json`,
`soft_anchor_consumption_contract_summary.csv`,
`soft_anchor_consumption_contract_cases.csv`, and
`soft_anchor_consumption_contract_failures.csv`.

Thirteen consumption policies were directly testable: no consumption, silent
safety, possible top-1 hints, loose top-1 hints, anchor-neighborhood hints,
ambiguous top-3 sets, clarification, structured LLM self-selection, UI-only
top-3, current-turn recall, durable-only fact consumption, decayed reminders,
and ask-or-show hybrid. Six planned policies were recorded as not testable from
this artifact alone because they require additional traces: retrieval
annotation, context packing, retrieval neighborhood expansion, group anchors,
cross-modal evidence, and correction-aware recovery.

The first scoring pass was too conservative because it treated every surfaced
no-anchor hint as harmful. That is only true for asserted-context consumption,
where the engine acts as if an anchor has been resolved. It is not true for the
intended surface: SoftAnchor context on retrieved memories containing full
memory text, uncertainty, and possibly multiple candidate continuities. The
human, LLM, or downstream agent decides which candidate is usable.

We therefore split the metric into two views. In the **asserted-context** view,
no-anchor surfacing is harmful because the system has implied a referent. In the
**SoftAnchor context** view, no-anchor surfacing is counted as context/noise
load; harm is reserved for wrong-only or stale-only context on reference cases.

With that corrected interpretation, directly testable SoftAnchor context consumers
do pass the replay criterion:

| run | best SoftAnchor context variant | target surfaced | wrong-only contexts | optional contexts on no-anchor controls | p95 prompt chars |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| curated formation policies | C2 possible top-1 over `adaptive_soft_anchor_v1_no_generic` | 270 / 270 | 0 | 151 / 151 | 208 |
| all formation policies | C2 possible top-1 over `adaptive_soft_anchor_v1_no_generic` | 270 / 270 | 0 | 151 / 151 | 208 |

The strict asserted-context view still has `0` passes, which is expected: Soft
Anchor should not be consumed as a fact or hard bind. As SoftAnchor context, the
formed links are useful: the best variant surfaces all targets with no
wrong-only/stale-only reference contexts in the replay. The cost is that it also
surfaces optional context for every no-anchor control. That is not a correctness
failure if the context is phrased and rendered as optional memory support, but
it is a UX and context-budget question.

Interpretation: Soft Anchor consumption should be implemented as uncertain
retrieved-memory context, not as an automatic resolved anchor. When a memory is
retrieved, attaching the top candidate sentences and strengths is valid; the
consumer can choose, ignore, or ask. The next tests should therefore focus on
SoftAnchor context shape, context budget, and manual/LLM usefulness rather than
trying to make no-anchor context emission zero.

We then wired Soft Anchor into the engine as an always-on ingress formation
operation. This pass does not change production retrieval. `UpdateSoftAnchor`
runs only after `MemoryStorage`, consumes the current stored memory id and
representative embedding, compares the current signal against prior soft-anchor
state, and writes `soft_anchors` / `soft_anchor_links` rows. The product line is
explicit: Soft Anchor formation is in the engine, retrieved and working memories
now expose optional `SoftAnchor` context, and retrieval ranking remains
unchanged. Hard anchor binding and retrieval reranking remain out. The demo chat
mirrors those entries in the memory event UI and includes them as nested
`<soft_anchor>` elements under retrieved memories in the prompt snapshot, with
instructions that they are optional continuity likelihoods rather than resolved
facts.

Implementation verification:

```bash
cmake --build build -j 8 --target cortext
cmake --build build -j 8 --target cortext_tests
cmake --build build -j 8 --target cortext_chat
./build/tests/cortext_tests "[cortext][hydration][soft_anchor]"
./build/tests/cortext_tests "[operations][soft_anchor]"
./build/tests/cortext_tests "[operations]"
./build/tests/cortext_tests "ES-AIST GGUF executes native text image and audio kernels" -s
ctest --test-dir build -R cortext_tests --output-on-failure
```

The focused Soft Anchor tests pass and cover default formation, creation from
the first ES-style 1536d signal, and continued-link update from a similar
signal. The broader operations slice passes. The ES-AIST multimodal runtime
test confirms native GGUF/GGML execution for text, image, and audio and verifies
the corrected 768/768 ES slices. The full `cortext_tests` CTest target passes
in `133.41 s`. The chat demo rebuilds with Soft Anchor context and the ES-AIST
signal path.

#### Direct Webcam and Microphone Chat Ingress

The demo chat now has a direct webcam/microphone ingress path. This path is
separate from voice chat: it does not run speech-to-text, diarization, speaker
labeling, or reply generation. On macOS it uses AVFoundation to capture camera
frames as RGB images and microphone samples as mono float PCM. The media worker
then feeds those signals through the existing Cortext multimodal APIs:
`Cortext::ProcessImage` for camera frames and `Cortext::ProcessAudio` for
microphone chunks.

This is a UI/example integration rather than a retrieval-policy change. Video
defaults to `1` FPS, can use `CORTEXT_CHAT_WEBCAM_FPS` as the startup default,
and can be adjusted/persisted from the chat Settings tab; audio is captured as
`16 kHz` mono chunks with a `2 s` chunk duration. The capture queue is bounded to
eight pending items so model ingest cannot accumulate an unbounded backlog, and
database explorer refresh from direct media ingest is throttled to once per
second. Production retrieval ranking remains unchanged; the engine now receives
live camera/audio signals directly instead of requiring an intermediate text
transcript.

Verification:

```bash
cmake --build build -j 8 --target cortext_chat
```

The chat target rebuilt successfully. The only warnings were existing
OpenTelemetry deprecation warnings from vendored headers.

We then measured the direct media encoder ceiling using the same benchmark
binary extended to cover image and audio. On the Apple M3 Max / Metal GGML path,
the default `ES-AIST-81M_q8_0.gguf` encoder processed short text at `2.20 ms`
per embedding (`454.60` embeddings/s), `640x480` RGB images at `303.58 ms`
per embedding (`3.29` images/s), and `2 s` / `16 kHz` mono audio chunks at
`488.31 ms` per embedding (`2.05` chunks/s) before audio preprocessing
optimization. The explicit `ESS-AIST v9 q8` artifact was similar for image
throughput: `306.52 ms` per `640x480` image (`3.26` images/s), while `320x240`
images were still `297.13 ms` (`3.37` images/s), indicating the model graph
rather than input copy dominates this path.

We then optimized the audio GGUF path by caching the Hann window and sparse mel
filterbank and by skipping FFT/filterbank work for guaranteed-silent padded tail
frames. The default ES-AIST q8 audio path improved to `157.66 ms` per `2 s`
chunk (`6.34` chunks/s) while still using the full audio GGML graph. Therefore
the webcam Settings slider is a throughput control, not a video recording rate:
`1 FPS` is the safe default, `2-3 FPS` is the practical continuous image range
on this host, and higher values are burst/diagnostic settings where the bounded
ingest queue may drop old frames if Cortext falls behind. Audio at 2-second
chunks is no longer the limiting path after this optimization.

We also compared this result with the adjacent `emel.cpp` embedding generator
on the same host. Its TE-75M q8 image lane runs at about `88.0 ms` per image
(`~11.4 FPS`), with the split dominated by `~83.6 ms` of encode time and only
`~4.4 ms` of image preparation. That implementation uses a persistent native
MobileNet/EfficientAT lane over GGUF-loaded tensors: weights are bound once,
convolution kernels are prepacked, HWC scratch buffers are reused, and
pointwise/depthwise/BN/ReLU work is fused in native kernels. A Cortext
experiment that only folded GGML graph batch-normalization into convolution
weights did not materially improve image throughput (`~312 ms` per image) and
regressed audio, so it was not retained. The conclusion is that the `>10 FPS`
webcam target requires a persistent native GGUF-backed vision lane rather than
the current generic GGML convolution graph.

We then added the first ES-AIST native HWC image lane. The path keeps the same
model contract: image pixels are resized/normalized to the ES-AIST 384 x 384
input, the MobileNetV4-style image stack runs over GGUF-loaded tensors in native
HWC layout, and the existing ES-AIST projection plus L2 normalization still
produce the 1536d vector. On Apple, dense convolution and pointwise stages use
Accelerate-backed row-major GEMMs. In Release, the CPU backend improved from
`313.49 ms` per image (`3.19 FPS`) on the old full-image GGML graph to
`87.68 ms` (`11.41 FPS`) on the native HWC lane. Removing the redundant
HWC-to-row copy from every 1x1 convolution and moving convolution outputs
directly into HWC tensor storage raised the CPU backend to `82.43 ms` per image
(`12.13 FPS`). Moving the image projection onto the host tensor path kept the
lane CPU-first even when Metal is available for text/audio and measured
`82.24 ms` (`12.16 FPS`), exceeding the emel reference class while staying
CPU-first. With default backend selection the same native lane measured
`83.14 ms` (`12.03 FPS`). CPU audio remains realtime-compatible at `336.67 ms` per `2 s` chunk
(`2.97` chunks/s, about `5.9x` realtime). This reaches the emel single-thread
target class without changing the signal model. The remaining runtime work is
to make the lane structurally more like emel: persistent scratch buffers,
packed kernels, and fused depthwise/BN/ReLU instead of per-block temporary
matrices.

Frame-level parallelism then moved the image path past the requested webcam
throughput target. We extended the release benchmark with `--parallelism`, where
each worker owns its own ES-AIST encoder instance and the benchmark measures
wall-clock throughput over independent frames. On the same CPU-backed native HWC
lane, 2 workers measured `42.16 ms` effective per frame (`23.72 FPS`), 3 workers
measured `27.27 ms` (`36.67 FPS`), and 4 workers measured `22.16 ms` (`45.13
FPS`). This is a throughput result rather than a single-frame latency result:
serial image latency remains about `80-85 ms`. The chat demo now permits a
`30 FPS` webcam setting, while full Cortext ingestion still needs bounded
single-writer staging if we want to sustain that rate through storage and UI
accounting without dropping older frames.

Finally, we pulled down a real public MP4 (`sample-10s.mp4` from Samplelib) and
ran decoded media through Cortext's actual image/audio ingestion calls. The
source was `10.216 s`, H.264/AAC, and was decoded to 303 `640 x 480` RGB frames
at `30 FPS` plus `163,469` `16 kHz` mono float samples. The artifacts are under
`build/video_media_perf/`, including `source_ffprobe.json`,
`cortext_video_media_perf.json`, and `cortext_video_media_perf_10fps.json`.

The full 30 FPS visual replay used one Cortext instance and called
`ProcessImage` serially for every decoded frame, followed by `ProcessAudio` for
2-second chunks. Visual ingest averaged `83.74 ms` total per frame (`78.89 ms`
encode, `4.82 ms` process/storage, `0.03 ms` hydrate), with p95 `88.76 ms`.
That is `11.88 FPS` effective and only `0.398x` realtime for a 30 FPS stream.
Audio averaged `344.47 ms` per 2-second chunk, p95 `368.55 ms`, or `4.94x`
realtime. The combined serial replay was `0.370x` realtime.

The same decoded video sampled at 10 FPS is the practical edge of the current
full-engine path. Visual ingest averaged `79.91 ms` per frame, p95 `82.56 ms`,
or `1.25x` realtime for the sampled visual stream. With the same audio chunks,
the combined serial pass was `0.998x` realtime. The conclusion is therefore
precise: ES-AIST encoder throughput can exceed 30 FPS with frame-parallel
workers, and audio is realtime, but continuous 30 FPS Cortext ingestion still
requires a bounded multi-worker pre-encode stage feeding a single-writer memory
commit path, or deliberate frame dropping.

We then implemented a benchmark-only `SignalFilter` target to test this as a
general ingress pattern rather than a video-only exception. The target supports
one modality-specific evidence adapter per modality and a shared adaptive
policy. In `--modality all`, the image, audio, and text filters run in parallel;
with accepted-signal processing enabled, each modality uses its own benchmark
Cortext instance and database, so the result measures parallel modality pressure
without claiming production single-writer semantics.

On the same downloaded video frames/audio and a 120-line text stream, with
1-second audio chunks, the adaptive policy accepted 79 of 303 image frames
(`7.82` accepted frames/s), 7 of 11 audio chunks (`0.685` chunks/s), and 108 of
120 text lines (`0.900` lines/s). Parallel processing of accepted signals
measured: image `82.69 ms` mean and `86.88 ms` p95 over 79 accepted frames
(`1.53x` realtime), audio `354.62 ms` mean and `394.26 ms` p95 over accepted
1-second chunks (`4.12x` realtime), and text `6.61 ms` mean with `14.68 ms` p95
(`167.40x` realtime under the synthetic 1-line/s text clock). This supports
`SignalFilter` as a general benchmark surface. The immediate value is visual
rate control; 1-second audio chunks are a practical realtime hearing default,
and text filtering should remain conservative and focus on generic or
near-duplicate suppression rather than throughput.

We then reran the audio path as a salience ablation rather than a throughput
counter. The same real video audio was chunked at 250, 500, and 1000 ms, and the
benchmark derived auditable acoustic-event windows from waveform features
(short-window RMS deltas, max-local energy change, positive onset velocity, and
current energy). This does not pretend to label semantic events; it checks
whether adaptive hearing catches focus-grabbing acoustic changes while adapting
to ambient volume. The aggregate artifacts are
`build/audio_signal_filter_real_video/audio_signal_filter_ablation_summary.json`
and `build/audio_signal_filter_real_video/audio_signal_filter_ablation_summary.csv`.

At 250 ms, the all-pass policy accepted 41 chunks and hit all 4 detected events
with event precision **0.488** and ambient accept rate **1.000**. The fixed
threshold accepted 7 chunks, but hit only **0.50** of events. The adaptive
policy accepted 13 chunks, hit **1.00** of events, improved event precision to
**0.538**, and reduced ambient accept rate to **0.286**. Accepted-signal
Cortext processing for this 250 ms adaptive policy averaged **124.51 ms** total
with p95 **143.17 ms** over 13 chunks, or **6.30x** realtime for accepted audio.
The 500 ms and 1000 ms adaptive paths also hit all detected events, but they
were coarser: 500 ms accepted 10 chunks at event precision **0.600**, while
1000 ms accepted 7 chunks at event precision **0.714**. The practical
interpretation is that 250 ms windows are the better always-on hearing default
when sub-second focus matters; 1-second windows remain a cheaper fallback.

The 250 ms Focus/Sensitivity sweep moved in the expected direction. With
Sensitivity **0.2**, medium/high Focus became too strict and event recall fell
to **0.75**. At Sensitivity **0.5** or **0.8**, adaptive filtering preserved
full event recall while retaining far fewer chunks than all-pass. This supports
the human-hearing analogy: the filter should adapt to ambient level, Focus
should sharpen acceptance, and Sensitivity should prevent quiet-but-real events
from being dropped.

We then promoted the validated audio and visual policies into the engine as a
general `SignalFilter` component rather than chat-side special cases.
`ProcessAudio` and `ProcessImage` now evaluate their filters before expensive
encoding/storage and return `signal_filter_*` diagnostics when a chunk or frame
is skipped. The implementation is intentionally modality-extensible: audio and
image have active adaptive policies by default, while text remains a
pass-through registry slot until a text-side filter is promoted. The image
adapter uses a bounded `32 x 24` luma grid with fixed per-cell samples, so its
cost is bounded and does not scale with every input pixel.

We removed the synthetic multimodal accumulation and episode-boundary benchmarks from the active evidence path. For this question, fake embeddings are not informative enough: the only valid benchmark is real media passed through the actual Cortext ingress APIs.

We therefore added `cortext_real_multimodal_episode_bench` plus
`tools/prepare_real_multimodal_episode_assets.py`. The asset script downloads
public Wikimedia media, converts images to `384x384` RGB and audio to `16 kHz`
mono float32 PCM, and records source URLs, licenses, and SHA-256 hashes. The
benchmark calls `Cortext::ProcessImage`, `ProcessAudio`, and `ProcessText`; it
does not construct embeddings directly and does not set forced boundaries.

The real-media results are more cautious:

| scenario | dog image+name fused | dog image+audio fused | all dog modalities fused | event split success | mixed-event memory |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| dog image + text + Bailey audio | 1 | 0 | 0 | n/a | 0 |
| dog image/text/audio then car image/text/audio | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| dog image/audio then car image/audio | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

The latest audit writes `real_multimodal_episode_groups.csv`, one manual review
row per formed memory, and adds programmatic checks for mixed event labels and
invalid byte concatenation. Only **1 / 3** cases passed all checks. The
storage-byte contract did pass: `mixed_memory_blob_violations=0` and
`audio_only_concat_violations=0`. Mixed-modal memories are therefore not being
serialized as one invalid byte stream; image/audio/text payloads remain
inspectable as signal rows, and audio-only concatenation remains coherent.

The episode grouping contract did not pass. Two real sequences still mixed
offline event labels inside one memory. In `real_dog_name_then_car_crash`,
memory `3` grouped `dog_name_audio` with `car_crash_image` and
`car_crash_text`. In `real_dog_name_audio_then_car_crash_audio`, memory `1`
grouped `dog_image`, `dog_name_audio`, and `car_crash_image`.

Interpretation: modalities can be grouped during episodes, and audio-only bytes
can be concatenated safely, but the current real encoder + accumulator/write
timing does **not** yet reliably separate natural multimodal episodes. The
failure is not that the database cannot represent mixed modalities; it is that
the engine still lets a same-source audio/visual accumulator cross a real event
shift. The next implementation target is natural multimodal write timing:
same-episode audio arriving after a text write must either attach back to the
current episode or close cleanly before a subsequent visual event.

We also reran the real-media benchmark as an explicit no-signal-filter
ablation. This path reports `signal_filter_used=false` and processes every real
input through `ProcessImage`, `ProcessAudio`, or `ProcessText`. The full
dog-then-car sequence still processed `6/6` events and reproduced the same
failure: dog image+audio fusion remained `0`, event split success remained `0`,
and one mixed dog/car memory remained. Therefore the current failure is not an
artifact of the realtime `SignalFilter` work.

We then added a benchmark-only modality-agnostic graph probe to answer whether
the graph/consolidation substrate can be built from data Cortext already has
when runtime labeling is disabled. The target is
`cortext_modality_agnostic_graph_bench`; it uses the same real Wikimedia
image/audio assets and calls only `Cortext::ProcessImage`,
`Cortext::ProcessAudio`, and `Cortext::ProcessText`. It does not call production
consolidation, does not change production graph behavior, does not use
synthetic embeddings, and uses the offline dog/car group annotations only for
scoring.

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_modality_agnostic_graph_bench \
  --assets-dir build/real_multimodal_episode_assets \
  --video-dir build/video_media_perf \
  --models models \
  --output-dir build/modality_agnostic_graph_bench

python3 tools/modality_agnostic_real_db_surface_audit.py \
  --output-dir build/modality_agnostic_graph_bench
```

Artifacts:

- `modality_agnostic_graph_summary.json`
- `modality_agnostic_graph_manifest.json`
- `modality_agnostic_graph_cases.csv`
- `modality_agnostic_graph_edges.csv`
- `modality_agnostic_graph_clusters.csv`
- `modality_agnostic_consolidation_cases.csv`
- `modality_agnostic_consolidation_units.csv`
- `modality_agnostic_real_db_surface_audit.json`
- `modality_agnostic_real_db_surface_audit.csv`
- `modality_agnostic_real_db_memory_units.csv`
- `modality_agnostic_real_db_signal_units.csv`

We then widened this into an exhaustion pass over every real surface currently
normalized enough to run without changing production behavior: the four
Wikimedia image/audio/text scenarios, three real Samplelib video/audio stream
scenarios (`1 fps` frames, `1 s` audio chunks, and interleaved AV), four real
dialogue-corpus text scenarios (`PersonaChat`, `Taskmaster`, `TopicalChat`, and
`EmpatheticDialogues`), a real RAVDESS speech-corpus slice, and a read-only
audit of the existing chat memory database. The generated benchmark run covered
`12` real ingress scenarios, `166` stored signal-evidence rows, and `58`
long-term memory rows. The aggregate run wrote `runtime_label_rows=0`,
`fact_assertion_rows=0`, and `fact_evidence_rows=0`, so the new benchmark
remained label/fact-free.

The real chat DB audit adds a separate production-shaped structural data point:
`examples/chat/chat_memory.db` contained `13` memories and `51` linked signals
(`26` image, `22` audio, `3` text), with `12` multimodal memory-row units, `2`
soft anchors, and still `0` labels/facts. The prior `video_media_perf` SQLite
files were empty for memory/signal graph purposes; the real Samplelib stream is
therefore represented by the new direct-ingress scenarios rather than those
older perf DBs.

The widened benchmark compared blob-only similarity, memory-embedding
similarity at three thresholds, memory-embedding plus temporal adjacency,
signal-aware temporal adjacency, and Soft Anchor continuity:

| variant | node coverage | signal coverage | edges | cross-group edges | mixed clusters |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| blob-only similarity | 0.79 | 0.74 | 174 | 0 | 0 |
| memory embedding similarity `0.78` | 1.00 | 1.00 | 185 | 0 | 1 |
| memory embedding similarity `0.65` | 1.00 | 1.00 | 209 | 0 | 1 |
| memory embedding similarity `0.90` | 1.00 | 1.00 | 98 | 0 | 1 |
| memory similarity + temporal | 1.00 | 1.00 | 231 | 1 | 2 |
| signal-aware temporal | 1.00 | 1.00 | 46 | 1 | 2 |
| Soft Anchor continuity | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

Interpretation: a graph rooted in memory blobs or text labels is the wrong
primitive for multimodal data. Blob-only coverage improved from the first tiny
Wikimedia pass because the wider run now includes text memories, audio-only
memory blobs, and stream payloads; it still missed `12 / 58` memory rows and
`43 / 166` signal-evidence rows, and blob similarity is a payload-shape
primitive rather than a stable semantic or multimodal graph relation. Memory
embeddings covered the surface at all tested thresholds, but the threshold
sweep did not remove the underlying mixed episode. Naive temporal edges still
created the dog/car cross-event edge. The current Soft Anchor rows are not
production graph edges,
and they should not be treated as hard identity edges, but they are usable as
optional continuity evidence: in this widened run they still avoided adding the
dog/car temporal cross-edge. They also still cannot repair a memory that was
already formed as a mixed dog/car episode; that failure belongs to
accumulator/write timing, not graph traversal.

The resulting graph direction is modality-agnostic: memory nodes should carry
representative embeddings and bounded episode metadata; signal-evidence edges
should preserve the original image/audio/text payload rows; Soft Anchor links
should be weak likelihood edges that can annotate retrieval results and graph
context without asserting identity; and durable graph labels/facts should remain
disabled until a multimodal label extractor exists. Consolidation should consume
this structure later, not replace it with text-only summaries.

The same benchmark now emits sidecar consolidation units over the exact same
real-data run. These units are not production consolidation output. They answer
what consolidation *could* safely consume while runtime labels are disabled:
formed memory rows, one unit per signal-evidence row, or graph clusters from the
sidecar graph variants.

| consolidation unit variant | memory coverage | signal coverage | units | mixed units | multimodal units | unit precision |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| memory row units | 1.00 | 1.00 | 58 | 1 | 10 | 0.983 |
| signal evidence units | 1.00 | 1.00 | 166 | 0 | 0 | 1.000 |
| cluster blob-only similarity | 0.79 | 0.74 | 7 | 0 | 0 | 1.000 |
| cluster memory embedding similarity `0.78` | 1.00 | 1.00 | 14 | 1 | 6 | 0.929 |
| cluster memory embedding similarity `0.65` | 1.00 | 1.00 | 13 | 1 | 6 | 0.923 |
| cluster memory embedding similarity `0.90` | 1.00 | 1.00 | 26 | 1 | 6 | 0.962 |
| cluster memory + temporal | 1.00 | 1.00 | 12 | 2 | 5 | 0.833 |
| cluster signal-aware temporal | 1.00 | 1.00 | 12 | 2 | 5 | 0.833 |
| cluster Soft Anchor continuity | 1.00 | 1.00 | 58 | 1 | 10 | 0.983 |

Interpretation: signal-evidence rows are the safest consolidation substrate
because they preserve every modality payload and never create mixed dog/car
units in this slice, but they do not perform episode fusion. Memory-row and Soft
Anchor cluster units preserve multimodal fusion and full coverage, but they
inherit the one mixed episode already formed by the accumulator. Temporal
cluster units are worse because they merge adjacent dog/car memories in the
dog-then-car sequence. Therefore the benchmark-supported consolidation contract
is two-layered: use `Memory` as the candidate consolidation unit only when its
signal evidence is internally coherent; always keep `SignalEvidence` rows as
the auditable source of truth; treat Soft Anchor as optional continuity context;
and fall back to signal-level or ambiguous consolidation when a memory contains
mixed evidence. The graph can be modality-agnostic now, but durable
cross-modal consolidation still depends on better natural episode/write timing
or a future multimodal extractor.

Exhaustion matrix for this pass:

| angle | covered evidence | result |
|---|---|---|
| real still image + text + audio | Wikimedia dog and car scenarios | multimodal memory representation works; event split remains imperfect |
| real image/audio interleave | Wikimedia dog/audio then car/image | accumulator can still form one mixed memory |
| real video stream | Samplelib `1 fps` frames from decoded MP4 | graph coverage holds on stream-like visual ingress |
| real audio stream | Samplelib `1 s` audio chunks | signal-evidence units remain precise; memory rows are the fusion point |
| real AV stream | Samplelib interleaved frame/audio chunks | widened graph metrics still favor SignalEvidence as audit truth |
| real speech corpus | RAVDESS Actor 16 WAV files decoded and resampled in-benchmark | `60` real WAV events produced `54` audio signals and `12` long-term audio memories |
| real dialogue corpora | PersonaChat, Taskmaster, TopicalChat, EmpatheticDialogues first held-out conversations | text corpora added `62` stored signals and `31` long-term memories without labels/facts |
| real chat DB | `examples/chat/chat_memory.db` | `13` memories / `51` signals / `12` multimodal memory units / `0` labels/facts |
| blob graph | memory-row blobs only | insufficient coverage |
| embedding graph | thresholds `0.65`, `0.78`, `0.90` | full coverage, but thresholding does not solve mixed episodes |
| temporal graph | immediate adjacency | creates cross-event errors |
| Soft Anchor graph context | soft-anchor links as weak continuity | avoids new temporal cross-edge but is not a repair mechanism |
| consolidation granularity | memory rows, signal rows, graph clusters | signal rows safest; memory rows useful only when internally coherent |
| existing DB unit splits | memory row, memory-modality, memory-source, signal row | chat DB shows most memories are multimodal, so consolidation needs signal-level audit fallback |

This still does not prove universal robustness across every external corpus or
every possible capture condition. It does close the local benchmark gap for the
available normalized media and dialogue surfaces: real still image/text/audio,
real video, real streamed audio, real AV interleave, real speech WAVs, real
dialogue text, and an existing production-shaped chat DB. The conclusion for
the current multimodal graph path is therefore narrow but now better covered:
with labeling disabled, the only representation that survives all covered
angles is a two-layer graph of `Memory` candidate units plus `SignalEvidence`
source rows, with Soft Anchor retained as weak context and with signal-level
fallback for mixed memory rows.

We then added `cortext_audio_video_accumulator_bench` to separate audio capture
chunking from memory duration. The benchmark writes controlled audio/image
signals through the accumulator/storage path and audits a live chat database,
recording memory span, `n_signals`, per-signal audio duration, and
memory-level PCM duration for audio-only memories.

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_audio_video_accumulator_bench \
  --output-dir build/audio_video_accumulator_bench \
  --audit-db examples/chat/chat_memory.db
```

The controlled audio results show the distinction clearly:

| scenario | memories | chunk | observed memory shape |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `audio_10x_1s_final_flush` | 4 | 1.0 s | three 3-signal / 3.0 s audio memories plus one 1.0 s tail |
| `audio_5x_1s_force_each` | 5 | 1.0 s | five 1-signal / 1.0 s audio memories |
| `audio_chunk_sweep_250ms` | 2 | 0.25 s | one 3-signal / 0.75 s memory plus one 0.25 s tail |
| `audio_chunk_sweep_500ms` | 2 | 0.5 s | one 3-signal / 1.5 s memory plus one 0.5 s tail |
| `audio_chunk_sweep_1000ms` | 2 | 1.0 s | one 3-signal / 3.0 s memory plus one 1.0 s tail |
| `audio_chunk_sweep_2000ms` | 2 | 2.0 s | one 3-signal / 6.0 s memory plus one 2.0 s tail |

Interpretation: the one-second observation is primarily a signal-chunk and UI
exposure issue, not a hard memory-storage limit. Webcam audio currently arrives
as one-second PCM signals, and the DB view exposes per-signal playback, so each
playable signal row is one second. However, memory storage can and does attach
multiple audio signals to one memory and concatenates PCM for audio-only
memories. The deeper accumulator issue remains that the default boundary/write
path tends to flush controlled audio after roughly three chunks, and mixed
image/audio memories need a media-aware consumer that can assemble the memory's
audio signal set instead of treating individual signal payloads as complete
memories.

We repaired that consumer/storage contract next. Mixed media memories now keep
their image/audio/text payloads as grouped `signals` rows rather than writing a
single invalid concatenated memory blob. Memory-level blobs are only emitted for
coherent byte streams: text, audio-only PCM, or a single payload. In the chat DB
view, expanded memories now show media counts and a combined memory-audio
playback control that concatenates all audio signals in serial order; image
payloads remain loaded only on demand.

We also added an explicit processing retention contract for no-storage live
queries. Public `ProcessText`, `ProcessTextAt`, `ProcessAudio`, and
`ProcessImage` calls default to `Retention::Durable`; callers must explicitly
pass `Retention::Ephemeral` to process a signal without allowing durable memory
storage. The write gate treats ephemeral signals as hard no-store decisions
before flush, spike-bypass, or force-write logic, memory storage has a
defensive retention check, and the accumulator does not attach ephemeral payload
records to later durable writes. The chat Playground uses this mode for
text/audio/video/image probes, while normal combined webcam ingress remains
durable. This lets the demo exercise WM/STM/LTM state and cross-modal retrieval
without polluting the database with every manual probe.

## Stability Sweep (Long Horizon)

We swept Stability with **F=0.5, S=0.5**, using **2 conversations × 360 turns** (`max_total=720`). Stability adjusts persistence and gating strictness, so we track interrupt behavior and candidate volume.

| T | interrupt_turn_rate | precision | recall | fp_rate | fn_rate | retrieval_avg_candidates | retrieval_semantic_overlap_mean |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.3 | 0.483 | 0.995 | 0.870 | 0.0053 | 0.1296 | 31.20 | 0.528 |
| 0.5 | 0.483 | 0.995 | 0.879 | 0.0053 | 0.1215 | 27.28 | 0.526 |
| 0.7 | 0.455 | 0.994 | 0.823 | 0.0056 | 0.1767 | 29.35 | 0.527 |

**Observations:** Higher Stability slightly reduces interrupt rate and recall (more false negatives), consistent with stricter gating; mid‑range T preserves recall while keeping precision stable. Candidate counts remain in the same band, indicating Stability primarily affects decision thresholds rather than retrieval breadth.

## ES-AIST Label Centroid Regeneration

After moving the multimodal encoder path to ES-AIST, we audited the existing
centroid assets and found that the deployed baked centroids under
`data/affect/*_256.npy`, `data/emotion/*_256.npy`, and
`data/audio_emotion/*_256.npy` remain 256-dimensional legacy assets. They are
not comparable to the ES-AIST 1536-dimensional output contract:

| view | slice |
|---|---:|
| `semantic_key` | `z[0:768]` |
| `entity_key` | `z[768:1536]` |
| `full_key` | `z[0:1536]` |

We therefore added a reproducible centroid-source builder:

```bash
python3 tools/build_label_centroid_sources.py \
  --out-dir build/label_centroid_sources
```

The builder ingests the checked-in SALT table, English WordNet 2025 XML, the
existing label bank, and the text-emotion sample files that produced the old
emotion centroids. It writes prompt rows, label rows, a summary, and a
reproducibility manifest with input SHA-256s. The generated source pack contains
`75,578` label records and `353,637` prompt rows:

| source | labels | prompt rows |
|---|---:|---:|
| `data/label_bank/labels.jsonl` | 6,478 | 12,956 |
| `data/english-wordnet-2025.xml` | 68,472 | 286,718 |
| `data/salt.csv` | 622 | 33,588 |
| `data/emotion/_tmp_text_emotion` | 6 | 20,375 |

We then added `cortext_label_centroid_bench`, which encodes the source prompts
with native ES-AIST GGUF kernels, builds centroids in each ES view, evaluates
held-out prompts against the centroid bank, and writes the centroid artifacts and
failure examples. The benchmark records that the old 256d centroids are
incompatible with the ES-AIST space rather than silently reusing them.

Full SALT run:

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_label_centroid_bench \
  --source-records build/label_centroid_sources/label_centroid_source_records.jsonl \
  --models models \
  --output-dir build/label_centroid_bench_salt \
  --source-filter salt.csv \
  --train-prompts-per-label 44
```

| view | top-1 | top-5 | top-10 | MRR | mean rank |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `semantic_key` | 0.6413 | 0.8701 | 0.9256 | 0.7432 | 3.99 |
| `entity_key` | 0.5783 | 0.8199 | 0.8868 | 0.6861 | 5.36 |
| `full_key` | 0.6260 | 0.8596 | 0.9183 | 0.7301 | 4.25 |

This run encoded `33,588` prompt rows for `622` labels. Mean encode latency was
`2.16 ms` and p95 was `3.06 ms`. SALT is mostly a sound/scene label source, so
the semantic view being strongest is expected. The failure examples are mostly
near-neighbor confusions such as horn/bell/music subclasses rather than random
label drift.

Label-bank 1k sanity run:

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_label_centroid_bench \
  --source-records build/label_centroid_sources/label_centroid_source_records.jsonl \
  --models models \
  --output-dir build/label_centroid_bench_label_bank_1k \
  --source-filter data/label_bank/labels.jsonl \
  --max-labels 1000 \
  --train-prompts-per-label 1
```

| view | top-1 | top-5 | top-10 | MRR | mean rank |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `semantic_key` | 0.4390 | 0.6510 | 0.7140 | 0.5339 | 39.60 |
| `entity_key` | 0.5230 | 0.6980 | 0.7480 | 0.6038 | 45.39 |
| `full_key` | 0.5240 | 0.7000 | 0.7510 | 0.6067 | 38.82 |

Here the entity/full slices clearly improve over semantic-only, which is the
expected direction for name/entity-style labels. Mean encode latency was
`1.75 ms`, p95 `3.27 ms`.

WordNet 200-label sanity run:

| view | top-1 | top-5 | top-10 | MRR | mean rank |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `semantic_key` | 0.6300 | 0.8650 | 0.9150 | 0.7367 | 3.36 |
| `entity_key` | 0.6150 | 0.8900 | 0.9250 | 0.7288 | 3.67 |
| `full_key` | 0.6350 | 0.8650 | 0.9300 | 0.7473 | 3.19 |

Text-emotion centroid redo:

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_label_centroid_bench \
  --source-records build/label_centroid_sources/label_centroid_source_records.jsonl \
  --models models \
  --output-dir build/label_centroid_bench_text_emotion \
  --source-filter data/emotion/_tmp_text_emotion \
  --train-prompts-per-label 1000 \
  --max-eval-prompts-per-label 500
```

| view | top-1 | top-5 | MRR | mean rank |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `semantic_key` | 0.3583 | 0.9430 | 0.5774 | 2.53 |
| `entity_key` | 0.3597 | 0.9413 | 0.5792 | 2.53 |
| `full_key` | 0.3630 | 0.9447 | 0.5795 | 2.52 |

Interpretation: the old 256d centroid files should not be reused for ES-AIST
signals. Regenerating centroids in the ES-AIST contract is reproducible and
fast enough for offline build artifacts. The regenerated centroids are useful as
label priors: semantic is best for SALT sound/scene labels, entity/full are best
on the existing label-bank sample, and WordNet behaves as a broad lexical sanity
check with many legitimate near-synset confusions. The text-emotion result is a
useful caution: the correct emotion is usually in the candidate set, but mean
ES-AIST centroids alone are not a strong six-way affect classifier. Replacing
the old emotion centroids should therefore either preserve the old contrastive
and purification recipe in ES-AIST space or move to a true multimodal label
head/centroid bank.

We then repaired the production centroid path rather than leaving those assets
in a benchmark-only state. Production retrieval currently stores
`RetrievalEmbeddingView(encoded)`, which is the first 256 ES-AIST dimensions,
renormalized. The baked centroid bundle therefore must remain 256-dimensional
until the store schema and public centroid contract change, but the source
vectors must be regenerated from the same ES-AIST slice. We added:

```bash
python3 tools/centroid_vectors/build_aist_sliced_centroids.py \
  --models models \
  --text-embedder build/tools/text_embedder/cortext_text_embedder \
  --audio-embedder build/tools/aist_audio_embedder/cortext_aist_audio_embedder \
  --out-root data \
  --work-dir build/aist_sliced_centroids

python3 tools/centroid_vectors/centroid_vectors.py embed
```

The first command rewrites `data/emotion/*_256.npy`,
`data/affect/*_256.npy`, and `data/audio_emotion/*_256.npy` from the active
ES-AIST encoder's `[0:256]` retrieval slice. Text emotion centroids reuse the
existing emotion source files, apply global mean-centering, purification, and
contrastive class-vs-other centroids. Affect centroids are rebuilt from the
emotion pools plus deterministic valence/arousal/goal/violation prompt banks.
Audio emotion centroids are rebuilt from real RAVDESS WAV media through a new
native `cortext_aist_audio_embedder`, then sliced and normalized in the same
way. The second command rebakes `src/data/embedded_centroid_vectors.cpp` so
runtime affect metrics, sensitivity updates, graph affect retrieval, and audio
emotion priors all use the ES-AIST-compatible 256d assets.

Validation: every required regenerated `.npy` file has shape `(256,)`, finite
values, and norm `1.000000`; `cortext_tests '[operations][centroids]'`,
`cortext_tests '[augmem][affect]'`, and `cortext_tests '[data][affect]'` all
pass. This does not make centroid labels a full multimodal labeling system, but
it removes the incompatible EmbeddingGemma/legacy centroid mismatch from
the production engine.

### Benchmark-Only 256d Label Vector DB

We next tested whether the label system should move from one centroid per label
to an embedded 256d label-vector database. This was kept completely outside
production. The new benchmark executable:

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_label_vector_db_bench \
  --source-records build/label_centroid_sources/label_centroid_source_records.jsonl \
  --models models \
  --output-dir build/label_vector_db_salt_topk \
  --source-filter salt.csv \
  --prototype-candidates-per-label 24 \
  --max-prototypes-per-label 16 \
  --max-eval-prompts-per-label 8
```

writes:

* `label_vector_db_256.f32`: row-major normalized 256d prototype vectors;
* `label_vector_db_rows.csv`: row-to-label/prototype metadata;
* `label_vector_db_labels.csv`: label metadata and prototype ranges;
* `label_vector_db_manifest.json`: embeddable artifact contract;
* evaluation cases, failures, latency, and metrics JSON.

The scoring comparison uses the same ES-AIST `[0:256]` retrieval slice as the
production centroid path. We compared `centroid_256` against prototype max and
top-3 prototype pooling. The best prototype variant is shown for each slice:

| slice | labels | prototype rows | eval prompts | DB MiB | centroid top-1 | centroid top-5 | best prototype variant | prototype top-1 | prototype top-5 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|
| SALT 16-prototype | 622 | 9,952 | 4,976 | 9.72 | 0.5878 | 0.8260 | `prototype_top3_mean_16_256` | 0.5117 | 0.7562 |
| WordNet 2k | 2,000 | 7,469 | 2,275 | 7.29 | 0.1938 | 0.3745 | `prototype_max_1_256` | 0.1837 | 0.3380 |
| text emotion | 6 | 192 | 3,000 | 0.19 | 0.3287 | 0.9310 | `prototype_max_2_256` | 0.2610 | 0.8910 |
| label-bank 1k | 1,000 | 1,000 | 1,000 | 0.98 | 0.3360 | 0.5440 | `prototype_max_1_256` | 0.3360 | 0.5440 |

We also emitted a full all-source benchmark-only DB artifact:

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_label_vector_db_bench \
  --source-records build/label_centroid_sources/label_centroid_source_records.jsonl \
  --models models \
  --output-dir build/label_vector_db_full_2proto \
  --source-filter all \
  --prototype-candidates-per-label 2 \
  --max-prototypes-per-label 2 \
  --skip-eval
```

This artifact contains `75,578` labels and `151,156` 256d prototype rows. The
raw vector matrix is `147.61 MiB`, with `15 MiB` of row metadata and `6.4 MiB`
of label metadata. It encoded in `170.72 s`, with mean text encode latency
`1.12 ms` and p95 `2.33 ms`.

Interpretation: a label-vector DB is easy to generate and small enough to
discuss as an embedded optional asset, but the direct nearest-prototype policy
does **not** beat the centroid path on the current text-derived label sources.
Top-k prototype pooling reduces the damage from noisy exemplars, but still
trails the centroid on SALT, WordNet, and text emotion. The label DB should
therefore not replace centroids as the first production label scorer. The more
defensible design is a hybrid: keep centroids for cheap label priors and use a
prototype/vector DB as an inspectable backing store for richer future consumers,
especially once image/audio-derived label exemplars or pre-projection feature
heads are available.

### Benchmark-Only Open-Name Vector Probe

We then tested the specific hypothesis that open names might be recoverable
without an autoregressive extractor by embedding a large forename bank and
retrieving nearest names with the current plain encoder. This remained
benchmark-only and did not change production retrieval, soft anchors, labels, or
facts.

Command:

```bash
python3 tools/name_vector_retrieval_probe.py \
  --output-dir build/name_vector_retrieval_probe \
  --top-names 5000 \
  --force
```

The script uses `data/surnames/forenames.csv`, keeps the top `5,000` aggregate
forenames plus forced probe names, and embeds five templates per name:
bare name, `a person named X`, `someone called X`, `X's house`, and
`the dog named X`. The runtime encoder was the current default
`ES-AIST-81M-GGUF` text path
(`models/ES-AIST-81M-preview-GGUF/ES-AIST-81M_q8_0.gguf`), producing `1536d`
vectors. The probe embedded `25,005` name-template rows and `30` memory-like
test utterances: `15` with expected names and `15` no-name controls including
common-word lures such as `rose`, `summer`, `April`, `mark`, `bill`, and
`grant`.

Main results:

| variant | positive top-1 | positive top-3 | positive top-5 | negative p95 best score | zero-FPR top-5 recovery | 5% FPR top-5 recovery |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| name only | 0.1333 | 0.2000 | 0.4000 | 0.9057 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |
| person context | 0.2667 | 0.4000 | 0.4667 | 0.9057 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |
| name + named pet | 0.3333 | 0.5333 | 0.5333 | 0.9057 | 0.1333 | 0.1333 |
| all templates | 0.4667 | 0.6000 | 0.6000 | 0.9057 | 0.1333 | 0.1333 |
| all templates, common-word names filtered | 0.0667 | 0.0667 | 0.0667 | 0.8923 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |

Representative positives worked: `Jared's house` retrieved `Jared` at rank 1,
`That dog's name is Bailey` retrieved `Bailey` at rank 1, `Maya` and `Omar`
also retrieved at rank 1, and `Maria` appeared in the top 3 for
`Maria is bringing her dog Luna`. But several visible names were missed:
`Jordan`, `Sarah`, `Priya`, `Diego`, `Chen`, and `Grant` did not appear in the
top 5 under the all-template policy. The no-name controls also produced high
name-like scores, for example `We just hung out for a while` retrieved `Boy`
with score `0.9057`, and common-word controls retrieved plausible names such as
`Summer`, `River`, `April`, `Bill`, and `Grant`. Filtering names that are common
English words reduced some lures but destroyed recall for real names that are
also ordinary words.

Interpretation: a plain encoder plus a name vector DB is useful as a weak
proposal source, not as a standalone name extractor. It can surface obvious
candidate names for a human or LLM in some text cases, but it cannot safely
abstain from ordinary no-name memories without losing most recall. It also does
not solve private image/audio naming unless a name has already been linked in
the local memory state. This supports the hybrid architecture: keep name-vector
retrieval as an uncertain `possible_name` signal, but use span/ASR or a bounded
autoregressive path for reliable open-string extraction and promotion.

### Benchmark-Only Label Graph DB Consolidation

The next question was whether the full `75,578`-label vector DB becomes useful
when it is not treated as a one-shot nearest-label classifier, but as graph
evidence accumulated over memories and signal rows. We kept this benchmark-only.
Production retrieval, production consolidation, runtime labels, and facts remain
unchanged.

First, `cortext_modality_agnostic_graph_bench` now writes an embedding surface
sidecar:

* `modality_agnostic_graph_embedding_rows.csv`
* `modality_agnostic_graph_embeddings.f32`

Each row is either a `signal` node or a `memory` node with scenario id, node id,
memory id, modality set, offline scoring group, and a normalized 256d stored
embedding. Then the new script:

```bash
python3 tools/label_graph_db_consolidation_bench.py \
  --graph-dir build/modality_agnostic_graph_bench_label_surface \
  --label-db-dir build/label_vector_db_full_2proto \
  --output-dir build/label_graph_db_consolidation_signal_surface_sweep \
  --surface signal \
  --top-rows 768 \
  --top-labels 75
```

scores each node against the full label DB, emits memory-label edges, builds
label-overlap graph edges, and evaluates only with offline dog/car labels. It
also reruns with `--surface memory`, `--include-modalities text,image`, and
`--include-modalities audio,image`.

Artifacts:

* `label_graph_db_results.json`
* `label_graph_db_memory_labels.csv`
* `label_graph_db_label_summary.csv`
* `label_graph_db_edges.csv`
* `label_graph_db_clusters.csv`
* `label_graph_db_failure_examples.csv`
* `label_graph_db_memory_aggregate_labels.csv`

The memory-row-only pass is weak as a graph construction test because the real
Wikimedia scenarios usually contain only one dog memory and one car memory. It
therefore has almost no positive same-group memory-memory pairs to recover.
Still, it is useful as a label-surfacing check: over `58` memory nodes and `5`
offline-scored dog/car memories, the WordNet-only label DB hit the expected
dog/car label in top-10 for `4 / 5` memories and top-50 for `5 / 5`. No tested
memory-row label-edge rule recovered positive same-group graph edges.

The signal-level surface is more informative because the real image/text/audio
signals are separate positive evidence nodes before consolidation:

| surface | nodes | scored nodes | best expected label hit@10 | best graph edge rule | scored edge precision | same-group recall | cross-group rate | unit precision |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| memory nodes | 58 | 5 | 0.80 | none recovered positives | -- | 0.00 | 0.00 | -- |
| signal nodes, all modalities | 166 | 15 | 0.667 | WordNet token top-50 | 0.786 | 0.917 | 0.300 | 0.833 |
| signal nodes, text+image | 90 | 10 | 1.000 | WordNet token top-50 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.000 | 1.000 |
| signal nodes, audio+image | 100 | 11 | 0.545 | WordNet token top-50 | 0.625 | 1.000 | 0.500 | 0.750 |

This result says the label graph is not universally useless, but its current
safe operating region is narrow. Text and image rows produce useful WordNet
object/event evidence in this slice. The text+image ablation recovered every
scored same-group dog/car pair and created no dog/car cross-group pair. Audio is
the failure mode: the word-audio rows for `Bailey` and `crash` retrieved labels
such as `yester`, `lesser`, `bald`, and `ergative-absolutive language` instead
of the intended lexical/object labels. When audio is included, same-group recall
can remain high only by accepting dog/car cross-links.

Memory-level label aggregation shows the same pattern. Aggregating labels across
all signal rows inside a memory with a small support bonus reached `5 / 5`
`any_group_hit_top10` for WordNet, but only `4 / 5` `all_groups_hit_top10`: the
miss is the deliberately mixed audio/image interleave memory containing both
dog and car groups. Text-only aggregation is perfect on the `4` memories that
contain text, while non-text aggregation falls to `1 / 5` on the full dog/car
memory slice and `2 / 5` any-hit when restricted to audio+image.

Interpretation: a 75k label-vector DB can be useful as a candidate label graph
for text/image-supported memories and as an inspectable explanation surface. It
does not currently solve multimodal graph consolidation on its own. In
particular, the stored 256d audio embedding slice is not a reliable lexical or
object label signal, so a production graph built directly from these label edges
would need modality-quality weighting and would still have to fall back to
signal-evidence rows when the accumulator forms a mixed event. The defensible
near-term design is therefore not "replace consolidation with a label graph";
it is "attach tentative label candidates to signal/memory nodes, use them as
weak graph evidence when text/image agreement exists, and require a stronger
multimodal label source before durable graph labels/facts are enabled."

### ES-AIST Full-Slice Label Graph Diagnostic

The previous label-graph run used the stored `RetrievalEmbeddingView`, which is
the first `256` dimensions of the ES-AIST embedding. To avoid over-interpreting
that truncated surface, we added
`examples/benchmark/es_aist_label_graph_signal_bench.cpp`. This benchmark uses
the native ES-AIST q8 GGUF runtime directly, encodes the same real Wikimedia
dog/car image, text, and audio signals, and compares four ES views:

* `prefix256 = z[0:256]`
* `semantic768 = z[0:768]`
* `entity768 = z[768:1536]`
* `full1536 = z[0:1536]`

It then scores the signals against the full `75,578` label universe and emits:

* `es_aist_label_graph_results.json`
* `es_aist_label_graph_signal_labels.csv`
* `es_aist_label_graph_edges.csv`
* `es_aist_label_graph_failures.csv`

Run:

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_es_aist_label_graph_signal_bench \
  --models models \
  --assets-dir build/real_multimodal_episode_assets \
  --source-records build/label_centroid_sources/label_centroid_source_records.jsonl \
  --output-dir build/es_aist_label_graph_signal_all_labels_top50 \
  --max-labels 0 \
  --top-k 50 \
  --label-text-mode label \
  --label-match-mode label
```

The native q8 path used Metal kernels. Encoding the `75,578` label strings took
`82.23 s`; encoding the `16` real dog/car signal rows took `8.10 s`. The full
ES-AIST slices changed the label-surfacing picture:

| view | modality | hit@10 | hit@25 | hit@50 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| entity768 | audio | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.50 |
| entity768 | image | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| entity768 | text | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| full1536 | audio | 0.00 | 0.50 | 0.50 |
| full1536 | image | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| full1536 | text | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |

The image and text paths are strong across the wider ES-AIST views. Audio is
still not a dependable lexical/object label source. The audio examples here are
spoken words from Wikimedia (`Bailey` and `crash`), so this should not be read
as an acoustic-event failure only. It shows that the current audio embedding
should not be expected to replace ASR or a dedicated acoustic label head for
lexical graph labels.

Graph edges without modality or label-kind gating remained unsafe. On
`entity768`, token overlap at top-25 produced precision `0.667`, same-group
recall `0.714`, and cross-group rate `0.385`. At full `1536`, token overlap at
top-25 produced precision `0.643`, same-group recall `0.643`, and cross-group
rate `0.385`. The failure rows show the same pathology as the 256d run:
`Bailey` and `crash` audio often surface generic linguistic labels such as
`ergative-absolutive language`, which then create dog/car cross-links.

We also tested a plausible improvement: encode each label with aliases,
definitions, and up to four prompt/prototype strings, then match edges using
expanded aliases/definitions. That run wrote
`build/es_aist_label_graph_signal_expanded_all_labels`. It was slower
(`169.92 s` for labels) and worse: audio hit@50 fell to `0.00`, and
`entity768` top-25 graph precision dropped to `0.375` with cross-group rate
`0.769`. Expanded text introduced broad shared terms faster than it improved
the signal.

Finally, `tools/es_aist_label_graph_posthoc_ablation.py` tested whether the
graph can be made useful by constraining the evidence type rather than by asking
the model to solve every modality at once:

```bash
python3 tools/es_aist_label_graph_posthoc_ablation.py \
  --input-csv build/es_aist_label_graph_signal_all_labels_top50/es_aist_label_graph_signal_labels.csv \
  --output-dir build/es_aist_label_graph_signal_all_labels_top50_posthoc
```

The best healthy setting was narrow but clean: bare-label ES-AIST,
`entity768`, top-10 or top-25, core/strict label kinds, and no audio edges. On
