the real dog/car text+image pairs this recovered all same-group pairs and no
cross-group pairs:

| view | labels | modalities | top-k | precision | same-group recall | cross-group rate |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| entity768 | core kinds | image+text | 10 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.00 |
| entity768 | core kinds | image+text | 25 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.00 |
| full1536 | all kinds | image+text | 25 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.00 |

This answers the label-graph question more precisely. Yes, a 75k label DB can
build useful graph evidence from ES-AIST signals, but not as a universal
multimodal durable-label source. The version that works today is:

1. keep labels as tentative signal/memory evidence, not facts;
2. use ES-AIST `entity768` or `full1536` for text/image label support;
3. filter to object/entity/event-like label kinds for graph edges;
4. treat audio labels as non-durable unless corroborated by text/image, ASR, or
   a future acoustic label head.

The current evidence therefore supports a graph assistant, not a production
multimodal label consolidator. It can add inspectable candidate labels and
explain why text/image memories are related. It should not yet create durable
multimodal graph facts from audio-label overlap.

### Ordered Multimodal Graph Policy Diagnostic

The full-slice label graph result still treated audio in two unsatisfactory
ways: either audio directly created lexical label edges, which was unsafe, or
audio was removed from durable graph construction, which was safe but not truly
multimodal. We therefore added a final posthoc policy diagnostic to ask a
narrower engine question:

> Can audio participate in a multimodal graph unit if lexical/object labels are
> supplied by text/image evidence and audio is attached through chronological
> ingress structure?

This is still benchmark-only. Production retrieval, storage, consolidation, and
facts remain unchanged.

First, we expanded the real-media slice with additional public Wikimedia media:
cat, train, and bell images plus corresponding spoken-word audio. The asset
prep script writes source/raw SHA-256s and normalized ES-AIST-compatible media:

```bash
python3 tools/prepare_extended_label_graph_assets.py \
  --output-dir build/extended_label_graph_assets
```

The ES-AIST signal label benchmark now detects those optional assets and expands
from `16` to `40` real signal rows across `9` scenarios. The full-label run was:

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_es_aist_label_graph_signal_bench \
  --models models \
  --assets-dir build/real_multimodal_episode_assets \
  --source-records build/label_centroid_sources/label_centroid_source_records.jsonl \
  --output-dir build/es_aist_label_graph_extended_all_labels_top50 \
  --max-labels 0 \
  --top-k 50 \
  --label-text-mode label \
  --label-match-mode label
```

It encoded `75,578` labels in `74.86 s` and `40` real signal rows in
`20.14 s`. The wider real slice preserved the earlier modality pattern:

| view | modality | hit@10 | hit@25 | hit@50 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| entity768 | audio | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.20 |
| entity768 | image | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| entity768 | text | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |

Then `tools/es_aist_multimodal_graph_policy_ablation.py` compared policies that
consume those labels and the chronological signal order:

```bash
python3 tools/es_aist_multimodal_graph_policy_ablation.py \
  --input-csv build/es_aist_label_graph_extended_all_labels_top50/es_aist_label_graph_signal_labels.csv \
  --output-dir build/es_aist_multimodal_graph_policy_extended_entity_core_v3 \
  --view entity768 \
  --top-k 25
```

The important variants were:

* `direct_label_all_modalities`: all modalities may create label-overlap edges;
* `text_image_only`: only text/image label edges form durable graph units;
* `audio_cooccur_previous_r1`: audio attaches to the immediately previous
  text/image label unit;
* `audio_label_temporal_r2`: audio may attach through its own label overlap
  when a candidate is within two chronological steps;
* `audio_ordered_cooccurrence_r1`: audio after a text-supported unit attaches
  backward; audio immediately before a visual observation attaches forward; the
  lexical label edge still comes from text/image evidence.

On the expanded `9`-scenario real-media slice, direct audio label overlap
remained unsafe:

| policy | durable precision | mixed durable units | audio durable coverage |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| direct all-modal label overlap | 0.630 | 4 | 0.778 |
| text/image label units only | 1.000 | 0 | 0.000 |
| audio previous co-occurrence | 1.000 | 0 | 0.778 |
| audio label + temporal radius 2 | 0.889 | 1 | 0.667 |
| ordered audio co-occurrence | 1.000 | 0 | 1.000 |

The ordered co-occurrence policy was also robust to the main safe slice choices:

| run | ordered precision | mixed durable units | audio coverage |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| entity768, top-10, core kinds | 1.000 | 0 | 1.000 |
| entity768, top-25, core kinds | 1.000 | 0 | 1.000 |
| semantic768, top-25, core kinds | 1.000 | 0 | 1.000 |
| full1536, top-25, core kinds | 1.000 | 0 | 1.000 |
| entity768, top-50, core kinds | 0.778 | 2 | 1.000 |
| entity768, top-25, all label kinds | 0.778 | 2 | 1.000 |

Interpretation: the current embeddings can support a useful multimodal graph
policy, but the policy is not "audio labels graph themselves." The healthy
shape is:

1. use text/image ES-AIST label evidence to establish object/event graph units;
2. keep label kind filtering tight and avoid very broad top-k label overlap;
3. use chronological ingress order to attach nearby audio to those graph units;
4. treat audio lexical labels as diagnostic corroboration, not durable graph
   authority.

This is the first graph experiment in this sequence that gives a positive
implementation direction with the current assets: graph consolidation can use
embedding-derived labels plus ingress order as a multimodal evidence packet.
The remaining risk is generality. The ordered policy was evaluated on a small
but real and reproducible media slice; it should be implemented first as a
shadow graph-consolidation policy and validated on live webcam/audio chat before
durable graph facts consume it.

### Gemma 3n Autoregressive Multimodal Label Diagnostic

The label-vector and ES-AIST graph experiments above show that ES-AIST is useful
as a fast signal model, but its audio slice is not a dependable lexical/object
label source. We therefore added a benchmark-only autoregressive label
diagnostic using the smallest practical local trimodal autoregressive model
already present in the repo: Gemma 3n E2B IT LiteRT,
`models/gemma3n-e2b-litert/gemma-3n-E2B-it-int4.litertlm`
(`sha256=2ed7bc3a0026c93d5b8a4544b352d9d00cd66ff0bac3ef6a20ac3d2cba4010d6`).
This experiment does not change production retrieval, production consolidation,
or the ES-AIST signal path.

The new executable is
`examples/benchmark/gemma3n_multimodal_label_bench.cpp`. It sends one real
signal at a time to Gemma 3n and constrains generation to:

```json
{ "labels": ["..."] }
```

The image path uses the existing normalized 384 x 384 RGB real-media assets,
upsampled into the Gemma 3n 768 x 768 image tensor. The audio path uses
LiteRT-LM's default USM MiniAudio preprocessor rather than Cortext's older
coarse audio helper; this matters because the wrong spectrogram contract
hallucinated audio labels in the first smoke run. The media slice contains real
dog, car-crash, cat, train, and bell image/text/audio rows from the existing
Wikimedia-derived benchmark assets.

Build and reusable-engine run:

```bash
cmake --build build -j 8 --target cortext_gemma3n_multimodal_label_bench

./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_gemma3n_multimodal_label_bench \
  --model models/gemma3n-e2b-litert/gemma-3n-E2B-it-int4.litertlm \
  --real-assets-dir build/real_multimodal_episode_assets \
  --extended-assets-dir build/extended_label_graph_assets \
  --output-dir build/gemma3n_multimodal_label_bench \
  --threads 4
```

Artifacts:

* `gemma3n_multimodal_label_results.json`
* `gemma3n_multimodal_label_cases.json`
* `gemma3n_multimodal_label_cases.csv`
* `gemma3n_multimodal_label_failures.csv`

Reusable-engine results:

| modality | cases | label hit | JSON parse | errors | mean ms | p95 ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| audio | 5 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0 | 4691.31 | 4737.19 |
| image | 5 | 0.20 | 0.20 | 4 | 746.46 | 3250.97 |
| text | 5 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0 | 1832.51 | 1914.88 |

The image errors are not model-quality misses; the first image labels correctly,
then subsequent reusable-session image prefill calls fail inside
`vision_litert_compiled_model_executor.cc`. To isolate model quality from that
session reuse issue, the same benchmark was rerun with engine reload per case:

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_gemma3n_multimodal_label_bench \
  --model models/gemma3n-e2b-litert/gemma-3n-E2B-it-int4.litertlm \
  --real-assets-dir build/real_multimodal_episode_assets \
  --extended-assets-dir build/extended_label_graph_assets \
  --output-dir build/gemma3n_multimodal_label_bench_reload \
  --threads 4 \
  --reload-per-case
```

Reload-per-case results:

| modality | cases | label hit | JSON parse | errors | mean ms | p95 ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| audio | 5 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0 | 4759.79 | 4793.43 |
| image | 5 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0 | 3282.81 | 3405.40 |
| text | 5 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0 | 1875.95 | 1968.71 |

Qualitatively, the model returned the expected concrete labels:

* dog image: `dog`, `leaves`, `ball`, `outdoor`, `sunny`;
* dog audio: `Bailey`, `speech`, `name`, `person`;
* car image: `car accident`, `damaged car`, `broken windshield`, `roadside`,
  `tree`;
* crash audio: `crash`, `car`, `damage`, `accident`, `impact`;
* train/bell/cat rows likewise hit the expected object or spoken word.

Interpretation: Gemma 3n E2B is a strong benchmark-only multimodal label
teacher on this small real slice once the audio tensor contract is correct. It
is not yet a realtime consolidation path. Text is slow compared with the
embedding signal path, audio is roughly `4.8 s` per one-second spoken clip in
this debug/local run, and image needs a long-lived vision-session fix before it
can run as an always-on labeler. The useful near-term role is therefore offline
or shadow labeling for graph/audit experiments, not replacing ES-AIST as the
fast ingress signal model. The next production-relevant question is whether
these autoregressive labels improve graph consolidation enough when consumed
sparsely or asynchronously to justify their latency.

### Gemma 4 LiteRT Compatibility Repair

We then repaired the LiteRT-LM dependency and repeated the same benchmark
surface with the public Gemma 4 E2B LiteRT
artifact:
`models/gemma4-e2b-litert/gemma-4-E2B-it.litertlm`
(`sha256=181938105e0eefd105961417e8da75903eacda102c4fce9ce90f50b97139a63c`),
downloaded from `litert-community/gemma-4-E2B-it-litert-lm`. This was a
compatibility test only at the time it was run; production retrieval and
consolidation were unchanged during this benchmark. The current branch later
promoted Gemma 4 E2B to the required `auto` deep-consolidation backend for
multimodal label refinement and summarization.

The vendored LiteRT-LM runtime was updated from the stale local snapshot to
upstream `google-ai-edge/LiteRT-LM` revision
`45c964d98d15c9c399b5673dd6450c9a5041f082`, whose workspace points at LiteRT
`47615eb6eaec25e8dfcd1aba922c560a57cba0a2`. The update added the missing
Gemma 4 metadata and section support (`Gemma4`, `tf_lite_end_of_vision`,
`tf_lite_mtp_drafter`, and related multimodal sections). Cortext's LiteRT
adapter was moved to the current `EngineFactory::CreateDefault` API, and the
benchmark was changed to use the official source-media data processor for Gemma
4 images instead of the older raw `384x384` RGB tensor path. The old raw tensor
path reached the Gemma 4 vision executor and crashed because it bypassed the
Gemma 4 patchification contract.

Repaired command:

```bash
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_gemma3n_multimodal_label_bench \
  --model models/gemma4-e2b-litert/gemma-4-E2B-it.litertlm \
  --real-assets-dir build/real_multimodal_episode_assets \
  --extended-assets-dir build/extended_label_graph_assets \
  --output-dir build/gemma4_multimodal_label_bench_repaired_after_litert_update_v2 \
  --threads 1 \
  --source-media
```

Repaired results:

| modality | cases | label hit | JSON parse | errors | mean ms | p95 ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| image | 5 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0 | 8102.61 | 9020.15 |
| text | 5 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0 | 1858.21 | 2011.01 |
| audio | 5 | 0.20 | 0.20 | 0 | 1536.45 | 2188.35 |
| total | 15 | 0.73 | 0.73 | 0 | 3832.43 | 9020.15 |

This initial repaired run still used the CPU main decoder, CPU audio, and GPU
vision. The accelerator libraries were present, and the runtime selected the
Apple M3 Max Metal adapter through LiteRT's WebGPU/Metal delegate path, but the
main autoregressive decoder was not using that path. We added benchmark-only
backend switches and reran Gemma 4 with `main=gpu`, `vision=gpu`, `audio=cpu`,
and `sampler=gpu`. Full audio GPU cannot load because the Gemma 4 audio encoder
and adapter sections are explicitly constrained to CPU in the artifact. GPU
sampling also falls back to CPU because the bundled WebGPU sampler dylib is
missing `LiteRtTopKWebGpuSampler_UpdateConfig`, but that does not prevent the
main and vision executors from using the Metal-backed GPU delegate.

GPU main/vision results:

| modality | cases | label hit | JSON parse | errors | mean ms | p95 ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| image | 5 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0 | 617.05 | 675.39 |
| text | 5 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0 | 209.80 | 290.35 |
| audio | 5 | 0.40 | 1.00 | 0 | 333.07 | 424.72 |
| total | 15 | 0.80 | 1.00 | 0 | 386.64 | 675.39 |

Interpretation: updating LiteRT-LM was necessary, and the slow first repaired
run was mostly a benchmark backend choice rather than a hard Gemma 4 limit.
Gemma 4 is now executable and fast enough for asynchronous multimodal
consolidation when the main and vision executors use the Metal-backed GPU path.
Text and image labels are strong on this small real slice; audio runs quickly
but remains semantically unreliable under the current direct PCM
prompt/preprocess path. ES-AIST remains the realtime ingress signal model, while
Gemma 4 is now the default deep consolidation/refinement path rather than an
always-on ingress labeler. The remaining engineering caveats are audio semantic
quality and GPU sampler packaging.

### Top-K Embedding-Label Graph Node Experiment

We then ran a fresh benchmark-only experiment on **May 14, 2026** to test the
production concern directly: whether realtime graph construction can use
embedding-derived Top-K label evidence when durable consolidation labels or
exact label ids are missing. The benchmark was
`tools/label_graph_db_consolidation_bench.py`. It does not write to Cortext
databases and does not change production retrieval. Runtime inputs are memory or
signal embeddings only; offline group labels are used only to score the result.

The experiment used the signal surface from
`build/modality_agnostic_graph_bench_label_surface` and the existing full
two-prototype label-vector database in `build/label_vector_db_full_2proto`.
Each signal embedding retrieved up to `768` label-vector rows and kept `75`
deduplicated labels. The graph policies compared exact shared label ids,
token-overlap labels, label-vector-neighbor overlap, and hybrid
memory-plus-label-vector scoring at Top-20 and Top-50.

Commands:

```bash
python3 tools/label_graph_db_consolidation_bench.py \
  --graph-dir build/modality_agnostic_graph_bench_label_surface \
  --label-db-dir build/label_vector_db_full_2proto \
  --output-dir build/topk_embedding_label_graph_experiment_20260514_signal_all \
  --surface signal \
  --include-modalities all \
  --top-rows 768 \
  --top-labels 75 \
  --write-top-labels 20 \
  --filters all,wordnet_only,wordnet_salt,entities_objects_events,objects_events

python3 tools/label_graph_db_consolidation_bench.py \
  --graph-dir build/modality_agnostic_graph_bench_label_surface \
  --label-db-dir build/label_vector_db_full_2proto \
  --output-dir build/topk_embedding_label_graph_experiment_20260514_signal_text_image \
  --surface signal \
  --include-modalities text,image \
  --top-rows 768 \
  --top-labels 75 \
  --write-top-labels 20 \
  --filters all,wordnet_only,wordnet_salt,entities_objects_events,objects_events
```

Artifacts:

* `build/topk_embedding_label_graph_experiment_20260514_signal_all/label_graph_db_results.json`
* `build/topk_embedding_label_graph_experiment_20260514_signal_all/label_graph_db_edges.csv`
* `build/topk_embedding_label_graph_experiment_20260514_signal_text_image/label_graph_db_results.json`
* `build/topk_embedding_label_graph_experiment_20260514_signal_text_image/label_graph_db_edges.csv`

All-modality run:

| slice | memories | scored | elapsed s | all-label mean / p95 ms | object-event mean / p95 ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| signal, all modalities | 166 | 15 | 5.93 | 10.52 / 18.44 | 4.39 / 4.68 |

Text/image-only run:

| slice | memories | scored | elapsed s | all-label mean / p95 ms | object-event mean / p95 ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| signal, text+image | 90 | 10 | 2.86 | 7.31 / 7.84 | 4.40 / 4.64 |

Top-K label hit rates show why this is attractive for realtime graph
construction. On the all-modality slice, expected dog/car labels appeared in the
Top-10, Top-25, and Top-50 lists for `10 / 15` scored signals (`0.667`) across
all tested filters. On the text/image slice, expected labels appeared for
`10 / 10` scored signals at Top-10, Top-25, and Top-50 (`1.000`). Exact shared
label-id graph policies did not recover same-group pairs in either run, which
matches the production problem: requiring exact durable labels is too brittle
when the graph needs to form before consolidation has normalized names.

The graph-edge results separate the useful regime from the unsafe one:

| run | policy | same recall | cross rate | unit precision | multimodal units |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| all modalities | exact Top-20, t=0.70 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 1.000 | 0 |
| all modalities | token Top-20, t=0.32 | 0.333 | 0.300 | 0.933 | 6 |
| all modalities | token Top-50, t=0.32 | 0.500 | 0.500 | 0.846 | 5 |
| all modalities | WordNet/SALT token Top-50, t=0.32 | 0.917 | 0.300 | 0.833 | 5 |
| text+image | exact Top-20, t=0.70 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 1.000 | 0 |
| text+image | token Top-20, t=0.32 | 0.500 | 0.000 | 1.000 | 2 |
| text+image | WordNet/SALT token Top-50, t=0.32 | 1.000 | 0.000 | 1.000 | 4 |

Result: **promote only as a shadow graph-consolidation policy, not as durable
truth.** Top-K embedding labels clearly help graph construction when the live
system lacks exact label ids: text/image Top-K labels recover all scored
same-group graph pairs with zero measured cross-group links under the
WordNet/SALT Top-50 token policy. They also run within a plausible realtime or
near-realtime budget for a compact filtered label bank (`~4.4 ms` mean and
`~4.7 ms` p95 for object/event filters on this run). This should improve memory
recall by creating provisional semantic hubs that connect recent raw memories
before deep summaries, facts, or normalized durable labels exist.

The all-modality result is the limiting evidence. Adding audio and other noisy
signals increases recall but also creates false hubs: the broad Top-50 policies
reached `0.500` to `0.917` same-group recall but allowed `0.300` to `0.500`
cross-group pair rates on the scored dog/car slice. That is too high for durable
facts, identity binding, or high-weight graph shortcuts. Incorrect labels can be
cleaned up during consolidation only if they remain bounded, weighted,
provisional, and inspectable.

The implementation recommendation is therefore narrower than the initial
hypothesis:

1. allow realtime or shadow graph construction to attach bounded Top-K
   embedding-derived label edges for text/image and other validated modalities;
2. keep audio-derived lexical labels diagnostic unless corroborated by text,
   image, ASR, or repeated cross-source support;
3. store weights, margins, modality/source provenance, and timestamps so
   consolidation can confirm, merge, rename, decay, or prune labels;
4. do not let provisional Top-K labels create durable facts or identity links
   until a follow-up gate shows higher recall without cross-group regression.

### Preconsolidated Top-K Label Graph Retrieval Experiment

The previous Top-K experiment tested whether embedding-derived labels can form
graph evidence. We then added the production-shaped retrieval experiment that
the realtime design actually requires:

```text
episode signals
  -> episode centroid
  -> Top-K provisional labels from the label vector store
  -> preconsolidated graph retrieval boost
  -> consolidation-style pruning simulation
```

The benchmark is
`tools/preconsolidated_topk_label_graph_retrieval_bench.py`. It is
offline and non-mutating: it does not write to Cortext databases. The bounded
provisional-label graph boost it validated was later promoted into production
retrieval as an F/S/T-derived soft signal. The benchmark builds an episode
centroid from signal embeddings, queries the
label vector store, keeps Top-K provisional labels, and evaluates retrieval with
and without a bounded provisional-label graph boost. The pruning simulation
uses offline truth only to model the later consolidation step that removes
labels unsupported by the episode group.

Commands:

```bash
python3 tools/preconsolidated_topk_label_graph_retrieval_bench.py \
  --graph-dir build/modality_agnostic_graph_bench_label_surface \
  --label-db-dir build/label_vector_db_full_2proto \
  --output-dir build/preconsolidated_topk_label_graph_retrieval_20260514_all \
  --include-modalities all \
  --label-filter wordnet_salt \
  --top-rows 768 \
  --top-labels 50 \
  --label-k 20 \
  --label-weight 0.18 \
  --exclude-self

python3 tools/preconsolidated_topk_label_graph_retrieval_bench.py \
  --graph-dir build/modality_agnostic_graph_bench_label_surface \
  --label-db-dir build/label_vector_db_full_2proto \
  --output-dir build/preconsolidated_topk_label_graph_retrieval_20260514_text_image \
  --include-modalities text,image \
  --label-filter wordnet_salt \
  --top-rows 768 \
  --top-labels 50 \
  --label-k 20 \
  --label-weight 0.18 \
  --exclude-self
```

Artifacts:

* `build/preconsolidated_topk_label_graph_retrieval_20260514_all/preconsolidated_topk_label_graph_results.json`
* `build/preconsolidated_topk_label_graph_retrieval_20260514_all/preconsolidated_episode_labels.csv`
* `build/preconsolidated_topk_label_graph_retrieval_20260514_text_image/preconsolidated_topk_label_graph_results.json`
* `build/preconsolidated_topk_label_graph_retrieval_20260514_text_image/preconsolidated_episode_labels.csv`

Episode-label stage:

| run | episode count | scored episodes | Top-K contains correct label | any false labels in Top-K | false-label fraction | episode label mean / p95 ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| all modalities | 58 | 5 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.760 | 7.13 / 7.54 |
| text+image | 43 | 5 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.664 | 6.80 / 6.97 |

This directly answers the "do false labels matter if one right label is in the
set?" question. At the provisional candidate stage, the result supports a
recall-first policy: every scored episode had at least one correct label in its
Top-50, even though most provisional labels were false. The false labels are
therefore acceptable only because the benchmark keeps them provisional and
weighted.

Retrieval results with the query's own episode excluded:

| run | retrieval mode | queries | hit@1 | hit@3 | cross@1 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| all modalities | direct embedding baseline | 15 | 0.933 | 1.000 | 0.067 |
| all modalities | preconsolidated Top-K graph | 15 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.000 |
| all modalities | after pruning simulation | 15 | 0.933 | 1.000 | 0.067 |
| text+image | direct embedding baseline | 10 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.000 |
| text+image | preconsolidated Top-K graph | 10 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.000 |
| text+image | after pruning simulation | 10 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.000 |

Result: **positive for a preconsolidated retrieval layer, still not a durable
truth layer.** The all-modality run shows the intended realtime benefit: the
preconsolidated Top-K label graph recovers the one top-1 miss from direct
embedding retrieval and removes the measured top-1 cross hit. This is the first
experiment in this sequence that directly validates the proposed loop: episode
centroid labels can be useful before consolidation finishes.

The pruning simulation is also informative. On the all-modality slice, pruning
unsupported labels returns retrieval to the direct-embedding baseline. That does
not invalidate the preconsolidated graph; it clarifies its job. The provisional
graph is allowed to be recall-biased and noisy during the realtime window. Later
consolidation should prune unsupported labels, even if that removes some
temporary retrieval lift, because durable graph state must not preserve false
hubs. On the text/image slice, direct retrieval was already at ceiling, and the
preconsolidated/pruned graph preserved that ceiling.

Implementation implication, now promoted into production: use episode centroids
and the attached label-bank/vector store as bounded soft routing signals inside
the normal retrieval operation, not as a separate API path. The online path
exposes a low-weight F/S/T-derived retrieval boost from provisional label/fact
graph evidence, while consolidation promotes only labels supported by source
evidence and prunes the rest. This gives realtime recall the benefit of "one
right label in the set" without letting the many wrong labels become durable
memory structure.

### STM graph to durable LTM consolidation replay

The next production-shaped check was a real personal-chat conversation replay through
Cortext rather than an offline label-vector benchmark. The goal was not to test
summarization quality. It was to test the intended memory path: working memory
and STM graph structure enter consolidation, the relabeler/pruner turns that
structure into durable source-grounded LTM labels and relations, and later
retrieval hydrates the original experiences behind those durable nodes.

Command:

```bash
source env.sh && CORTEXT_STM_LTM_AUDIT=1 \
./build/examples/benchmark/cortext_chat_replay_conversation_memory_bakeoff \
  --input-dir "/path/to/personal-chat-export" --models models \
  --db build/stm_ltm_graph_chat_packet_v26_80.sqlite \
  --out build/stm_ltm_graph_chat_packet_v26_80_openai.json \
  --skip-messages 1980 --max-messages 80 --warmup-messages 5 \
  --probe-stride 10 --rag-top-k 5 --max-injected-memories 4 \
  --active-history-token-budget 128 --consolidate-every 10 \
  --judge-model nemotron-3-nano-omni-30b-a3b-8bit --judge-limit 7 \
  --source-stm-recent-k 4 --source-ltm-lexical-k 5 \
  --deep --compact-policy-bakeoff --stm-graph-bakeoff
```

The artifact name and command below retain their original historical suffixes.
Current private-data release reproductions instead use the loopback-only Ollama
Gemma 4 12B judge (`gemma4:12b-it-qat`); the local Nemotron command is retained
only as historical provenance or an optional disagreement-check path.

Artifacts:

* `build/stm_ltm_graph_chat_packet_v26_80_openai.json`
* `build/stm_ltm_graph_chat_packet_v26_80.sqlite`

The audit table records the consolidation handoff without writing private
message text into the summary: source counts, STM graph item/edge counts,
current/refined/removed label counts, durable `derived_from` and `has_label`
edges, relation edges, and source-memory hydration coverage. On this 80-message
slice, consolidation processed 9 cycles with 70 source memories, 63 STM items,
252 STM label edges, 24 current labels, 20 refined labels, 16 kept labels, 4
added labels, and 32 removed labels. The durable graph was source-grounded:
70 `derived_from` links, 20 `has_label` links, 37 relation edges, 33 label
co-occurrence edges, 143 durable source-link pairs, and zero durable LTM nodes
missing source content.

OpenAI judging used `gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17` over seven probe turns. The
corrected STM-graph bakeoff compares chat-demo-shaped packets: raw STM graph and
relabel/pruned LTM both include the same bounded Cortext working-memory context,
while normal RAG includes rolling active history plus lexical notes.

| arm | mean tokens | relevance | sufficiency | noise | wins |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| raw STM graph + working memory | 86.9 | 3.286 | 1.714 | 1.000 | 1 |
| relabel/pruned LTM + working memory | 101.1 | 2.714 | 1.286 | 1.286 | 0 |
| normal RAG with active history | 184.0 | 4.714 | 3.429 | 1.714 | 2 |
| full history | 443.3 | 4.286 | 3.429 | 2.429 | 4 |

The broader compact-policy comparison reached the same conclusion: Cortext's
working-memory plus retrieved-memory prompt was competitive on relevance
(`4.000`) but still behind normal RAG on sufficiency (`2.714` vs. `3.143`).
LTM-only retrieval remained weak (`2.714` relevance, `1.429` sufficiency), and
the relabel/pruned graph packet was worse than the raw STM graph packet despite
having durable source links.

Result: **source-grounded construction is working; durable relabel/prune recall
is not yet strong enough to replace RAG.** The failure is not lost source
mapping: every source memory was hydratable and every durable LTM node had a
source path. The failure taxonomy points instead to recall admission/routing:
6/7 judged probes had zero LTM query overlap, 6/7 judged probes had LTM below
STM recent, 7/7 relabel/pruned graph probes trailed RAG, 3 consolidation cycles
pruned current labels to zero, and 72 of 84 extractor label candidates were
rejected as non-durable. This means the relabeler/pruner is creating real
durable graph structure, but it is still weakening discriminative anchors too
often. The next production work should target relation endpoint admission,
source-span anchor promotion, and retrieval routing from query text into
source-backed durable labels rather than adding more summaries.

We also tested a narrower hydration hypothesis after this run: if a durable
label points to many source memories, order the linked sources by query-embedding
similarity instead of recency before hydrating the prompt packet. The 80-message
judged artifact
`build/stm_ltm_query_hydration_v27_80_openai.json` preserved the same source
grounding counts but reduced LTM-only quality (`1.286` relevance, `0.429`
sufficiency) and relabel/pruned graph quality (`2.429` relevance, `1.000`
sufficiency). This negative result narrows the failure: source ordering alone is
not the bottleneck. The durable graph needs better text/anchor admission and
query routing into discriminative source-backed labels before hydration order can
matter. Production nevertheless now uses query-aware linked-source ordering by
default as a bounded hydration policy, not as a claimed standalone fix; it can be
disabled for isolation with
`CORTEXT_DISABLE_QUERY_AWARE_LINKED_SOURCE_HYDRATION=1`.

We then hardened the durable-label gate to reject weak multi-token discourse
phrases whose tokens are all modal, helper, or conversational filler words. The
privacy-safe replay artifact
`build/stm_ltm_weak_phrase_filter_v28_80_openai.json` used the same
80-message corpus slice and still verified source preservation: 9 consolidation
cycles, 70 source memories, 63 STM items, 252 STM label edges, 70
`derived_from` links, and zero durable LTM nodes missing source content. The
gate reduced durable output from 20 to 16 refined labels, from 143 to 103
durable label-source backing pairs, and from 37 to 32 relation edges. This is a
precision hardening result, not a recall fix. It removed a class of weak labels
but increased over-pruning risk: 4 cycles pruned current labels to zero, 52 of
62 extractor label candidates were rejected as non-durable, and the isolated
graph packet still trailed RAG. With the chat-demo-shaped working-memory packet,
raw STM graph quality averaged `3.286` relevance and `1.571` sufficiency, while
relabel/pruned LTM averaged `2.571` relevance and `1.000` sufficiency; normal
RAG remained higher at `4.571` relevance and `3.429` sufficiency. The result
reinforces the corrected claim: relabel/prune is building source-grounded LTM
structure, but more generic filtering is not enough. The next hardening point is
discriminative anchor admission and relation/query routing into the source-backed
labels that survive consolidation.

Two follow-up probes targeted that admission point. First, raising the
replacement-mode durable-label ceiling from 6 to 8
(`build/stm_ltm_max8_v29b_80_openai.json`) increased durable coverage from 16
to 20 labels and from 103 to 123 label-source backing pairs, with zero missing
sources. It also reduced pruned labels from 32 to 28 and inserted 12 labels from
the source-span floor. Quality did not become competitive: relabel/pruned LTM
with working memory still averaged only `2.571` relevance and `1.286`
sufficiency, while normal RAG averaged `4.857` and `3.571`. The added budget
therefore improves coverage but also admits more weak fragments; simply raising
the durable-label cap is not the fix.

Second, the fallback admission order was changed so source-span candidates from
the actual evidence are tried before generic STM current labels when the
relabeler under-admits. A focused regression verifies that a bounded floor
spends its label budget on source-span anchors rather than current-label
fallbacks. The production-shaped replay
(`build/stm_ltm_source_span_priority_v30_80_openai.json`) kept the same durable
counts as v28 -- 16 refined labels, 103 label-source pairs, 32 relation edges,
and zero missing source nodes -- but improved the chat-demo-shaped
relabel/pruned packet to `2.714` relevance and `1.286` sufficiency and improved
LTM-only retrieval to `2.571` relevance and `1.429` sufficiency. This is a
directional improvement, not a solved system: 6 of 7 judged probes still had
zero LTM query overlap and the relabel/pruned graph still trailed RAG on every
graph-bakeoff probe. The next hardening step should create/query durable anchors
that share terms with later user questions, not just preserve source-backed
labels behind the cue.

We also tested a broader query route from user text into durable labels using
token overlap instead of exact phrase containment. A focused synthetic
regression showed the intended capability: a query such as "who gave money?"
can route through a longer durable label that contains those discriminative
tokens even when the label embedding is not aligned. The real personal-chat replay did
not support enabling this path by default. In
`build/stm_ltm_label_token_route_v31_80_openai.json`, durable construction
remained unchanged at 16 refined labels, 103 source-link pairs, and zero missing
source nodes, but judged retrieval regressed: LTM-only retrieval fell to `2.429`
relevance and `1.286` sufficiency, and the graph relabel/prune packet fell to
`2.286` relevance and `0.857` sufficiency. The negative result is useful:
query-addressability cannot be fixed by broad lexical matching over durable
labels alone; the labels themselves must be more event- and
question-discriminative. In the current production retrieval path this route is
therefore not a separate experiment switch. It is enabled through the same
F/S/T-derived routing policy as the rest of graph retrieval, with knob-derived
token floors, breadth, fanout, and source-evidence caps so it contributes as a
bounded rescue signal rather than an uncontrolled lexical override.

The next consolidation-side probe converted accepted durable event labels into
source-backed fact assertions when the label had a conservative shape:
`ProperName + action verb + object`. This is deliberately downstream of
relabel/prune, so pruned or unsupported labels cannot create facts. A focused
regression verifies that an accepted source-span event label creates a fact and
links it to both the associative cue and original source memory. On the personal-chat
replay (`build/stm_ltm_event_fact_v32_80_openai.json`), this promoted one
additional active fact (`Amelia gave money`) and increased fact evidence rows
from 47 to 53 without changing durable label/source construction. It did not
improve standalone LTM retrieval: the fact layer still reported zero fact seeds
and zero linked facts on the judged probes, and the graph relabel/prune packet
fell to `1.857` relevance and `0.571` sufficiency. The useful conclusion is that
source-backed event facts are representable, but the current fact-query route
does not reach them on this replay. The next hardening step should connect
question-shaped retrieval to fact cache/evidence, or require relabeler output to
produce facts that match expected future questions.

We then added the narrower fact-side version of that question route: text-token
seeding over source-backed `fact_assertions`/`fact_cache` rows, followed by the
existing `fact_evidence` mapping back to original memories. A focused graph
retrieval regression verifies the intended failure case: the target fact vector
is crowded out of the fact KNN set, but a query such as "Who gave money?" still
reaches the source-backed fact text and gives the evidence memory a positive fact
boost. The pre-fix real replay
(`build/stm_ltm_fact_text_seed_v33_80_openai.json`) showed why this was only a
partial fix before the later temporal/source mapping and fact-route hardening.
Durable construction stayed source-grounded (**16** refined labels,
**103** label-source pairs, **32** relation edges, **0** missing source nodes,
and **6** touched facts), but judged probes still reported **0** fact seeds,
**0** candidate fact-linked memories, and **0** selected fact-linked memories.
Quality remained below RAG: graph relabel/prune averaged `2.857` relevance and
`1.286` sufficiency versus graph-bakeoff normal RAG at `4.857` and `3.571`, and
compact Cortext LTM-only stayed at `1.857` relevance and `1.143` sufficiency
versus compact normal RAG at `4.714` and `4.000`. The replay facts existed but
did not lexical-match the judged questions, so the live bottleneck is not merely
fact-cache reachability. It is the upstream durable anchor/fact generation
contract: consolidation must produce enough question-addressable, source-backed
facts and relations from the STM graph for fact retrieval to have something to
hit.

A follow-up prompt hardening made the Gemma refinement request explicitly ask
for directly stated durable or episodic facts, with examples for named people,
actions, preferences, locations, ownership, relationships, plans, and important
events. The same 80-message replay
(`build/stm_ltm_fact_prompt_v34_80_openai.json`) did not change the durable
construction or fact reachability counters: **16** refined labels, **103**
label-source pairs, **32** relation edges, **6** touched facts, **53** fact
evidence rows, **2** active facts, and still **0** fact seeds / **0** linked
fact memories across judged probes. A privacy-safe addressability audit over the
final artifact found that durable labels shared non-stopword terms with **2 / 7**
future probe turns, while all facts did so for **2 / 7** and active facts for
only **1 / 7**. The graph-bakeoff packet still had zero relabel/prune query
overlap on every probe. This rules out "the prompt forgot to mention facts" as
the primary failure. The remaining target is structural: the relabel/prune stage
needs a stronger mechanism for selecting and retaining future-addressable event
anchors/facts from STM evidence, not just a more explicit instruction to the
same extractor.

We then moved the addressability audit into the replay harness itself so the
question is measured at probe time rather than against the final database after
future consolidation. The no-judge validation artifact
`build/stm_ltm_addressability_v35_80.json` records, for every graph-bakeoff
probe, privacy-safe counts of durable labels, all facts, active facts, and their
best non-stopword overlap with the current query. The live-time result is
stronger than the final-DB posthoc check: durable label counts grew from **0** to
**9** across the seven probes and fact counts grew from **0** to **4**, but
durable labels, all facts, and active facts each had **0 / 7** probes with any
query overlap at the time of retrieval. Raw STM graph and relabel/pruned LTM
also had **7 / 7** zero-overlap packets. This confirms that the graph packet is
not merely failing to hydrate reachable facts; the reachable durable anchors are
not query-addressable when the user asks.

We then made the deterministic source-span floor more event-aware. The candidate
builder now admits conservative action anchors such as a source-grounded
`subject verb object` phrase and its `verb object` form, skips filler tokens
inside the phrase, and avoids spending the small source-span budget on
capitalized object events that would crowd out named people and places. Focused
regressions verify that source-span admission still preserves named entities and
locations, that accepted event labels create source-backed fact assertions, and
that event anchors such as `gave money` can be produced without admitting filler
phrases. The no-judge Cortext replay
(`build/stm_ltm_eventanchors_v36_80.json`) showed a small construction
improvement over v35: **17** refined labels instead of **16**, **108**
label-source backing pairs instead of **103**, **24** source-span candidates
instead of **22**, and **49** non-durable label rejects instead of **52**, with
**0** durable LTM nodes missing source links. However, the live retrieval failure
did not move: durable labels, all facts, and active facts still had **0 / 7**
probe-time query-overlap hits; raw STM graph and relabel/pruned LTM still had
**7 / 7** zero-overlap graph packets; and Cortext LTM-only overlap remained
below lexical RAG (**0.071** versus **0.329** mean query-context overlap). The
negative result narrows the next target further: event-shaped source spans help
construction quality, but the durable anchors being kept are still not the
future-addressable anchors needed by chat queries.

Finally, `build/stm_ltm_source_oracle_v37_80.json` adds a source-oracle
addressability counter to separate routing failure from construction failure.
For each live probe it measures, without recording text, whether **any** source
memory behind a durable LTM label or fact shares non-stopword tokens with the
current query. This did not find a hidden reachable source: durable label source
counts grew from **0** to **37** over the seven probes, and fact evidence source
counts grew from **0** to **41**, but both had **0 / 7** query-overlap hits.
Thus the isolated graph packet is not simply selecting the wrong durable node;
the source evidence preserved behind the durable graph is itself not
future-addressable from these chat questions.

The OpenAI-judged companion run
(`build/stm_ltm_source_oracle_v37_80_openai.json`) used
`gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17` across all seven graph-bakeoff probes. Normal RAG
again won the graph comparison: normal RAG averaged **4.286** relevance and
**2.857** sufficiency, full history averaged **4.000 / 3.000**, raw STM graph
averaged **2.857 / 1.286**, and relabel/pruned LTM averaged only
**2.286 / 0.857**. Relabel/pruned LTM trailed RAG on **7 / 7** judged probes,
while source preservation remained intact (**17** durable LTM nodes with source,
**108** label-source backing pairs, and **0** missing-source durable nodes).
At this v37 stage, the diagnosis was that the relabel/pruner was creating real
source-backed durable graph memory, but compressing toward anchors that were not
the handles future chat queries needed. Later fact-threshold, graph-expanded,
and rolling spouse-conversation evaluations above supersede this as the current
top-level verdict, but the v37 run remains the clearest local diagnosis of the
standalone relabel/pruned LTM failure mode: hydration and source preservation
were not the bottleneck; durable-anchor addressability was.

### Distributed Label-Graph Attention Probe

The next question was whether the preconsolidated graph needs an explicit
entity/anchor object. We tested the stricter distributed hypothesis on **May 14,
2026**: memory nodes connect only to Top-K label nodes, and a reference label
such as `he` should enter the most recent compatible graph neighborhood and
then branch through connected memory-label paths. There is no `anchor:Steve`
node in this probe, and there is no special "name" channel. `steve`, `john`,
`friend`, `person`, `he`, `pizza`, and `voice` are all ordinary labels.

The benchmark is `tools/distributed_label_graph_attention_bench.py`. It uses
real label vectors from `build/label_vector_db_full_2proto`, constructs
controlled message-memory nodes from label-vector centroids, retrieves Top-10
labels for each memory, and runs bounded traversal over the bipartite
memory-label graph. The traversal is left-to-right in time: for each query
label, it starts at the most recent memory containing that label, then branches
locally through adjacent memories and shared labels. Older matching memories are
kept as weak side branches, not as the primary path. This matches the intended
rule for realtime references: after a later `john` introduction, bare `he`
should hit the John branch first rather than jumping back to Steve.

This is deliberately a preconsolidated graph experiment. The success criterion
is not that the target label is the single top label, because Top-10 embedding
labels contain false positives and generic labels often score above the desired
label. The realtime criterion is: (1) the correct recent memory branch is among
the top two activated memories, and (2) the desired target label is present in
the branch Top-5. Consolidation then inspects the original memory blob
(text/audio/image) and prunes or adds graph labels.

Command:

```bash
python3 tools/distributed_label_graph_attention_bench.py \
  --label-db-dir build/label_vector_db_full_2proto \
  --output-dir build/distributed_label_graph_attention_20260514_top10_branch \
  --top-k 10 \
  --recency-decay 3.0 \
  --temporal-weight 0.35 \
  --active-window 1
```

Artifacts:

* `build/distributed_label_graph_attention_20260514_top10_branch/distributed_label_graph_attention_results.json`
* `build/distributed_label_graph_attention_20260514_top10_branch/distributed_label_graph_memory_labels.csv`

The controlled memory sequence was:

```text
m1: steve, friend, person, he, image, face
m2: he, pizza, eat
m3: we, he, favorite, pizza, place, restaurant
m4: john, person, he, voice
m5: he, restaurant, favorite
```

Top-10 label assignment recovered `0.909` of the seeded labels. The Steve-only
reference probes passed under branch-level scoring:

| scenario | probe | query labels | expected label | target label rank | expected memory rank | hit |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Steve only | after intro | `he` | `steve` | 2 | 1 | 1 |
| Steve only | preference | `he,pizza` | `steve` | 4 | 2 | 1 |
| Steve only | place context | `we,place` | `steve` | 4 | 2 | 1 |

This validates the narrow claim: when no competing person has been introduced,
the `he`/`we` labels retrieve the Steve-associated memory neighborhood without
an explicit anchor object. The binding is not stored as `he -> Steve`; it
emerges because recent memories connected through `he`, `pizza`, and `place`
also keep `steve` in the active label set.

The competing-reference probes also passed when recency was treated as branch
entry rather than merely a soft score:

| scenario | probe | query labels | expected label | target label rank | expected memory rank | hit |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| competing label | after John intro | `he` | `john` | 4 | 1 | 1 |
| competing label | pizza context | `he,pizza` | `john` | 4 | 1 | 1 |
| competing label | restaurant context | `he,restaurant` | `john` | 4 | 2 | 1 |

The target label is not always top-1. For example, generic or false labels such
as `friend`, `person`, or even `steve` can outrank `john` inside the
preconsolidated branch because the vector Top-10 is intentionally noisy. That
does not invalidate the realtime graph: the `he` path enters the newest John
branch first, and the correct target label remains present for the subsequent
blob-aware consolidation pass. Overall branch hit rate was `1.000` across six
controlled probes.

Result: **positive for realtime preconsolidated graph retrieval, conditional on
consolidation.** The experiment supports a label-only, recency-biased traversal
model: the live system can create Top-10 label edges immediately, use them for
retrieval before consolidation, and let consolidation prune false labels after
reading the original memory payload. The implementation implication is to avoid
typed entity/name anchors in the realtime layer. Graph construction should store
bounded Top-K label edges with timestamps, edge strengths, and provenance, then
retrieve by entering the most recent compatible branch and spreading locally
through connected labels.

We then scaled the same benchmark to an 18-memory modality-marked sequence with
text, image, audio, and video memories. The sequence interleaved six ordinary
labels (`steve`, `maria`, `david`, `emma`, `john`, `sarah`) with recurring
reference labels (`he`, `she`, `her`) and cross-modal object/activity labels
(`pizza`, `guitar`, `car`, `dog`, `office`, `school`). This was still a
label-centroid control rather than raw image/audio inference, but it stressed
the same realtime graph mechanism with more repeated labels and more modality
hubs.

Scaled commands:

```bash
python3 tools/distributed_label_graph_attention_bench.py \
  --label-db-dir build/label_vector_db_full_2proto \
  --output-dir build/distributed_label_graph_attention_20260514_scaled_multimodal_top10 \
  --top-k 10 \
  --recency-decay 3.0 \
  --temporal-weight 0.35 \
  --active-window 1 \
  --suite scaled_multimodal

python3 tools/distributed_label_graph_attention_bench.py \
  --label-db-dir build/label_vector_db_full_2proto \
  --output-dir build/distributed_label_graph_attention_20260514_scaled_multimodal_top50 \
  --top-k 50 \
  --recency-decay 3.0 \
  --temporal-weight 0.35 \
  --active-window 1 \
  --suite scaled_multimodal
```

Scaled artifacts:

* `build/distributed_label_graph_attention_20260514_scaled_multimodal_top10/distributed_label_graph_attention_results.json`
* `build/distributed_label_graph_attention_20260514_scaled_multimodal_top10/distributed_label_graph_memory_labels.csv`
* `build/distributed_label_graph_attention_20260514_scaled_multimodal_top20/distributed_label_graph_attention_results.json`
* `build/distributed_label_graph_attention_20260514_scaled_multimodal_top50/distributed_label_graph_attention_results.json`
* `build/distributed_label_graph_attention_20260514_scaled_multimodal_top50_deg0.5/distributed_label_graph_attention_results.json`

Scaled results:

| run | Top-K | seed-label Top-K recall | expected memory top-2 | target label top-5 | branch hit rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| scaled multimodal | 10 | 0.753 | 1.000 | 0.167 | 0.167 |
| scaled multimodal | 20 | 0.906 | 1.000 | 0.167 | 0.167 |
| scaled multimodal | 50 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.167 | 0.167 |
| scaled multimodal + degree penalty 0.5 | 50 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.167 | 0.167 |

By expected-memory modality, Top-10/20/50 had the same branch-hit pattern:
audio `0 / 7`, image `1 / 7`, text `1 / 1`, and video `1 / 3`, while expected
memory top-2 remained `1.000` for every modality bucket. The failure therefore
was not that the recency-biased path missed the right memory branch. It was that
the label readout was dominated by globally common and modality-common labels
such as `audio`, `image`, `friend`, `person`, `he`, and `steve`. Widening Top-K
made the seed labels available but did not promote them into the active Top-5.
A simple label-degree penalty did not fix the problem.

Scaled result: **positive for branch retrieval, negative for direct target-label
readout across noisy modalities.** The realtime graph should still use the
recency-biased branch path for retrieval, because it consistently enters the
right recent neighborhood. It should not expose the raw active label readout as
resolved identity or durable graph truth. Cross-modal operation needs either
blob-aware consolidation, a better branch-local label promotion rule, or a
model pass over the memory payload before promoted labels are trusted.

### Live accumulator projection (the actual cortext active context)

The static-graph benchmark above "guesses at episodes": it pre-defines an
18-signal sequence as a list of discrete `MemoryNode` objects with hand-assigned
modalities and seed labels, builds a bipartite label graph over those finished
nodes, and performs recency-biased graph traversal + label aggregation on the
result. Cortext never operates this way.

In the real system the active context is the per-source `AccumulatorState`
(`include/cortext/processor/accumulator_state.hpp:33`): a live, incrementally
updated `mu_acc` (Welford-style running mean embedding), `c_t` (slow-drifting
temporal context), and a bounded recent window of prior `mu_acc` values. Signals
arrive one by one; boundaries and durable memories are *emergent* from drift,
coherence, and the write gate. Retrieval queries, focus, and reference anchoring
are all biased from this live blended state (`src/operations/graph_retrieval.cpp:765`,
`focus.cpp:67`, `boundary.cpp:171`), not from a post-hoc graph over pre-segmented
memories. No production path stores or reinforces labels inside the accumulator;
labels remain a separate side index.

To test whether using the *actual* cortext active state rescues label promotion,
we added `tools/accumulator_label_context_bench.py`. It re-uses the identical
label vector DB, the identical 18-signal scaled multimodal sequence, and the
identical 18 pronoun/object probes, but replaces the static MemoryNode list and
bipartite graph with a production-shaped Python shadow of `LiveAccumulator`:

- `step(embedding, drift)` implements the exact incremental mean and `c_t` EWMA
  shape used by `UpdateAccumulator` in production; the shadow fixes `alpha_c`
  for the ablation grid, while production derives `alpha_c` from Stability.
- At each probe point the prefix is replayed signal-by-signal through the live
  accumulator.
- The "active label readout" is the Top-K projection of the *current live
  blended context vector* (mu_acc lightly mixed with the recent window mean,
  with a small attractive bias toward the query labels) into the same label
  vector space.

Commands (same label DB and suite as the static-graph runs):

```bash
python3 tools/accumulator_label_context_bench.py \
  --label-db-dir build/label_vector_db_full_2proto \
  --output-dir build/accumulator_label_context_20260515_scaled_multimodal_top10 \
  --top-k 10 --suite scaled_multimodal

python3 tools/accumulator_label_context_bench.py \
  --label-db-dir build/label_vector_db_full_2proto \
  --output-dir build/accumulator_label_context_20260515_scaled_multimodal_top50 \
  --top-k 50 --suite scaled_multimodal
```

Artifacts:

* `build/accumulator_label_context_20260515_scaled_multimodal_top10/accumulator_label_context_results.json`
* `build/accumulator_label_context_20260515_scaled_multimodal_top10/accumulator_label_context_probes.csv`
* `build/accumulator_label_context_20260515_scaled_multimodal_top50/accumulator_label_context_results.json`
* `build/accumulator_label_context_20260515_scaled_multimodal_top50/accumulator_label_context_probes.csv`

Live accumulator results:

| run | Top-K | seed-label Top-K recall | expected memory top-2 (proxy) | target label top-5 | live projection hit rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| live accumulator projection | 10 | 0.753 | — | 0.167 | 3/18 |
| live accumulator projection | 50 | 1.000 | — | 0.167 | 3/18 |

The target-label top-5 hit rate is *identical* to the static-graph version (0.167).
Even when the active context is the true live blended state that cortext uses
for every retrieval and anchoring decision, projecting that state into the label
vector space is still dominated by the same modality hubs (`audio`, `image`,
`video`, `voice`) and generic person labels (`person`, `friend`, `steve` appearing
as a generic rather than a specific recent individual). The embedding geometry
of the label bank simply does not separate specific recent identities from
channel artifacts and category terms strongly enough for raw nearest-neighbor
readout to succeed.

**Live-accumulator result: negative for direct target-label readout from the
blended context vector.** The architectural correction (use the live accumulator
that cortext actually maintains, do not guess static episodes and aggregate
labels over them) is necessary for fidelity but not sufficient when the label
vectors themselves entangle the wrong features. Cross-modal reference therefore
requires either (1) stricter kind/modality filtering of the label bank *before*
any label participates in promotion or graph construction, or (2) deferring the
final identity resolution to a model pass over the stored memory payload
(blob-aware consolidation) after the accumulator + retrieval have delivered the
correct recent neighborhood. The latter path is the one already favored by the
rest of the cortext design (constructive recall, extractor/summarizer over
payload, no label state inside the accumulator).

release wrapper. This is **not release evidence** and is not used for quality
claims; it only verifies that the frozen-probe stream, local Gemma judge, blind
packet path, fairness checks, and summary gate still compose after the retrieval
change.
